sampled_files.README.md:
# nanopi **No Node. No Python. No `node_modules`.** A coding-agent CLI you can `scp` onto a box that has no runtime — a single ~4 MB static Rust binary, ported from [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi). Runs on Alpine, on CentOS 6, and anywhere `npm install` isn't an option. [![Release](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi?style=flat-square&color=blue)](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/releases/latest) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue.svg?style=flat-square)](LICENSE) ![Binary](https://img.shields.io/badge/binary-~4%20MB-brightgreen?style=flat-square) ![Static musl](https://img.shields.io/badge/static-musl-informational?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/rust-stable-orange?style=flat-square&logo=rust&logoColor=white) [![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/ci.yml?branch=main&style=flat-square&label=CI)](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/actions/workflows/ci.yml) **English** · [简体中文](README_zh.md)

TUI on Linux (macOS / Linux terminal)

TUI on Windows — captured from nanopi.exe on Windows 10/11

--- ## Why nanopi? - 🚫 **Zero runtime dependencies** — no Node, no Python, no package manager. Download one file, `chmod +x`, run. - 🖥 **Runs on ancient boxes** — glibc 2.12+ (CentOS 6), or the fully static musl build on Alpine and anything else - 🪶 **~4 MB static binary** — musl + LTO + strip (the download is 1.6 MB, UPX-packed) - 🧬 **PI-parity** — mirrors [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi)'s surface: JSONL sessions, hooks, skills, `-p`, `/fork`, `/resume` - 🔌 **Multi-provider** — any OpenAI-compatible endpoint (DeepSeek, ollama, vLLM, …) plus native Anthropic; `provider` / `api_kind` in `config.toml` pick the vendor and wire protocol explicitly when the base_url sniff isn't enough. A **leading** `…` block in the reply text (R1-lineage models — R1, its distills, QwQ, GLM, etc. — served through any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) is split out and rendered as thinking; a `` appearing after other text is left literal. `inline_think_tags = true | false` overrides the default (on). - 🛠 **Streaming tool calls** — `read` / `write` / `edit` / `bash`, rendered live in a ratatui TUI - 🪝 **Claude Code-protocol hooks** — JSON-on-stdin, exit-2-to-block shell hooks, using PI's event names (`tool_execution_start` / `tool_execution_end` / `input` / …) - 🧠 **Agent Skills** — [spec-compliant](https://agentskills.io/specification) `SKILL.md` discovery + `/skill:name` expansion - 🎛 **Orchestrator by default** — in the TUI the main agent scouts the code, handles quick lookups itself, and delegates real work to dedicated agents shown live under the input box ## Background — why nanopi exists Pi is a great coding agent, but its upstream chose not to support certain environments that real users need: | Upstream issue | User request | Upstream status | |---|---|---| | [pi#8591](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/8591) | musl-linked builds for Alpine | not planned | | [pi#6546](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/6546) | Avoid glibc version mismatch on older Linux | not planned | | [pi#6075](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi/issues/6075) | Startup time is too slow | not planned | Three separate people asked for musl builds, old-glibc compatibility and a lighter startup; upstream closed all three as *not planned*. That is a reasonable call for them — Pi targets modern machines — but it leaves the old-hardware case unserved. **nanopi is a Rust rewrite for exactly that case:** - **Static musl build** — zero runtime deps, runs in Alpine containers (see [`release.yml`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/.github/workflows/release.yml) for the CI matrix) - **glibc 2.12+ (CentOS 6)** — the dynamic build covers old servers; the musl build covers everything else - **~4 MB** — Rust + LTO + `opt-level = "z"` + `panic = abort` + strip; the published binary is UPX-packed down to 1.6 MB - **Prebuilt for** `linux-x86_64`, `linux-x86_64-musl`, `linux-aarch64-musl`, `android-aarch64`, `macos-aarch64` and `windows-x86_64`. Each Linux and Android target also ships a `-wasm` variant with the plugin runtime compiled in. ## Install ### Prebuilt binaries Grab a build from [Releases](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/releases/latest): ```bash # Adjust VERSION to the tag you want (e.g. v0.9.1) VERSION=v0.9.1 curl -L -o nanopi \ "https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/releases/download/${VERSION}/nanopi-${VERSION}-linux-x86_64-musl" chmod +x nanopi ./nanopi --version ``` Per release, prebuilt binaries ship for: - `nanopi--linux-x86_64-musl` — fully static Linux, works on anything (recommended) - `nanopi--linux-x86_64` — dynamic glibc Linux, slightly smaller - `nanopi--linux-aarch64-musl` — static arm64: Raspberry Pi and arm64 servers - `nanopi--android-aarch64` — Android (Termux or `adb shell`). Prefer this over the musl build on a phone: it links bionic, so DNS resolves through the system resolver with no extra setup - `nanopi--macos-aarch64` — Apple Silicon (M1+) - `nanopi--windows-x86_64.exe` — Windows 10/11 Every Linux and Android asset above also has a `-wasm` twin (e.g. `nanopi--linux-x86_64-musl-wasm`) built with `--features wasm`. Take it only if you use `[[extensions]]` WASM plugins — it carries the wasmtime runtime and is ~7.2 MiB against the stock build's ~4 MB. macOS and Windows are stock-only; for plugin support there, build from source with `cargo build --release --features wasm`. ### DNS on hosts without `/etc/resolv.conf` nanopi resolves names with the bundled hickory resolver, which reads `/etc/resolv.conf` and nothing else. Android has no such file — DNS is done by netd — so a **static musl** build on a phone fails every request with `error reading DNS system conf for hickory-dns: io error: os error 2`. The `android-aarch64` asset handles this for you: on Android nanopi switches off hickory and resolves through libc `getaddrinfo`, which on a bionic-linked binary reaches netd. (Linking bionic is not sufficient on its own — reqwest picks the resolver from a compile-time feature flag, so the switch has to be made at runtime. See `src/net.rs`.) The static musl build cannot do this: musl's own resolver reads the same missing file and then defaults to `127.0.0.1:53`. So on a phone, prefer `android-aarch64`. If you are on the musl build instead, give it nameservers explicitly: ```bash export NANOPI_DNS=223.5.5.5,119.29.29.29 # or any IP[:port] list # or, persistently: printf 'nameserver 223.5.5.5\nnameserver 119.29.29.29\n' > ~/.nanopi/resolv.conf ``` `NANOPI_DNS=system` forces the default behaviour, for a host that has a working `/etc/resolv.conf` but a stale `~/.nanopi/resolv.conf`. Note that explicit nameservers bypass any VPN's resolver, which can matter for split-horizon DNS. macOS Intel isn't prebuilt (GitHub runner supply is scarce); build from source with `cargo build --target x86_64-apple-darwin`. On macOS the download is unsigned, so Gatekeeper blocks it. Clear the quarantine attribute and ad-hoc sign it: ```bash xattr -d com.apple.quarantine ./nanopi--macos-aarch64 2>/dev/null || true codesign --force --sign - ./nanopi--macos-aarch64 ``` ### Build from source ```bash # One-time host setup curl --proto '=https' --tlsv1.2 -sSf https://sh.rustup.rs | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain stable --profile minimal source "$HOME/.cargo/env" rustup target add x86_64-unknown-linux-musl sudo apt install -y musl-tools build-essential # Debian/Ubuntu # Build cargo build --release --target x86_64-unknown-linux-musl ./target/x86_64-unknown-linux-musl/release/nanopi --version ``` ## Quick start ```bash export OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-... export OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://api.deepseek.com/v1 export OPENAI_MODEL=deepseek-v4-flash # Interactive TUI (default) nanopi # One-shot -p mode (Claude Code semantics) nanopi -p "read /etc/hostname and tell me what you see" # JSON output for scripting nanopi -p --output json "say hi" # Prompt piped on stdin echo "explain this error" | nanopi -p # Resume: last session / by id / fork nanopi --continue nanopi --session nanopi --fork ``` ## CLI | Flag | Default | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `--base-url` | `https://api.openai.com/v1` | OpenAI-compatible API root | | `--model` | (required) | Model id | | `--api-key` | `$OPENAI_API_KEY` | Bearer token | | `-m`, `--message` | (piped stdin) | User message; first positional arg also accepted. In `-p` mode, falls back to piped stdin | | `-p`, `--print` | false | Non-interactive mode | | `--output` | `text` | `-p` output: `text` \| `json` | | `--continue` | false | Resume the most recent session | | `--session ` | — | Resume by session id | | `--fork ` | — | Fork an existing session | | `--no-hooks` | false | Disable all hooks | | `-a`, `--approve` | false | Trust project resources for this run | | `-N`, `--distrust` | false | Distrust project resources | | `--skill ` | — | Load a skill file/dir (repeatable) | | `-S`, `--no-skills` | false | Disable skill discovery | | `-C`, `--no-context-files` | false | Disable AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md discovery | | `--system-prompt ` | — | Replace the built-in system prompt | | `--append-system-prompt ` | — | Append to the system prompt (repeatable) | | `--profile ` | active profile | Use a config profile for this run only (see [Profiles](#profiles)) | | `--foreground [id]` | — | Bring a session working in the background back to the TUI (see [Background mode](#background-mode-background-nanopi---foreground)) | | `--background` | — | List the sessions working in the background and exit | ## Profiles A profile is a complete, independent global config in its own folder, so you can keep e.g. a work gateway, a personal key and a local model side by side and switch between them without restarting. Everything that belongs to a profile (its key file, an unfinished wizard draft) lives in that folder. ```text ~/.nanopi/config.toml the "default" profile (the usual config file) ~/.nanopi/api_key default's key file, as `nanopi init` writes it ~/.nanopi/profiles/work/config.toml profile "work" ~/.nanopi/profiles/work/api_key work's key file (mode 600; folder is mode 700) ~/.nanopi/profiles/local/config.toml profile "local" ~/.nanopi/active_profile the profile chosen with /profile use (absent = default) ``` Profiles written as flat files by an earlier build (`profiles/.toml`) are moved into their folder (`profiles//config.toml`) on the next start. Nothing changes if you never create a profile: `default` *is* `~/.nanopi/config.toml`, and there is no `profiles/` directory or `active_profile` file until you make one. In the TUI: | Command | Effect | |---|---| | `/profile` or `/profile list` | List profiles; `*` marks the active one | | `/profile create ` | Set up a new profile with the setup wizard (below) | | `/profile create --copy` | New profile as a copy of the active one's `config.toml`, to edit by hand | | `/profile use ` (alias `switch`) | Switch now **and** remember it for the next start | `/profile create ` asks the same questions as the first-run wizard, right in the TUI: provider (OpenAI, DeepSeek, Anthropic, Gemini via gateway, Ollama or custom), model, and API key (skipped for localhost; shown masked in the scrollback). It then sends one tiny test request, and only when that succeeds writes `profiles//config.toml` and `profiles//api_key`. On a failed test you can retry, edit the answers, or abort. Esc or Ctrl-C cancels; answers already tested are kept as a draft in the folder and offered as defaults next time. The same wizard runs outside the TUI with `nanopi --profile init`, which also creates the profile if it does not exist yet. `/profile use` checks the target first (it must parse and resolve a model and an API key) and changes nothing if it does not. Then it swaps the model, `base_url`, API key, `api_kind` and `provider` on the live session — the conversation continues — and reloads hooks, skills and extensions from the new profile. Agents started afterwards use the new profile too. The footer shows `profile:` whenever the active profile is not `default`. `[agent]` limits and `[experimental] orchestrator` take effect at the next start (use `/orchestrator` to flip that one now). Which profile is used, highest priority first: `--profile ` (this run only, never saved) → `NANOPI_PROFILE` → `~/.nanopi/active_profile` → `default`. An unknown `--profile` is an error (except with `init`, which creates it); a saved profile whose config was deleted falls back to `default` with a warning. Only the global config is per-profile. The project's `./.nanopi/config.toml` is still merged on top of whichever profile is active, and `settings.toml`, sessions, skills, trust decisions and `mcp.json` are shared. At startup CLI flags and `OPENAI_*` env vars still override the profile, as they always have; on a `/profile use` the profile wins and those env vars only fill keys the profile leaves out. Names may use `A-Z a-z 0-9 - _` (up to 64 characters). ## Model catalogue (`~/.nanopi/models.json`) nanopi needs a model's **context window** for two things: the usage bar in the status line, and deciding when to auto-compact the conversation. It ships a built-in table of ~163 models, but that table is baked into the binary — a model released after your build shows `?/128.0k` and auto-compaction falls back to a cruder char-count heuristic. On first interactive run nanopi writes `~/.nanopi/models.json`. Add anything it doesn't know to `custom`: ```json { "generated_by": "0.16.1", "custom": [ { "id": "some-new-model", "vendor": "openai", "context_window": 2000000 } ], "builtin": [ "… the shipped table, for reference …" ] } ``` `custom` wins over `builtin` by id, so it also corrects a wrong window. Lookup is a case-insensitive longest-prefix match, so `my-model` also covers `my-model-20260101`. `builtin` is regenerated whenever nanopi's version changes — the previous file is copied to `models.json.bak` first, and your `custom` entries (and any extra top-level keys you added) carry over untouched; `_comment` is nanopi's own text and is rewritten, the old one stays in the `.bak`. That split is what stops the file going stale: upgrade nanopi and you get its newer models, while keeping your own. Edits made directly inside `builtin` work only while `generated_by` matches the running version: once nanopi is upgraded the old `builtin` is ignored (even in `nanopi -p`, which cannot rewrite the file) and then replaced, so put anything you want to keep in `custom`. A malformed file is never overwritten — nanopi reports the line and falls back to the built-in table for that run. `nanopi -p` reads the file but never creates or refreshes it, so a scripted run has no side effects. To refresh the shipped table from source: `python3 scripts/gen-models.py ` (from [models.dev](https://models.dev/api.json)). It unions rather than replaces, so an existing entry is never dropped. ## Orchestrator mode In the TUI, the main agent is an **orchestrator**. Besides the four dispatch tools (`agent`, `list_agents`, `stop_agent`, `send_message`) it has `read`, `grep`, `find`, `ls` and `bash`, which it uses to: - **scout** — look at the relevant code and environment first, so each brief names the right files, symbols and constraints; - **triage** — handle a quick lookup or check itself (answering a question about the code, reading a log, running one command) when that is faster than dispatching, and delegate anything that changes files, takes many steps, or can run in parallel. It has no `write` or `edit` tool and is told never to modify files through `bash`: every change to a file is made by a dedicated agent it briefs, dispatches, monitors, and whose report it synthesises for you. Agents run in the background, so the orchestrator hands work off and gives you the turn back rather than blocking on them. Live agents appear in a strip at the bottom of the dock, under the footer: ``` ● main 3 agents working · Ctrl+G details ○ yearning-dump read raw.json 12s ○ msg-framework-dev bash cargo test 1m05s ○ write release notes queued 0s ``` Each worker row shows the agent's name, its latest tool call (refreshed about once a second), and elapsed time. `Ctrl+G` prints the full detail — activity history, turns/tokens, worktree/branch, report path — into scrollback. An agent disappears from the strip when it finishes; its report is delivered into the conversation, which is where you read results. **Esc stops the orchestrator's turn, not the agents.** Esc (and Ctrl-C during a streaming turn) interrupts only the orchestrator; every dispatched agent — background, foreground, `parallel` or `chain` — keeps running and reports when it finishes. Agents are stopped only by `/agents stop ` (or `/agents stop all`), by the orchestrator's own `stop_agent` when you ask it to, or by quitting nanopi. Bare `/agents` opens a picker over every agent of the run, finished ones included; Enter prints that agent's detail card (state, time, model, task, recent activity, report, paths), and `/agents show ` prints one directly. `/agents list` is the plain-text version. See [docs/agents.md](docs/agents.md). Parallel agents that write code can each get their own git worktree (`isolation: "worktree"`), merged back automatically, with conflicts escalated to you. To go back to the classic single-agent flow — where the main agent reads, edits, and runs commands itself — use `/orchestrator off` in-session, or set it at startup: ```toml [experimental] orchestrator = false ``` A `⎈ solo` badge in the status line marks that the mode is off; the default gets no badge. Caps for the spawned children live under `[agent]` (see `config.toml.example`). This is TUI-only: `nanopi -p` ignores the setting entirely and always keeps its full tool set, so scripted runs are never silently restricted. ## Goals and loops (`/goal`, `/loop`) Two ways to keep a session working without prompting each step, after Claude Code's commands of the same names. **`/goal `** starts working toward the condition right away. After every turn a separate model call (no tools) reads the condition and the conversation and returns *met*, *not met* or *impossible*, with a reason. Not met → nanopi starts the next turn with the reason as guidance; met or impossible → the goal clears and the result is printed. The evaluator only sees the conversation, so name a check the work itself shows: ```text /goal all tests in tests/auth pass (cargo test exits 0) and no other test file changes ``` | Command | Effect | |---|---| | `/goal ` | Set (or replace) the goal and start; up to 4,000 characters | | `/goal` | Status: condition, time, turns judged, tokens, last reason | | `/goal clear` | Clear it (also `stop`, `off`, `reset`, `none`, `cancel`) | The goal **pauses** — stays set but stops driving turns — when you interrupt a turn (Esc), after 3 judged turns in a row with no tool call, after an error a retry would repeat (rate limit), after 3 failed automatic retries, or when the check itself fails. Your next message resumes it. Transient errors (dropped connection, cut-off stream) are retried after 30 s, 60 s, 120 s; errors you must fix (bad key, unknown model, context overflow) clear the goal. While background agents run, the check waits for their report. `/new`, `/resume` and forking clear the goal. The footer shows `◎ goal 3m05s`. `nanopi -p "/goal "` runs the whole loop in one invocation (notes on stderr) and exits non-zero unless the goal is met. Set `NANOPI_GOAL_MODEL` to judge with a cheaper model on the same endpoint. **`/loop [interval] [prompt]`** re-runs a prompt while the session is open: | Input | Behaviour | |---|---| | `/loop 5m check whether the deploy finished` | Every 5 minutes (also `… every 2 hours`; units s m h d, minimum 1m) | | `/loop check CI and fix what broke` | Self-paced: each iteration ends with the model choosing the next delay (1–60 min) or stopping | | `/loop` or `/loop 15m` | `.nanopi/loop.md`, else `~/.nanopi/loop.md`, else a built-in maintenance prompt (continue unfinished work, tend the branch, small cleanup) | | `/loop status` | Show the loop | | `/loop stop`, or Esc on an empty prompt | Stop it | | ask in chat ("stop the loop") | The model ends it with its `stop_loop` tool, which it also uses on its own once the loop's task is done | Iterations start only when the session is idle — never mid-turn, and a missed one runs once, not once per missed interval. The first runs at once. A self-paced loop gives the model a `schedule_wakeup` tool for as long as the loop runs; an iteration that neither reschedules nor stops gets one fallback check 20 minutes later, and the loop ends if that one does not reschedule either. One loop per session (a new `/loop` replaces it); loops expire after 7 days and do not survive a restart. The first line of a `/skill:` prompt is kept intact so the skill still expands. ### Background mode (`/background`, `nanopi --foreground`) A session with a running `/goal` or `/loop` can keep working without the TUI: | Command | Effect | |---|---| | `/background` | Hand the goal / loop to a background worker and quit. Mid-turn, it happens when the turn ends (Esc cancels both); with agents running (the orchestrator's usual state), once they have reported — the TUI then quits by itself | | `/background now` | Stop the running agents and hand off at once; the worker's next goal turn is told which agents were stopped (and where their briefs are) so it can dispatch them again | | `/background cancel` | Cancel a hand-off that is still waiting | | `nanopi --background` (or `/background list`) | List background sessions: status, what they run, last progress line | | `nanopi --foreground [id]` | Stop the worker after its current turn (Ctrl-C while waiting cancels that turn), then open the TUI on the session — history replayed, goal and loop restored, work continuing. Without an id: the newest one started in this directory | The worker is a detached `nanopi` (its own session, so closing the terminal does not stop it) resuming the same session file. It runs goal turns and loop iterations exactly as the TUI would, and exits on its own when the goal is met, judged impossible or paused, or the loop ends; `--foreground` then just shows the result. State and log live in `~/.nanopi/background/.json` and `.log` (`tail -f` the log to watch). Nothing can ask you anything in the background: sudo in `ask` mode is refused, as in `nanopi -p`. Agents are children of the process that started them, so the TUI's agents cannot move to the worker — hence the wait (or `now`); the worker dispatches its own. A reboot ends the worker — `--foreground` still restores the goal / loop from its state file. ## sudo nanopi never runs a session as root. If your account has **passwordless** sudo (checked at startup with `sudo -n true`), the model may prefix the individual commands that need root with `sudo -n` — never `sudo su`, `sudo -i` or a root shell. By default every such command is shown in the TUI and runs only after you press y; n, Esc or Enter refuse it, and the model is told not to retry. ```toml [sudo] mode = "ask" # "ask" (default) | "auto" (no confirmation) | "never" agents = false # let dispatched agents use sudo (they cannot ask) ``` - **Print mode** (`nanopi -p`) cannot ask, so `"ask"` refuses there; `"auto"` allows. - **Agents** never ask; they may use sudo only with `agents = true`. - **Password sudo** is not supported yet: the command is refused and the model gives you the command to run yourself. - **Running as root**, nothing is gated — sudo adds nothing. - A project's `.nanopi/config.toml` can only make this **stricter**, never looser, so a cloned repository cannot turn on unattended root. Spotting sudo inside a shell command is heuristic (it catches `a && sudo b`, `env X=1 sudo …`, `xargs sudo`, `bash -c "sudo …"`, but not a script that runs sudo internally). It guards against accidents; your sudoers policy is the real boundary. ## MCP servers nanopi is an [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) client: tools served by external MCP servers show up as ordinary tools named `mcp____`. Servers are listed in `~/.nanopi/mcp.json` (under `NANOPI_HOME` if you set it) in the same `mcpServers` shape Claude Code and most other clients use, so an existing block pastes in unchanged. The file is global only and nanopi never writes it. ```json { "mcpServers": { "fs": { "command": "npx", "args": ["-y", "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem", "/home/me/projects"], "env": { "LOG_LEVEL": "warn" } }, "playwright": { "type": "http", "url": "http://127.0.0.1:8931/mcp" }, "gateway": { "type": "http", "url": "https://mcp.example.com/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ${GATEWAY_TOKEN}" } } } } ``` **stdio** (`command`, `args`, `env`): nanopi launches the server as a subprocess. That subprocess runs with your full privileges — unlike a WASM plugin it is not sandboxed — so only list servers you would run by hand. `env` values are used verbatim; `${VAR}` is not expanded there. **Streamable HTTP** (`url`, optional `headers`): nanopi connects to a server that is already running (a shared browser, a team gateway). `"type": "http"` is optional when `url` is present. A server may answer as plain JSON or as an SSE stream; both work. - `${VAR}` in `headers` values and in `url` is replaced from the environment, so a token lives in your shell, not in `mcp.json`. An unset variable skips that server with a diagnostic (the literal `${VAR}` is never sent); an empty one expands to nothing. `$${` writes a literal `${`. Nothing else is expanded. - **Cleartext is loopback-only for credentials.** `http://` to a host that is not loopback (`127.0.0.0/8`, `::1`, `localhost`) is refused when the server carries any header, URL userinfo, or a credential-looking query parameter; use `https://`. `http://` to loopback is fine, and so is `http://` to a remote host with no credentials at all. - `/mcp` shows every server in `mcp.json` and where it stands: *connected* (with tool names), *failed* (with the reason), or *skipped* (an invalid entry, an unset `${VAR}`, a refused cleartext URL, `type: sse`), with the same masking as below. It reads cached state, so it is safe to run mid-turn. With the orchestrator on it notes that the tools are used by the agents you dispatch. - `/tools` (with the orchestrator off) shows each tool's origin. For an HTTP server that is the URL with userinfo shown as `***@` and everything after `?` shown as `?***`; header names and values are never printed. - **Sessions are ended on exit.** The server's `Mcp-Session-Id` session is closed with an HTTP `DELETE` when the TUI quits (including on SIGTERM or SIGHUP, which take the same orderly path as `/quit` and exit 143 / 129), when a `-p` run ends, and on Ctrl-C or SIGTERM in a `-p` run. `kill -9` cannot, and leaves the session for the server to expire. A server that drops the session mid-run (`404`) is re-initialized once and the failed call retried. - Redirects are not followed, and loopback targets bypass `http_proxy`. Not supported yet: the older HTTP+SSE transport (`"type": "sse"` is reported and skipped), OAuth (static `headers` only), the standing `GET` stream that carries server-initiated messages (so a server's `tools/list_changed` is not seen; the tool list is read once at startup) and stream resumability (`Last-Event-ID`), an interactive `/mcp` (reconnecting a server, enabling or disabling one: `/mcp` is read-only, `mcp.json` is read once at startup, and `/reload` does not re-read it), WebSocket, and MCP `prompts`/`resources`. All servers connect concurrently at startup under one 15 s budget. A server that fails to start, or an entry that is invalid, is reported and skipped; it never stops nanopi from starting or hides the others. `--tools` restricts the tool set, which excludes MCP tools. **With the orchestrator** the main agent has no MCP tools of its own (only the built-in scouting tools), but it sees their names and descriptions and can grant them to the agents it dispatches by naming them in the `agent` tool's `tools` list. Those agents are separate processes that never connect to a server themselves: every call goes through the main process, which holds the one connection (one session, for HTTP), checks the grant, and returns the result. The channel carries tool names, schemas and results only: a child is never sent a server's `env`, URL or `headers`, and nanopi removes from the child's environment every variable that `mcp.json` references as `${VAR}` (in a `url` or a `headers` value), so `echo $GATEWAY_TOKEN` in a child prints nothing. Every other variable is inherited as before, and `PATH`, `HOME`, `OPENAI_API_KEY` and `NANOPI_*` are never removed, even if you reference one. **This is not a sandbox.** A child that has `read` or `bash` can read `~/.nanopi/mcp.json` itself, where a stdio server's `env` values and any literal header value are plaintext (the same trust class as an API key in `config.toml`), and on Linux it can read its parent's `/proc//environ`, since both run as you. Use `${VAR}` rather than a literal for a secret, and treat an agent with `read` or `bash` as able to read anything you can. This channel is Unix-only; on Windows the servers work in the main process but agents cannot be granted their tools. With `/orchestrator off` (or in `nanopi -p`) the tools are simply in the main agent's tool set. ## Skills Nanopi implements the [Agent Skills spec](https://agentskills.io/specification). Drop a `SKILL.md` into `~/.nanopi/skills//`: ```markdown --- name: greet description: Greet the user warmly. Use for hellos. --- Say "hi, friend" — nothing else. ``` Invoke explicitly, or let the model discover it via the auto-appended `` block in the system prompt: ```bash /skill:greet # expands SKILL.md into the message /skill:greet in french # extra args are appended ``` **Locations** (earlier wins on name collisions): - User: `~/.nanopi/skills/` - Project: `/.nanopi/skills/` (only when trusted via `-a` or persisted decision) - CLI: `--skill ` (files or dirs; loads even with `--no-skills`) ## Custom system prompt `--system-prompt ` replaces the built-in identity/guidelines prompt; `--append-system-prompt ` (repeatable, values joined by a blank line) adds text after it. Both accept literal text OR a path to an existing file. Either flag suppresses the matching file discovery below entirely — no merge. Without a flag, nanopi discovers: - `/.nanopi/SYSTEM.md` (only when the project is trusted via `-a` or a persisted decision), then `~/.nanopi/SYSTEM.md` — for `--system-prompt`. - `/.nanopi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md` (same trust rule), then `~/.nanopi/APPEND_SYSTEM.md` — for `--append-system-prompt`. Project beats global; the global file needs no trust gate (it's your own machine, not a cloned repo). Context files, skills, and the "Current working directory: …" line still apply on top of a custom prompt — only the identity/tools/guidelines section is replaced. Caveat: a replaced prompt drops the auto-generated "Available tools: …" line, and some models skip tool calls without it, so mention the tools you expect the model to use. ## Hooks nanopi has two extension systems, and as of v0.12.0 they can both see every lifecycle event — the difference is what they're allowed to do with it: | | add tools | add commands | see events | veto / transform | hold state | cost per fire | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | shell hooks | ✗ | ✗ | ✓ (11) | ✓ | ✗ — fresh process | fork + exec | | WASM plugins | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ (11, opt-in, observe-only) | ✗ | ✓ — `Store` persists | one function call | In one sentence: **WASM plugins observe, shell hooks can refuse** — see [`docs/v0.12-events.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/v0.12-events.md) §8 for why nanopi keeps both instead of merging into one system like PI's `ExtensionAPI`. Shell hooks fire around tool calls, using Claude Code's hook *protocol* (JSON on stdin, exit code 2 to block, `tool_name` / `tool_input` / `hookSpecificOutput` fields) — but PI's *event names*, not Claude Code's. Configure in `~/.nanopi/settings.toml`: ```toml [[hooks.tool_execution_start]] matcher = "^bash$" command = "logger 'nanopi about to shell out'" ``` Keys are `snake_case` (`tool_execution_start`, not `ToolExecutionStart`). `matcher` is a regex, and what it is tested against depends on the event: the tool name, the session id, the turn number, or the compaction reason. `input` is the one event with nothing to match against — a user message is not a tool call — so `matcher` there must be `"*"`, and any other value is a startup error rather than a hook that silently never fires. Full protocol in [`docs/v0.5-research.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/v0.5-research.md) §6. ### Renamed in v0.12 nanopi used to borrow Claude Code's names for four hooks. v0.12 renames them to PI's names, with no alias and no deprecation period — a config using an old key on the left fails to load at startup, and the error names the replacement on the right: | Old key (retired — hard error) | New key | |---|---| | `pre_tool_use` | `tool_execution_start` | | `post_tool_use` | `tool_execution_end` | | `user_prompt_submit` | `input` | | `session_end` | `session_shutdown` | ### Lifecycle events (v0.11.0) In addition to the Claude Code-protocol trio above, nanopi exposes four lifecycle hooks that mirror Pi's `before_agent_start` / `turn_start` / `turn_end` / `message_end`: | Hook key | Fires | Blockable? | |---|---|---| | `before_agent_start` | Once per turn, after compaction but before the user message enters context | yes (returns early with a synthetic message) | | `turn_start` | Top of each agent-loop iteration | no (advisory) | | `turn_end` | Bottom of each agent-loop iteration | no (advisory) | | `message_end` | Once after the for-loop completes | no (advisory) | For all four, the `matcher` runs against the turn number string (so `^1$` fires only on the first turn), and stdin carries `{ "turn_count": N, ... }` plus event-specific fields. Full enumeration in [`config.toml.example`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/config.toml.example). Two more fire around context compaction: `session_before_compact` and `session_compact`. Both are advisory, and their `matcher` runs against the reason string (`threshold` or `manual`). ## WASM extensions (v0.11.0) Shell hooks can observe and veto, but they can't add a tool the model is allowed to call. Extensions can. A nanopi extension is a WebAssembly component — written in Rust, Go, C, or anything else that compiles to WASM — whose exported tools show up in the model's tool list next to `bash` and `read`. **This is opt-in at build time.** The stock release binary has no WASM runtime, so it stays ~4 MB; `[[extensions]]` entries are ignored with a warning. To use them: ```bash cargo build --release --features wasm ``` Then declare the components in `config.toml`: ```toml [[extensions]] path = "~/.nanopi/extensions/my-tool.wasm" ``` A plugin exports two required functions, and optionally two more ([`wit/nanopi-extension.wit`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/wit/nanopi-extension.wit)): | Export | Signature | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `list-tools` | `() -> string` | JSON array of `{name, description, parameters}`. Called once at load. `parameters` is a JSON Schema handed to the model verbatim. | | `execute-tool` | `(name: string, args-json: string) -> string` | Runs a tool, returns `{"content": "...", "is_error": false}`. | | `list-commands` | `() -> string` | *Optional.* JSON array of `{name, description}` — slash commands the user can type. | | `execute-command` | `(name: string, args: string) -> string` | *Optional.* Runs a command, returns one of `{"print": "..."}`, `{"send_user_message": "..."}`, `{"error": "..."}`. | **Tools vs commands.** A tool is something the *model* decides to call; a command is something *you* type. Commands show up in the `/` palette with the plugin's name attached, and are interactive-mode only — `nanopi -p` has no palette, though the plugin's tools still work there. **Seeing what loaded.** `/tools` lists every tool the model can actually call, tagged `[builtin]` or `[plugin:]` with the `.wasm` it came from. It reads the live registry — the same list handed to the provider — so it is the thing to check when a plugin tool seems missing. Asking the model to list its own tools is not a substitute: it cannot tell a plugin tool from a built-in one, and will guess. `print` goes straight to your scrollback: the model never sees it and it never enters the session transcript. `send_user_message` starts a turn as if you had typed it — always echoed verbatim first, so a plugin cannot put words in your mouth invisibly; typed mid-stream it steers the running turn instead, exactly like your own typing. `error` is shown to you and, like a trap, is never forwarded to the model. The two command exports live in a second WIT world, `extension-commands`, which `include`s the first. A tool-only plugin keeps targeting `extension` and keeps building unchanged — WIT cannot express an optional export, so widening the original world would have broken every existing plugin's *source* even though the host still loads its compiled *binary*. **Watching lifecycle events (v0.12.0).** A third, opt-in WIT world, `extension-events`, `include`s `extension-commands` and adds two more exports: | Export | Signature | Purpose | |---|---|---| | `list-events` | `() -> string` | *Optional.* JSON array of PI event names the plugin wants to observe. | | `handle-event` | `(event: string, payload-json: string) -> string` | *Optional.* Called for every event both requested here AND granted by config. Return value is ignored — this is observe-only, a plugin cannot veto or transform through it. | Delivery needs **both lists to agree**: the plugin's `list-events` and the config's `[[extensions]].events` (`config.toml.example` documents the full grant syntax). Either alone grants nothing — an unsatisfied request (exported but not granted) is reported at load, so a plugin that looks like it should be receiving events but isn't says why. The payload handed to `handle-event` is byte-identical to what a shell hook receives on stdin for the same event — same `HookInput` JSON, same builder. This is a bigger grant than it might look: an `input` subscriber sees every prompt verbatim, and a `tool_execution_start` subscriber sees every tool call's arguments — bigger than `allow_fs`. Combining `events` with `allow_network = true` on one plugin is warned about at startup, because it turns the plugin into a channel that can exfiltrate whatever those events carry. **Do not fetch from an event handler** — `host-http-get` is still reachable from `handle-event`, but a slow or hostile fetch there is bounded by the fetch's own 10s timeout stacked on top of the event budget below, not by epoch interruption (epoch instrumentation cannot preempt a running host function). Guest code in `handle-event` gets a 2s wall-clock budget — much tighter than a tool call's 30s, since an event handler sits on the turn's critical path and fires far more often. Delivery is **drop-on-busy, never blocking**: if a plugin's `Store` is already busy with an in-flight tool call, the event for that instant is dropped rather than queued, so one busy plugin can never stall an emit for the rest of the agent loop. Dropped events are counted per plugin and logged. `/tools` lists every plugin currently subscribed, under a "Watching events" section — the same inventory that already answers "what can the model call" now also answers "what is watching me". And may import these host functions: | Import | Signature | Gate | Purpose | |---|---|---|---| | `host-log` | `(level: u8, message: string)` | always | Write to nanopi's stderr. `0`=trace `1`=info `2`=warn `3`=error. | | `host-fs-read` | `(path: string) -> string` | `allow_fs` | Read a UTF-8 file inside the working directory. Returns contents, or a string starting with `error: `. | | `host-http-get` | `(url: string) -> string` | `allow_network` + `url_allowlist` | Fetch an `http`/`https` URL. Returns the response body, or a string starting with `error: `. | | `host-store-get` | `(key: string) -> string` | `allow_store` | Read this plugin's stored value for `key`. Absent reads as `""`. | | `host-store-set` | `(key: string, value: string) -> string` | `allow_store` | Replace this plugin's value at `key`. Returns `""` once the bytes are on the filesystem, or a string starting with `error: `. | | `host-notify` | `(text: string) -> string` | always | Put one line in the user's scrollback, prefixed by the host with this plugin's name. Rate-limited per turn. | | `host-set-context` | `(text: string) -> string` | `allow_context` | Declare text for the model's context, attributed to this plugin. Replaces the plugin's previous contribution; `""` clears it. Returns `""`, or a string starting with `error: `. | | `host-call-tool` | `(name: string, args-json: string) -> string` | `allow_tools`, per tool named | Run one of nanopi's built-in tools. Returns `{"content": "...", "is_error": false}` for a call that ran, or a bare string starting with `error: ` for one that did not. | | `host-send-user-message` | `(text: string) -> string` | `allow_send_message` | Start or steer a turn with this text, as if you had typed it. Always echoed to you verbatim, attributed to the plugin. Returns `""`, or a string starting with `error: `. | Payloads cross the boundary as JSON strings rather than WIT records — one primitive type keeps the ABI small enough that neither side needs a codegen step. A worked example lives in [`examples/wasm-plugin/`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/tree/main/examples/wasm-plugin), including the build command. [`examples/wasm-plugin-minimal/`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/tree/main/examples/wasm-plugin-minimal) is a smaller skeleton to copy — two tools, split into boilerplate and the part you replace. For plugins meant to be *used* rather than read: [`examples/wasm-plugin-memory/`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/tree/main/examples/wasm-plugin-memory) is durable project memory — facts are markdown files in `.nanopi/memory/` that you can diff and commit, and only the compact index enters the model's context, with `recall` fetching the full text of whatever looks relevant. [`examples/wasm-plugin-report/`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/tree/main/examples/wasm-plugin-report) records per-tool time and failures across sessions, which answers "why was that slow" — `tool_execution_end` carries a `duration_ms` that nothing else persists. All five plugins are indexed in [`examples/README.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/tree/main/examples) — a table of what each one does, the grants it needs, and which WIT world it targets. Step-by-step guides for writing, debugging, and gating a plugin are in the [wiki](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/wiki) (English and Chinese). **Sandboxing.** Components run inside wasmtime with no ambient authority — a plugin reaches the outside world only through host functions you opt into. `host-fs-read` is gated on `allow_fs = true`, and even then the path must resolve *inside* the working directory. Paths are canonicalized before that check, so `../` traversal and symlinks pointing outward are both refused. (The built-in `read` tool deliberately has no such guard, on the reasoning that the model can shell out anyway — but a plugin has no shell, so here the boundary is real rather than theater.) `host-notify` is ungated because it is output, not access — it reaches nothing and leaves nothing behind. What it can do is flood your attention, so it is bounded by a rate limit rather than a grant: past the per-turn allowance further lines are dropped and one `… N more suppressed` line says how many, and the suppressed calls come back as `error: ` strings so a plugin is never told it spoke when it did not. The prefix is applied by the host from the `.wasm` file stem and the payload is never parsed for it, so one plugin cannot impersonate another. It differs from `host-log` in where the text ends up: `host-log` writes raw stderr, which lands inside the TUI's managed region and is wiped by the next redraw, whereas `host-notify` scrolls into history and stays. `host-store-get` / `host-store-set` are gated on `allow_store = true` and are **keys, not paths** — the plugin supplies a map key and the host alone decides which file it lands in (`~/.nanopi/extensions//store.json`, one JSON object per plugin). So none of the confinement machinery above applies or is needed: there is no path for a plugin to point outward. Bounds are 1 MiB total, 1000 keys, and keys up to 128 chars; every refusal comes back in-band and stores nothing, so a plugin is never told it failed while the value went in anyway. A `""` return from `host-store-set` means the bytes reached the filesystem — the host commits with a temp file and a rename, so a crash leaves the whole old file or the whole new one, never a torn one. Two plugins whose `.wasm` files share a file stem where either has `allow_store` fail to load rather than silently sharing one store. `host-set-context` is gated on `allow_context = true`, and it is the one import that changes what the *agent* believes rather than what the plugin knows: the text a plugin declares is folded into the system prompt at the start of each turn. The host writes the attribution header — `[context contributed by extension "memory"]` — because without it the model cannot tell a plugin's injected instructions from your own. Each call **replaces** that plugin's previous contribution rather than appending, so it is idempotent state and ten turns cannot accumulate ten copies; `""` clears it. The bound is 4 KiB per plugin, in bytes, and it is small deliberately: this text enters *every* request for the rest of the session. An over-bound call is refused in-band and the previous contribution still stands, so being told "no" never costs you what you already had. Every change is announced in your scrollback naming the plugin — a contribution is invisible otherwise, since you never see the system prompt — and that announcement is accounted separately from the plugin's `host-notify` allowance, so a plugin cannot bury it by first flooding you with noise. Combined with `allow_network = true` this is the sharpest pair of grants nanopi has, and it warns at startup: a remote source could then shape how the agent behaves. `host-call-tool` is gated **per tool**, on `allow_tools` naming it. Empty (the default) denies everything, the same rule as `url_allowlist`. Per tool rather than per plugin because the tools are not equivalent: `allow_tools = ["find", "read"]` lets an indexer walk and read but not write or exec, while `allow_tools = ["bash"]` is arbitrary command execution that walks straight past `allow_fs`'s cwd confinement and `url_allowlist`'s per-host approval — nanopi prints an escalated warning at startup when it sees `bash` there, because that grant makes every other grant on that plugin decorative. Built-ins only: a plugin cannot call another plugin's tool, and a name that is not a built-in is a **load error** naming the valid ones rather than a silent no-op. The return shape is the honest half of the contract: a JSON frame means the call ran (including a call that ran and failed), and a bare `error: ` means it never happened. Nothing traps. Calls are bounded at 30s — the epoch budget bounds guest code and cannot preempt a host function already executing — and a `bash` child the timeout abandons may outlive it, which is a known limit rather than a claim. Your `[[hooks.*]]` still run, so a plugin does not outrank your own policy; a block comes back as `error: blocked by hook: `. Each call that ran is announced in your scrollback naming the plugin and the tool, on the host's own budget so a `host-notify` flood cannot bury it — necessary because a plugin's calls are deliberately **not** in the session transcript (a `tool_call` entry the model never emitted is the exact shape that made sessions unresumable), which means `--continue` will not show what a plugin did. `/tools` lists what every loaded plugin holds, under "Plugin grants"; a plugin granted nothing still gets a row, reading `no grants`. `host-send-user-message` is gated on `allow_send_message = true`, and it is the only capability nanopi has that **spends your money**. Every other grant lets a plugin learn something, change what the agent believes, or run a tool you could have run yourself; this one causes turns you are billed for. It warns at startup on its own, without needing a second grant to pair with, which no other grant does. If a turn is running the text steers it, arriving as a fresh user message at the next iteration boundary — the same path a line you type mid-stream takes, deliberately, because a plugin should not get a parallel mechanism to the one `b90b27f` repaired. If no turn is running, it starts the next one, queued **behind** anything you have already typed: a line you watched land outranks something software decided to spend your budget on. It is never dropped. Three bounds, all announced, none silent. One unconsumed message per plugin, which clears when the text actually reaches a turn rather than when the call returns. No message during a turn that plugin's own message started — per plugin, not globally, so an auditing plugin can still speak during a turn a rules plugin started. And at most 20 turns per plugin per session, which the spec's original two rules did not provide: a `turn_end` subscriber that sends once per turn satisfies both of them forever, because each new turn's origin is a new turn and each message is consumed before the next. The cap is a backstop against a runaway subscriber, not a budget, and it survives a plugin trapping — otherwise trapping would be how a plugin buys another twenty turns. The text is always echoed to you verbatim, attributed, and there is no quiet path: what the host accepts you see, and what it refuses the plugin is told about in-band with a reason. Under `nanopi -p` there is no turn loop to reach, so the call is **refused** rather than quietly dropped — a plugin must never believe it sent something it did not. `host-http-get` is gated twice: on `allow_network = true`, and then on the URL's host matching `url_allowlist`. An **empty allowlist denies everything**, so switching the capability on does not by itself reach anything. Matching is on the parsed host, not a substring — `https://evil.com/?x=api.github.com` and `https://api.github.com@evil.com/` are both refused against an allowlist of `api.github.com`. Entries are patterns, because a plugin that fetches whatever the model hands it has no finite host list to enumerate: | Entry | Matches | |---|---| | `github.com` | the host **and** its subdomains, any port | | `*.github.com` | subdomains only — the apex `github.com` is refused | | `*` | any `http`/`https` host | `*` is the escape hatch, and it is a real one: it turns the second gate off, leaving `allow_network` as the only check — link-local metadata endpoints included. nanopi prints a warning at startup naming the plugin whenever it sees `*` with networking on. A star anywhere else (`api.*.com`) is refused rather than widened, so a typo can't quietly broaden the gate. `*` widens hosts only; the scheme check is separate, so `file://` stays outside the network capability under every pattern. Only `http`/`https`; requests time out at 10s so a plugin cannot hang a turn; redirects are **not** followed, since a 3xx would otherwise walk the fetch onto a host you never approved. Refusals and failures come back to the plugin in-band as `error: `-prefixed strings rather than as traps. A trap in a plugin is reported to the model as a failed tool call — it does not take down nanopi, and a `.wasm` that fails to load is skipped with a warning rather than blocking startup. **Runaway plugins.** Guest code gets a ~30s wall-clock budget per tool call, enforced by wasmtime's epoch interruption. Exceeding it is a trap, which surfaces to the model as a failed tool call and leaves the plugin callable — the instance is rebuilt, so one bad call does not disable it for the rest of the session. Without the budget, a plugin containing an infinite loop would wedge nanopi permanently: the guest holds a real thread with no yield points, so Esc cannot reach inside it. The budget applies to **guest** code only. Epoch interruption is instrumentation compiled into the guest, so it cannot interrupt a host function that is already running — a plugin blocked inside `host-http-get` or `host-fs-read` is bounded by those functions' own limits (a 10s request timeout; regular-files-only and a 1 MiB cap, which is what stops a FIFO from blocking forever), not by the epoch deadline. Worst case for one call is therefore the budget plus one host call, not the budget alone. **Name collisions.** A plugin may not register a tool whose name already exists. Collisions are reported and skipped, so a plugin cannot quietly replace `bash`. Commands are stricter, and the two rules genuinely differ. A **tool** collision is first-wins: the tool already registered stays and the newcomer is skipped. A **command** collision refuses *both* claimants — if two plugins each register `/deploy`, neither gets it, because silently picking a winner would mean `/deploy` runs whichever plugin happened to load first. A command whose name belongs to a built-in like `/compact` is skipped. Every case prints a warning naming the plugin(s), and never affects that plugin's other commands or any of its tools. Plugins are loaded at startup and on `/new`, `/resume`, `/fork`, `/import` — and, as of v0.12.0, on `/reload`, which re-reads `[[extensions]]` and hot-swaps the live registry. **Hot reload.** `/reload` loads the new `.wasm` files *first*, then unregisters the old tools and commands, then registers the new ones — so a plugin whose file has stopped loading keeps the instance that is already running, and `/reload` says so in red rather than leaving you with neither the old plugin nor the new one. It reports what it did: how many plugins reloaded, how many tools and commands they brought, which plugins the config no longer lists (unregistered), and which failed. Grants are re-read from the config, so revoking `allow_network` takes effect on `/reload`; a failed plugin keeps its old grant row, because that row describes what is actually still running. A tool call already in flight when a reload lands is **refused, not executed and not silently substituted**: the plugin's old instance recognises that it has been replaced and returns an `error:` string naming the reload as the reason, both before the call starts and after the guest returns. The second check is the one that matters — you are never told a call succeeded when its result came from code that has since been replaced. Side effects the call already had (a file written, an HTTP request sent) stand, and the refusal says so. Events are not delivered to a replaced instance at all. Host-side plugin state survives a reload, deliberately: the plugin's host-store files (they are on disk, and a reload is not a factory reset), and the `plugin_send` loop guard and spent per-session message budget (otherwise `/reload` would be a budget refund, and a plugin could reload itself out of its own limit). The one exception is a plugin's system-prompt contribution, which is dropped if the plugin is gone from the config or has lost `allow_context` — keeping it would put text in the prompt that nothing live can account for. ## Versions | Version | Status | Size | Notes | |---|---|---|---| | **v0.16.1** | current | 2.0 MB | `/goal` (work until a verified condition), `/loop` (fixed or self-paced), background mode (`/background`, `--foreground`); config profiles; per-command sudo gate; hybrid orchestrator; cut-off replies reported; shared input history | | v0.15.0 | released | — | MCP servers (stdio + Streamable HTTP, `/mcp`); interactive `/agents` picker; orderly SIGTERM/SIGHUP exit | | v0.14.0 | released | 1.8 MB | Orchestrator as the default main agent; user-editable `models.json`; context usage bar | | v0.13.0 | released | — | Orchestrator mode; background agent dispatch; agents strip (Ctrl+G) | | v0.12.x | released | — | One hook-event vocabulary, plugin capabilities, hot-reloadable extensions (`.release-notes-v0.12.0.md`); explicit DNS, `sh`/ripgrep fallbacks (0.12.1) | | v0.11.0 | closed | ~1.6 MB | WASM extensions with gated `host-fs-read` / `host-http-get` and plugin-registered slash commands; Pi lifecycle hooks (`before_agent_start`, `turn_start`, `turn_end`, `message_end`); mid-stream steering; configurable tool exec mode | | v0.10.0 | released | 1.6 MB | Custom system prompt (`--system-prompt`, `SYSTEM.md`); explicit `api_kind` beats the vendor sniff; readable tool failures in `-p`; UPX-packed release | | v0.9.x | released | ~3.9 MB | First-run wizard, `/settings` + `/keybindings`, 8-vendor dispatch, retry envelope (0.9.2–0.9.3); v0.9.1 fixed the v0.9.0 tool loop | | v0.9.0 | released | ~4.0 MB | Skills (PI-parity), `--skill`/`--no-skills`, folded TUI card, `UserPromptSubmit` hook | | v0.8.x | released | ~3.9 MB | Full ratatui TUI, `/fork`, `--continue`/`--session`, hooks, JSONL sessions | | v0.5.0 | released | ~3.0 MB | Tools (read/write/edit/bash), `-p` mode, JSON output, hooks | | v0.1.0 | released | 2.4 MB | Single-file OpenAI streaming demo (kept as `nanopi_v0_1` binary) | Sizes are the published musl artifact. From v0.10.0 that artifact is UPX-packed (`make`), so 1.6 MB is not comparable to the unpacked figures above it — the same build is 4.4 MB before packing. The v0.11.0 figure is approximate: it is measured from a development build, not a published tag. `—` marks sizes not recorded here. ## Roadmap No feature checklist. nanopi is the lightweight Rust take on Pi: the aim is to carry Pi's core surface in one small static binary, not to match everything Pi does. A feature gets in when it earns the weight it adds. Known gap: Linux aarch64 is not in the CI matrix yet — build it yourself with `cargo build --release --target aarch64-unknown-linux-musl` (see above). ## Cargo mirror (China) Add to `~/.cargo/config.toml` for faster crate downloads: ```toml [source.crates-io] replace-with = "rsproxy-sparse" [source.rsproxy-sparse] registry = "sparse+https://rsproxy.cn/index/" [target.x86_64-unknown-linux-musl] linker = "musl-gcc" ``` ## Design notes - **musl + LTO + panic=abort + strip** → small static binary. rustls avoids the OpenSSL dep. - **Hand-written SSE parser** — no `reqwest-eventsource`, keeps the dep tree lean. - **JSONL over JSON** — append-only files survive crashes mid-write. - **Provider abstraction** landed in v0.6; native Anthropic + any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. See [`docs/v0.5-research.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/v0.5-research.md) and [`docs/PLAN.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/PLAN.md) for design + implementation notes, and [`docs/claims-and-races.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/claims-and-races.md) for what nanopi is allowed to claim about its own actions — plus the race table behind those rules, and [`docs/plugin-capabilities.md`](https://github.com/ChrisZhangJin/nanopi/blob/main/docs/plugin-capabilities.md) for the outbound surface a plugin gets (and the per-tool grant that keeps the sandbox worth paying for). ## Credits - [Pi](https://github.com/earendil-works/pi) — the upstream TypeScript agent nanopi ports. - [Claude Code](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code) — hook protocol, `-p` mode, skills spec. - [ratatui](https://github.com/ratatui-org/ratatui) & [crossterm](https://github.com/crossterm-rs/crossterm) — the TUI foundation. ## License [MIT](LICENSE) © Chris Zhang

repository.readme:
ClickHouse Loom

Shared memory, document search and code intelligence for AI agents.
For Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and your own agents.

English · 简体中文 · 日本語 · 한국어 · Português (Brasil) · Español

What Loom is for · Benchmarks · Get started · Capabilities · Integrations · Documentation

Loom is an open-source, self-hosted MCP server that gives your agents long-term, shared memory: what one agent learns in a session, the next agent or tool can find. In an authenticated team deployment, each agent uses a token scoped to namespaces and read or write roles. [Check shared memory and denied access](./docs/getting-started/connect-a-coding-agent.md#share-a-team-namespace-with-separate-credentials). Agents connect through MCP, HTTP, Python or TypeScript. Self-host with Docker or [on Kubernetes with the Helm chart](./docs/operations/kubernetes.md); agent context and index data live in [ClickHouse](./docs/use-cases/self-hosted-clickhouse.md), and a deployment can choose [Postgres at first boot](./docs/operations/postgres.md) for live memory and knowledge state. The dashboard brings memories, repositories, tasks and runs into one place. ## What Loom is for - **Long-term memory shared across your coding agents**, with plugins that load context at session start and capture the session as it runs. [Agent memory](./docs/use-cases/agent-memory.md) · [Connect a coding agent](./docs/getting-started/connect-a-coding-agent.md) - **Memory for an agent application**, per user, from the Python or TypeScript SDK. [Your first agent](./docs/getting-started/first-agent.md) - **A multi-user MCP memory server** with namespaces, roles and tokens. [Multi-user mode](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md#start-in-multi-user-mode) · [Namespaces and sharing](./docs/features/namespaces-and-sharing.md) - **A code index of your repositories** that coding agents query for definitions, callers and change impact. [Code index](./docs/use-cases/code-intelligence.md) · [Language support and limits](./docs/features/code-index/overview.md#language-support) - **Memories linked to the code they are about**, which follow it through refactors, are flagged when it changes and appear when an agent reads or edits it. [Memory linked to code](./docs/use-cases/memory-linked-to-code.md) - **Lower model cost for coding agents**, as [measured](#measured-results) below. [Coding-agent cost](./docs/use-cases/coding-agent-cost.md) - **Document search with citations (RAG)**, including PDF, `.docx` and `.pptx` files the extractor service converts. [Document search](./docs/use-cases/document-search.md) - **Shared context for multi-agent workflows**: shared memory, task inboxes and decisions. [Multi-agent](./docs/use-cases/multi-agent.md) - **Memory, recall, audit and erasure for autonomous agents.** [Autonomous agents](./docs/use-cases/autonomous-agents.md) - **A record of agent work**, with searchable conversations (when recording is on), session briefs to resume from, runs with their goals, outcomes and model costs when supplied, and PR and tracker history. [Runs and PR history](./docs/use-cases/runs-and-pr-history.md) **Memory for a software factory.** Loom gives implementation and review agents shared lessons, issue context and source provenance across sessions. Scope each principal's access with tokens, await required writes and task handoffs in your application, and recheck code-linked lessons against the current source before review. The same service supports multi-agent workflows and autonomous bots; your orchestration runs the agents, tests and approvals. Offering a tool does not guarantee the model uses it. [Multi-agent workflow](./docs/use-cases/multi-agent.md) · [Autonomous-agent memory](./docs/use-cases/autonomous-agents.md) Every use case, and when another tool fits better: [use cases](./docs/use-cases/index.md). Read [Choosing memory for a software factory](https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/discussions/939) for memory architecture choices, data ownership and operating responsibilities. Loom is not an in-process library for one agent's short-lived memory, nor an agent framework. [When Loom does not fit](./docs/getting-started/overview.md#when-it-does-not-fit) ## Measured results | Evaluation | With Loom | Without Loom | Efficiency gain | Scope | | ------------------------------ | --------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------- | ---------------------------------- | | Coding-agent answer quality | **0.84** | 0.78 | **20% lower** model cost | 24 questions × 3 paired runs | | Coding-agent file localization | **96.4%** | 91.4% | **21% lower** model cost | 36 questions × 10 paired runs | | Memory vs full-history answers | **94%** | 90% | **91% fewer** reader prompt tokens | 100 paired LongMemEval-S questions | Both coding setups use Claude Code (`claude-sonnet-5`) on the ClickHouse codebase; cost is the whole session's model bill, excluding Loom's server-side model calls, hosting and indexing. Answer quality measures coverage of a verified answer's key points, with a contradiction penalty. File localization counts whether the right file is among the up to three files the agent is asked to name at the end of its answer. The memory row compares retrieved memories with full conversation history using the same `gpt-5` reader. Token savings exclude memory construction; the 94% vs 90% accuracy difference is descriptive, not statistically established. **Separately, Loom's `memory.ask` configuration scored 96.6% answer accuracy on all 500 LongMemEval-S questions.** This is a product evaluation with its own configured answer models, not the fixed-reader comparison above. Results are specific to the tested workloads. [Protocols and reproducible artifacts](./docs/benchmarks/results.md) · [detailed results](#benchmark-details) · [evaluate on your workload](./docs/getting-started/evaluate.md) ## Get started ### 1. Choose your Docker setup - **Personal use—the default:** no login, localhost-only access and a `dev/local` namespace. One person can connect multiple agents. - **Team use:** authenticated accounts and namespace access controls. [Start in multi-user mode from the first boot](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md#start-in-multi-user-mode). Both modes support the same Loom features, including configured LLMs and embeddings. Single-user is not a reduced-feature edition. You can also [switch an existing installation without deleting its data](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md#2-open-the-dashboard); grant new accounts access to the existing namespaces. To try it with nothing installed, open it in a codespace: [![Open in GitHub Codespaces](https://github.com/codespaces/badge.svg)](https://codespaces.new/ClickHouse/loom?quickstart=1) ([what it runs and who can reach it](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md#try-it-in-github-codespaces)) For the default personal installation, with Docker installed (on Windows, in a WSL 2 terminal where `docker` works: Docker Desktop with its WSL integration on, or Docker Engine installed in the distribution): ```bash curl -fsSL https://github.com/ClickHouse/loom/releases/latest/download/install.sh -o loom-install.sh && sh loom-install.sh && rm loom-install.sh ``` Run it from your home directory, or another [directory only you can write to](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md#fast-path-released-image-no-clone). The installer starts Loom and ClickHouse, applies migrations and prints the dashboard URL: **http://localhost:7777/**; on a new install it then checks that a memory saves and reads back. On a terminal it also offers to connect the coding agents it finds (Claude Code, Codex, VS Code) and, on a new install, opens the dashboard. The image includes the server, workers, dashboard and Python, TypeScript and Go compiler indexers, plus the C++ one on `amd64`; TypeScript dependencies are prepared automatically. [Quickstart and pinned releases](./docs/getting-started/quickstart.md) The installation lives in `~/.loom` (`LOOM_INSTALL_DIR` chooses another directory): the Compose file and the startup settings in `~/.loom/.env`. Running the install command again upgrades in place and keeps your `.env` settings. Keep single-user mode localhost-only. For shared access, follow the [team deployment guide](./docs/operations/deployment.md#identity-modes), including TLS. ### 2. Configure models and API keys **The stock installation boots without keys or network.** Storage, the dashboard, structural code indexing and semantic search work, on a small local embedding model the image carries; the fake LLM gives no AI-generated answers. | Component | Configure for real use | Without configuration | | ---------- | -------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Embeddings | Provider, embedding model, dimensions and API key. | `local` (bge-small on CPU): semantic retrieval, weaker than a hosted model. | | LLM | Provider, model and API key. | `fake-echo-1`: no meaningful extraction, summaries or answers. | Open **Settings → Models & keys**, choose both providers and models, enter their keys, then click **Test & apply**. No Docker restart is needed; changing the embedding space rebuilds the existing index. The dashboard's embedding choices are hosted providers: to keep `local` and add an LLM, set the LLM lines in `~/.loom/.env` instead ([Models and keys](docs/getting-started/models-and-keys.md#claude-for-the-llm)). **One OpenAI API key can serve both roles.** Claude needs a separate embedding provider. OpenAI, Gemini and OpenAI-compatible embedding endpoints are supported. Your agent's CLI login or subscription does not supply Loom's provider keys. Prefer environment configuration? Edit `~/.loom/.env`, then recreate the server: ```bash docker compose --project-directory "$HOME/.loom" up -d --force-recreate loom ``` A key alone does not change the pinned models (the local embedder and the fake LLM); set the provider and model too. Saved dashboard settings take precedence over `.env`. Follow [models and API keys](./docs/getting-started/models-and-keys.md) for provider recipes and health checks. **Everything else is in one file.** [`loom.example.yaml`](./loom.example.yaml) lists every setting with its default and what it does, by area: the ClickHouse connection, timeouts and budgets, rate limits, workers, and the `*_enabled` switches that turn features on and off. Set any of them as `LOOM_` in `~/.loom/.env` and recreate the server; a deployment that mounts a config file can set them in a copy of this file instead ([how settings are read](./docs/operations/deployment.md#how-settings-are-read)). One marked `live` also changes while Loom runs: `loom settings set `, or Admin → Deployment settings. `loom settings list --changed` shows what differs from the defaults and where each value came from ([runtime settings](./docs/operations/runtime-settings.md)). ### 3. Connect your agents If the installer connected your agent, skip the commands below. On the machine running a personal installation, the plugins need no token: ```bash # Claude Code claude plugin marketplace add ClickHouse/loom claude plugin install loom@loom # Codex codex plugin marketplace add ClickHouse/loom codex plugin add loom@loom ``` Start a new session; the first one connects to `http://localhost:7777`. In Codex, run `codex` interactively once and approve the plugin's hooks; until then only the tools work. Tell the agent something worth keeping, then ask about it in the next session. For Cursor, on a Teams or Enterprise plan, a team admin can import this repository as a team marketplace; its [Cursor plugin](./docs/features/integrations/cursor.md#plugin), untested in Cursor, installs the MCP entry and Loom's skills. On the machine running a personal installation, the button below adds the [local MCP entry](./docs/features/integrations/cursor.md#mcp-tools), which needs no token: [![Add Loom to Cursor](https://cursor.com/deeplink/mcp-install-dark.svg)](https://cursor.com/en/install-mcp?name=loom&config=eyJ1cmwiOiJodHRwOi8vbG9jYWxob3N0Ojc3NzcvbWNwP3Rvb2xzZXQ9Y29kaW5nIn0%3D) For VS Code agent mode on the machine running a personal installation, the buttons below add the [local MCP entry](./docs/features/integrations/vscode.md#local-single-user-server), which needs no token: [![Add Loom to VS Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/VS_Code-Add_Loom-0098FF?logo=visualstudiocode&logoColor=white)](https://vscode.dev/redirect?url=vscode%3Amcp%2Finstall%3F%257B%2522name%2522%253A%2522loom%2522%252C%2522type%2522%253A%2522http%2522%252C%2522url%2522%253A%2522http%253A%252F%252Flocalhost%253A7777%252Fmcp%2522%257D) [![Add Loom to VS Code Insiders](https://img.shields.io/badge/VS_Code_Insiders-Add_Loom-24bfa5?logo=visualstudiocode&logoColor=white)](https://insiders.vscode.dev/redirect?url=vscode-insiders%3Amcp%2Finstall%3F%257B%2522name%2522%253A%2522loom%2522%252C%2522type%2522%253A%2522http%2522%252C%2522url%2522%253A%2522http%253A%252F%252Flocalhost%253A7777%252Fmcp%2522%257D) For a team server, pass `--config server_url=… --config token=…` to Claude Code, or point Codex at it as described in [connect a coding agent](./docs/getting-started/connect-a-coding-agent.md). Create tokens in **Settings → Tokens**. Cursor and other MCP clients, and [the SDK](./docs/getting-started/first-agent.md), are covered there too. ## Why Loom - **Memory that carries forward.** Share decisions and findings across agents and sessions. Each fact records who wrote it, version history and conflict review make corrections traceable, and a namespace can be rolled back to any point in time. [Memory](./docs/concepts/memory.md) - **Code intelligence with evidence.** Find definitions, callers, change impact and relevant tests; connect code to commits, pull requests and issues. Use source locations, completeness signals and per-tier freshness to check a result. [Code index](./docs/features/code-index/overview.md) - **Grounded retrieval.** Search permitted memories, documents, conversations and tracker records. Answers cite their sources; low-confidence retrieval can abstain. [Retrieval](./docs/concepts/retrieval-and-ranking.md) - **Multi-agent handoffs.** Assign work through durable task inboxes with leases, retries, review rules and outcomes. Your agents execute the workflow; Loom preserves the handoffs. [Task queues](./docs/features/tasks-and-decisions.md) - **Control over agent data.** Manage namespace access, provenance, retention, audit records and verified erasure. Context remains queryable in ClickHouse.
