When encoding, `.wav` writes PCM, `.aif`/`.aiff` and `.caf` write 16-bit PCM, `.flac` and `.mka` write FLAC, `.mp3` writes MP3 and `.m4a` writes AAC. For a cut to `.mka`, stream copy keeps the original audio codec and `--accurate` writes FLAC. Use `.mkv` for a Matroska cut with picture. `.wma` supports stream copy of WMA audio through `cut.py` and `metadata.py`. - **Extraction.** An audio extension on a video input drops the picture: `audio.py talk.mp4 -o talk.wav`, or `--voice -o talk.m4a` to clean it on the way (sound that starts after the picture keeps its place: the lead is written as silence). A tool that encodes a picture (and `metadata.py` for a source with one) refuses an audio extension (`output_extension_audio_only`). `--audio-stream N` picks a track; `probe` lists them under `audio_streams`. - **Join.** `join.py intro.wav episode.m4a outro.wav -o full.flac` resamples every clip to one rate and channel layout and crossfades them (`--transition none` for a butt join). Audio and video inputs cannot be mixed in one join. - **Sample-accurate trims.** `cut.py talk.wav --start 1.2345 --end 2.3456 --accurate` trims at the sample; the JSON reports `precision` (`packet` for a stream copy, `sample` for PCM / FLAC, `codec_frame` when a lossy encoder frames the audio again, `frame` for video) and the measured `duration_error_ms`. A `.wav` never receives compressed packets. - **Typed dynamics.** `audio.py --compress --comp-threshold -20 --comp-ratio 4`, `--limit --limit-ceiling -1`, `--gate --gate-threshold -45`. Each flag is one documented option of FFmpeg's `acompressor`, `alimiter` or `agate`, range-checked before ffmpeg runs; no filter string is accepted from the caller. - **Loudness.** `loudness.py talk.wav -I -16 --tp -1.5 -o talk.m4a` for podcast levels; `check.py talk.m4a --platform podcast` measures LUFS and true peak and reports the chapter markers and channel count. Picture tools (`fit`, `caption`, `overlay`, `graphics`, `color`, `export`, `look`) refuse an audio file with "input has no video stream" instead of inventing a picture. `scenes.py` measures an audio file (`audio_only: true`, one scene): `--beats`, `--audio-peaks`, `--speech` and `--highlights` run on the sound, and `--sheet` / `--shots` are refused. ## Built for agents ### What is SPEC? **SPEC** (Self-Producing Execution Contract) is the name this project's author, [kajisho5](https://github.com/kajisho5), gave the pattern the tool layer is built on: each tool's `input_schema` — the part of its contract that has to track the CLI exactly, flag for flag — is never hand-authored side by side with the code. It is derived, at run time, from the one thing that has to be correct for the CLI to work at all: the script's own `argparse` parser. Concretely, `scripts/_contract.py`'s `_capture_parser()` imports every tool script and intercepts its `parse_args()` call to get the live, fully-built parser object — flags, types, choices, defaults, required/positional, mutually exclusive groups, all of it. `input_schema` is built straight from that object. (The rest of a `ToolSpec` — `role`, `capabilities`, `inputs`, `outputs`, `output_schema` — comes from a hand-authored table, `TOOL_META`, since those facts aren't things a parser can express; only `input_schema` is parser-derived.) - **The contract**'s `input_schema` for every tool is generated from the live parser directly. - **SKILL.md is two-tier** (1.11.0): the file the agent loads every session keeps the workflow, the request→script table and one line per gotcha; the long-form detail lives in `references/gotchas.md` and the other `references/` files, read only when a job needs it. - **The MCP server** (`mcp/server.py`) carries no schema of its own; `tools/list` is translated straight from the contract, `input_schema` included. - **The docs** (`docs/contract.md`'s field reference, this README's tool table) describe the same shape. `tests/test_contract.py` runs on every CI run and fails the build if any of them drift out of sync with what the code actually does — it catches drift, it doesn't fix it for you. So adding a flag to a script's `argparse` block updates `input_schema` and the MCP tool definition with no second edit, and a docs page or `TOOL_META` entry that falls behind fails CI rather than drifting silently. There is no separate `input_schema` file to forget to update. ### Machine-readable contract ```bash npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json # or: python3 scripts/_contract.py --json npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json --static # without environment detection npx ffmpeg-skill contract --json --tool cut # one tool's entry under `tools` (repeatable): ~60 KB, not ~950 KB ``` The contract is generated from the code that runs, not maintained beside it. For each of the 42 tools (`ffmpeg-skill/`) it states: | Field | Meaning | |---|---| | `input_schema` | generated from the tool's argparse parser: properties, types, enums, defaults, required, positional order, mutually exclusive groups | | `output_schema` | what `--json` prints: `status`, `output`, `commands`, `probe`, `output_identity` (`{size, mtime_ns}` of the file written, on every tool but `probe`), plus tool-specific fields (`precision`, `checks`, `offset_seconds`, …) | | `role` | `analysis`, `analysis_and_execution`, `execution` or `verification` | | `capabilities` | the FFmpeg encoders, filters and bitstream filters the tool always needs, and the ones needed only for a flag or input | | `supports_dry_run`, `supports_json`, `supports_json_brief` | measured by the tests, not declared | | `verification` | which tools to run on the output afterwards (`probe`, `check`, `look`) | | `requires_visual_verification` | the picture changed; inspect the contact sheet | | `audio_only`, `video_required` | whether an audio-only input is accepted or refused | | `mutates_input` | always `false` | | `stability` | `stable` for the 12 core tools, `beta` for the other 30 (since 4.0.0) | | `idempotency_hint` | `bit_exact`, `content_equivalent`, `cached` or `environment_dependent` | Next to the tool list the document carries a top-level `deprecated` list (since 1.10): what the next major removes, since when, the replacement and the surface it lives on. It is empty in 3.0.0: Python 3.9 and FFmpeg 5.x, the two 2.x entries, moved to `removed` with what 2.0 removed, and `docs/contract.md` "What 2.0 changed" and "What 3.0 changed" are written from that. `contract_version` (2.0) is separate from the skill version, so a consumer can pin the shape and read the version for provenance. The document also states the invocation mapping (structured arguments → argv), the JSON shapes for success and failure (`{"status": "failed", "error": {"kind": "input | ffmpeg | output | missing_tool | timeout | verification | interrupted", "message": …}}`; a refusal adds `error.reason`, a stable code such as `output_exists` or `plan_inputs_changed`, and `error.details`, the facts behind it; warnings, fallbacks and skipped steps a run decided on its own are in `diagnostics`), and that no tool runs a shell or executes anything other than the named script, `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe`. Field-by-field reference: [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md). ### MCP ```json {"mcpServers": {"ffmpeg-skill": {"command": "python3", "args": ["/Users/you/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/mcp/server.py"]}}} ``` On Windows, `python3` is only on PATH if Python was installed from the Microsoft Store; a python.org install exposes `python` (or the `py` launcher) instead — if your MCP client reports the server failed to start, change `"command"` above to `"python"` (or the full path from `where python`). `mcp/server.py` is a stdio JSON-RPC transport with no tool table of its own. `tools/list` is derived from the contract at start-up, in contract order, with `inputSchema` translated from each tool's `input_schema`. By default it lists only the core 12 (`render`, `look`, `caption`, `export`, `check`, `fit`, `cut`, `audio`, `loudness`, `graphics`, `silence`, `probe`) so a client doesn't pay context for 30 schemas it rarely calls directly; set `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1` to list all 42. Every tool, listed or not, is callable through `tools/call`, which maps structured arguments to argv and runs the named script; a raw `argv` form is accepted for compatibility and marked non-canonical. `python3 mcp/server.py --list` prints the tools; `--call probe '{"inputs": ["a.mp4"]}'` runs one from the shell. No `inputSchema` lists `json` or `progress`: they are transport flags the server sets itself, not tool arguments (2.0; 1.x listed them unless `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_LEAN=1`). A client that still sends them is not refused. To receive encode progress during `tools/call`, send a string or integer in `params._meta.progressToken`. The server sends `notifications/progress` with that token and the current FFmpeg step's percent and ETA when available. The final tool result still arrives separately. Dry runs and calls without a token return their results without progress notifications. A structured value is never read as an option: one that starts with `-` (overlay text `-50%`) is passed as `--flag=value`, and positionals that start with `-` follow `--`. `probe`, `check` and `cropdetect` are annotated `readOnlyHint` and write no file over MCP (their `plan` is refused, structured or in a raw `argv`); every other tool is `destructiveHint`, because with `overwrite` it replaces an existing file. See `docs/contract.md` § MCP relationship. The server also advertises a `prompts` capability: five canned workflow recipes an agent can ask for by name instead of composing the individual tool calls itself — `reel`, `podcast`, `multicam`, `delivery_check`, `hdr`. `prompts/list` returns each one's name, description and arguments; `prompts/get {name, arguments}` fills the matching template and returns one text message naming the actual command lines to run and what to check afterward. These are recipes, not new tool calls — every command line a prompt names is one `tools/call` (or the CLI) can already run. For a small editing workflow, set the server's `env` to `{"FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_TOOLS": "probe,cut,fit,export,check"}`. This lists tools to inspect, cut, reframe, export and check a clip. Add `caption` for subtitles or use a recipe from `prompts/list`. Tool names are comma-separated and the response keeps contract order. `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1` takes precedence and lists all tools. Unlisted tools remain callable by name. See the [named list contract](docs/contract.md#default-toolslist-surface-core-12-opt-in-for-all-42). | `tools/list` profile | Measured JSON-RPC response | Rough tokens at 4 bytes per token | | --- | ---: | ---: | | Default 12 | 71.0 kB | 18,000 | | Full 42 | 190.9 kB | 48,000 | | Five-tool editing list above | 24.0 kB | 6,000 | The byte counts include the JSON-RPC envelope and the final newline. Token counts depend on the client and tokenizer. ### Capability detection ```bash npx ffmpeg-skill doctor # human-readable npx ffmpeg-skill doctor --json # available / missing / missing_optional / unknown / detection / errors / tools / gpu_encoders / ffmpeg_security ``` `doctor` reads `ffmpeg -encoders`, `-decoders`, `-filters` and `-bsfs` and resolves every capability the contract declares against this machine's build. Three states per capability: `available`, `missing`, `unknown`. Exit 0 when everything required is available, 1 when something required is missing, 2 when nothing is proven missing but a required capability is unknown. With detection on (the default), `contract --json` carries the same lists under `capabilities`. `doctor` also reports fonts: the default drawtext family, and `fonts.scripts` — one `available`/`missing`/`unknown` per writing system (ja, zh, ko, ar, he, hi, bn, ta, th, lo, ru, el, latin) with the file it would use — so "can this machine render Korean captions" is answered before the job, not after. `doctor --json`'s `tools` field folds that down to one answer per tool — `{"caption": {"usable": "no", "missing": ["filter:subtitles"], "fix": "..."}, ...}` — so "is `doctor` overall `ok`" and "can I run `caption.py` on this machine" are answered separately: a plain Homebrew `ffmpeg` is `ok` for tools that don't need `subtitles`/`drawtext`/`zscale`, while `caption`'s own `usable` is `"no"`. `doctor --json`'s `gpu_encoders` reports which GPU-backed encoders (`nvenc`, `videotoolbox`, `qsv`, `vaapi`, `amf`) this ffmpeg *build* was compiled with — read from `-encoders` alone, so it proves the capability shipped, not that the GPU/driver on this machine will actually accept a job (that needs a real encode, which `doctor`'s introspection never runs). It never affects `ok` or any tool's `usable`. The one GPU path a tool uses is Apple VideoToolbox, opt-in: `--hw` on every re-encoding tool (h264/hevc/prores on the GPU, AV1 stays on SVT-AV1), `FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1` to make it this machine's default for everything except `export.py`'s delivery presets (those take `--hw` explicitly, or `render.py --hw` for a whole project). It runs only on Apple Silicon and never by default, except on a build with no `libx264`/`libx265` (an LGPL ffmpeg that has only `h264_videotoolbox`/`hevc_videotoolbox`): there it is the only encoder, so every re-encoding tool and `export.py`'s presets use it without `--hw`, the result says `hw.source: "auto"`, and `doctor` lists the missing x264/x265 under `covered_by` instead of calling the tools unusable (`--no-hw` still asks for the CPU). It falls back to the CPU encoder — reported in the result's `hw.fallback`/`hw.notes` — only when VideoToolbox itself refuses a job (any other ffmpeg failure is reported as it happened, not retried); every result names the `encoder` that actually ran (`batch.py`, which encodes nothing itself: each `results` row), and a GPU encode adds a `notes` line that its quality is not CRF-equivalent. Measured on an M4 Max, 2–7× faster than x264/x265 `medium`; at matched SSIM (`tests/bench_vt.py`) 1.1–2.9× the bytes on SDR and 1.9–3.5× on HDR, which is why it is a flag and not the default (`docs/design-decisions.md`). `doctor --json`'s `hw` says whether this machine can run it (`platform_ok`) and whether it is the default here (`default_on`). `doctor` also compares the FFmpeg version with a small, dated table of high-severity FFmpeg CVEs (`doctor --json`'s `ffmpeg_security`; source [ffmpeg.org/security.html](https://ffmpeg.org/security.html), checked 2026-10-22). ffmpeg-skill does not ship FFmpeg, so a decoder bug in the build you have stays yours until you upgrade it. When the version is older than the first upstream release on its branch that carries a fix (today: CVE-2026-8461, the MagicYUV decoder heap write, fixed in 8.0.3, 8.1.2 and 9.0), `doctor` prints one `warning:` line on stderr with the update command and lists it under `ffmpeg_security.warnings`. It is advice, never a failure: `ok`, each tool's `usable` and the exit code do not change. A distribution package (Ubuntu `8.0.1-3ubuntu2`, Debian `+deb13u1`) may carry the fix as a backport under the old version number, so the line says the build is older than the fix, not that it is vulnerable. A version it cannot read (a git snapshot such as `N-12345-g…`) gets no warning, and nothing is fetched: the table ships with the skill. ## Gotchas and best practices The short list for humans. The agent-facing version, with the reasoning, is the "Things that look right but are wrong" and "Gotchas" sections of [SKILL.md](SKILL.md). - **Variable frame rate (phone and screen recordings).** `probe.py` flags it; every re-encoding tool conforms to a constant rate automatically. `cut.py` samples the frame timing before a copy and switches to frame-accurate mode when it is variable or too short to judge, because copy-cuts on VFR land on the wrong frame (`--vfr-guard average` restores 2.x's rule, re-encoding whenever the nominal and average rates differ; `--vfr-guard off` keeps the copy). Choose the rate yourself with `fit.py input.mp4 --fps 30` when the measured average is odd. - **Lossless cuts snap to keyframes.** A stream-copy cut can start up to one GOP earlier than asked. `cut.py` re-encodes when the snap exceeds 0.5 s (`--tolerance` changes the limit). For a strictly lossless file pass `--tolerance -1` (plus `--vfr-guard off` on a variable-frame-rate source), and expect the cut to land on the nearest earlier keyframe; the JSON result lists them under `nearest_keyframes`. A `--segments` join can still be re-cut: open-GOP video, a later segment of B-frame `.mp4`/`.mov` video that starts between keyframes (start it on a keyframe, or write `.mkv`), or a join that fails its check. A single `.mp4`/`.mov` copy keeps its edit list by default (since 3.0.0), so the picture starts where asked: the keyframe's pre-roll is stored but hidden by an MP4 edit list, which a player that ignores edit lists shows (`--no-edit-list` starts the file at the keyframe instead). - **Frame-exact without re-encoding the whole cut (H.264).** `cut.py --smart` re-encodes only from each cut point to the next keyframe and copies the GOPs between, matched to the source's profile, level, pixel format, B-frame depth and colour tags. It checks the result against the source (frame grid, copied packets, decoded frames). A source it cannot match (HEVC, 10-bit, interlaced, VFR, open GOPs) is re-encoded in full, and `smart.reason` says why. `probe.py --keyframes-near T` shows where the keyframes are. - **HDR stays HDR.** When the probe reports HDR (HDR10, HLG, Dolby Vision, BT.2020), the tools keep it rather than flatten it. Convert deliberately with `color.py --to-sdr` before H.264 deliverables or LUT work. `export.py` platform presets are SDR and warn on HDR input. - **Loudness targets.** −14 LUFS / −1 dBTP for YouTube and social platforms (the `loudness.py` default), `-I -16 --tp -1.5` for podcasts, `-I -23` for broadcast. A clip measured at −40 LUFS or below is room tone, not content; raising it raises the noise. Check true peak as well as LUFS: `check.py file --platform podcast` measures both. - **Alpha is kept only when asked, and a lost alpha is not verified.** The re-encoding tools write opaque H.264 by default. On a source whose alpha is used (ProRes 4444, QuickTime Animation, PNG, VP9 with alpha), `color.py`, `graphics.py` and `overlay.py` take `--keep-alpha` (ProRes 4444 by default, `--alpha-codec qtrle|png|vp9`, `--alpha-mode straight|premultiplied`) and read the alpha back; without it the result says `verified: false` with a failing `alpha` step, and `--drop-alpha` records that an opaque output is wanted. `background.py --transparent` makes the canvas to draw graphics on. - **Broadcast legal levels are measured, not assumed.** `check.py final.mxf --levels ebu-r103` (or `bt709`) counts every luma and chroma sample outside the legal range and FAILs when one frame has more than 1 % out (`--levels-tolerance`); the JSON `levels` adds min/max Y/U/V per `--levels-window`. `color.py --correct --legalize ebu-r103` clamps after the 4:2:0 conversion and measures what the encode left: a lossy encoder can push a few samples around a clamped edge back out, so the result says how many. - **Frame changes first, text second.** Captions and overlays burned before a crop or resize end up off-frame. Reframe, then caption. - **Cropping 16:9 to 9:16 discards 70 % of the width.** `fit.py --fit crop` centres by default; pass `--crop-x`/`--crop-y` toward the subject, or pad with `--fit pad --pad-fill blur`. Look at the contact sheet before deciding. - **Phrase-aware caption breaking (1.16).** `caption.py`/`graphics.py --wrap phrase` (the default) never breaks inside a word or on the wrong side of a hyphen, never leaves a lone digit, kana or punctuation pair on a line, prefers Japanese sentence ends and particles over a mid-word break, and never ends a line on an article or preposition. All four are penalties over break positions that already fit, so no line is widened and the line count never changes; `--wrap measured` restores 1.15's width-only wrap. The text itself is never rewritten or shortened. Since 1.16.1 a Thai run and a katakana word are never broken inside (Thai writes no space inside a phrase and there is no dictionary: the break goes where you put a space or `|`), and a line wider than the safe width is reported as `overlong` with the fix named. - **Caption size fitted to the cue (1.17, reachable from the templates since 1.17.1).** At a platform caption size a line holds about six em, so an ordinary sentence needs four lines and `--max-lines 2` used to cut it into consecutive cues — half the sentence arriving late. `caption.py --fit-size` (default `auto`) walks the size down until every cue fits, *before* laying the cues out, with a legibility floor of 4.5 % of the frame height (`--min-size`, default 13 ASS units). An explicit `--size` or a `brand.json` size is a statement about the look and is never overridden — which in 1.17.0 also silenced the fitter on every `render.py --template` run, since a template fills the size from the platform table; 1.17.1 marks that size as the default it is (`"fit_size": "on"` in the filled project), so the type shrinks and no cue is split. `--fit-size off` restores that earlier behaviour byte for byte, and the caption text is still never rewritten to make it fit. - **Beat-synced cuts (1.17).** `scenes.py --beats` reports the measured grid — tempo, beat times, and a confidence built from how far the winning autocorrelation lag stands above the others and how many onsets land on it. `cut.py --snap beats` (and a `"snap"` block in a `render.py` project) moves in/out points to the nearest beat within `--snap-tolerance` — and only onto the grid points a measured onset actually marks, never onto the regular grid's continuation through a passage with no music in it. Below `--min-confidence` it **refuses**: a cut point may move to a measured beat and may not appear from one, so speech and ambience get an honest "no steady pulse here" instead of an invented grid. A music bed is measured as it is delivered, WAV/FLAC/MP3 with no picture; on a synthetic click track at 90 and 120 BPM every beat is within 1 ms (WAV/FLAC) or 9 ms (MP3) of its click, `tests/test_analysis.py` holds it to 20 ms. - **Filler words (1.17).** `silence.py --filler --words transcript.json` removes "um" and "uh" through the same cut graph the silences use. Never without measured word timings — there is no heuristic that finds an "um" without them that would not also cut real speech — and `like`, `tipo` and `cioè` are deliberately not in the built-in lists, because a discourse marker is a content word. Built-in lists since 2.19: English, Japanese, Korean, Chinese, Spanish, German, French, Portuguese, Italian, Dutch, Polish, Russian and Turkish; any other language takes `--filler-words FILE`. Whisper stays optional: `--transcribe` with no engine installed refuses and names the five installs. - **Throughput (1.17).** `batch.py --jobs N` runs several files at once, capped at `min(N, cpu_count, 8)` and sharing one `--timeout` budget rather than one per item; the per-item table keeps its order. `render.py --cache DIR` reuses stages whose inputs and arguments did not change, so swapping an export preset re-runs export only. The cache is opt-in with no default directory, and the ffmpeg, skill and contract versions are part of every key, so a cache is never reused across them. - **Audiogram (1.16).** `waveform.py --image cover.png` (or `render.py --template audiogram`) puts the waveform over a still plate for an episode that has no picture, with `--platform` for the frame, `--title` and burnt-in captions. The image is a local file you give: nothing is fetched and no cover art is ever invented. - **Cut review.** `waveform.py clip.mp4 --at 12.4 --window 2 -o cut.png` marks the chosen cut time on a waveform PNG. Repeat `--at` for numbered images and use the exported cut's own time coordinates when inspecting the edited file. - **Emoji in captions and titles (1.15).** `caption.py`/`graphics.py --emoji-assets DIR` composites a PNG per emoji (Twemoji naming, `1f389.png`, or Noto's `emoji_u1f389.png`) on top of the text, because drawtext cannot load a colour emoji font at all and an installed one does not prove libass will draw it in colour — `doctor --json`'s `fonts.emoji` answers that from a render probe. Without assets the result's `emoji.mode` says which of three things happened: `color` when this build's libass draws the colour glyph (also for `--emoji mono` on such a build, with a warning), `mono` when it draws a monochrome one, and `none` when the emoji are left out of the text: with an `emoji_not_drawn` warning when that happened because nothing here draws the glyph, and with only an info line when `--emoji none` asked for it (and a `graphics.py` title that is nothing but emoji is refused). Nothing is ever downloaded. - **Indic and Thai text shaped correctly in titles and lower-thirds (1.15).** `graphics.py` renders Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Thai and Lao through libass automatically (`text_renderer: "ass"`), because drawtext never reorders matras or re-clusters marks; Arabic and Hebrew were already correct on a fribidi build. `--text-render drawtext` with such a script is refused, never rendered wrongly. - **Non-Latin text picks a font by script (1.12).** Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Hebrew, Devanagari, Thai, Cyrillic and Greek cues, titles and overlays resolve a font file that covers them automatically, and a machine with no such font fails the job (`kind: input`) instead of rendering boxes. `doctor --json`'s `fonts.scripts` says which languages this machine can render; `--lang ja|ko` disambiguates Han-only text, and `--lang zh-TW` (or `zh-HK`, `zh-Hant`) picks a Traditional Chinese face (2.19); an explicit `--font`/`--font-file` is always kept. - **Silence detection finds nothing?** The default threshold is −35 dBFS. The tool prints a hint with the track's measured level; raise the threshold (`silence.py --threshold -25`) or shorten `--min-silence`. - **Sync results carry a confidence.** Below 0.3, or an offset near the edge of the analysis window, is probably wrong: enlarge `--analyze-seconds` or find a clap. Recordings over ten minutes from separate devices need `sync.py --fix-drift`. - **Odd file names and unusable inputs are named, not passed to ffmpeg.** A still called `a%20b.png` or `logo%d.png` is read as that one file; a relative subtitle, LUT or font path with a colon works (`--srt ./a:b.srt`); an input whose name starts with `-` is read as a file (give it after `--` or as `./-name.mp4`). An input that is empty, a directory, not media or not readable by the user is refused with its own `error.reason` (`input_empty`, `input_is_directory`, `input_not_media`, `input_permission_denied`) and a hint; an output extension this FFmpeg build has no muxer for (`out.xyz`) is refused before anything runs (`output_extension_unknown`), dry runs included. - **Outputs are never overwritten silently.** An existing output path is refused (`kind: input`, `error.reason: output_exists`, before anything runs); pass `--overwrite` where a replacement is intended. - **Nothing happens silently.** A refusal names its `error.reason` and `error.details`; a stale output lock taken over, a run without a lock, a plan input nobody could fingerprint, a fallback (an odd-sized frame scaled to even, a substituted font, libaom for SVT-AV1), a skipped step and every warning are recorded in `diagnostics` and on stderr (codes: `json_output.diagnostic_codes`); tools that draw text name the font face they drew with (`font_used`; libass draws a glyph that face lacks from another, not named). A refused plan and a lock takeover also append a line to an audit log (`.audit.jsonl`, or `render.py --audit-log FILE`). A degraded or partial result says so: `render.py`'s `verified` is every stage's, an unmeasured loudness or a report section that could not be built is a failing verification step, `export.py` reports `trimmed`, `multicam.py`'s `cuts` name the camera rendered, and `batch.py` rows carry the failing step's `error`, `verified`, and a row for every input after Ctrl-C. - **Long masters need a longer `--timeout`.** The default is 1800 s per ffmpeg call, which is there to catch a hang. A full re-encode of an hour of 1080p at the default preset ran past it on a 4-core machine (see [A one-hour recording](#a-one-hour-recording)). Pass `--timeout 0` or a larger value, or `--fast`. Analysis and stream-copy cuts are far below it. - **Long chains belong in a plan.** Three hand-chained re-encodes lose quality and are hard to change; `render.py` runs the whole edit from one JSON file, and `--dry-run` shows every ffmpeg command before anything is written. ## FAQ ### Can I pass raw ffmpeg arguments, or a filter_complex? Each operation is a script whose flags are its argparse parser, and that parser is what `contract --json` and the MCP `inputSchema` are built from. CI fails the build when those drift from the scripts. A caller-supplied filter graph, `-vf` string, or other ffmpeg option is not an argument any script accepts. `doctor` reads `ffmpeg -filters` (and `-encoders`, `-bsfs`) and reports a filter a tool needs before a job runs into it. MCP does accept an `argv` array, and that array is the named script's own CLI flags, still bound to that script: the script's flags, never an ffmpeg command line and never a shell. ### What if I need an option no tool exposes? For immediate use, run FFmpeg directly outside the skill. To request support in the skill, open an issue with the FFmpeg option, the kind of footage it applies to, and the result you need. New options are added as typed flags with tests and appear in the CLI and MCP schemas through the same contract. ### Why 42 tools? Isn't that overkill? One tool per job, because each job promises something different, and the tool measures that promise after the run. `loudness.py` re-measures integrated loudness and true peak. `cut.py` reports how far a cut snapped to a keyframe. `silence.py` returns the ranges it kept. `export.py` checks the preset's maximum length. A value a tool cannot read fails that step as `not_measured`; it does not pass. One tool with a mode flag would need as large a schema, and its checks would be vaguer. An agent does not read 42 schemas. Over MCP, `tools/list` advertises the core 12 (bold below). The other 30 are called by name through `tools/call` when a job needs one, and `FFMPEG_SKILL_MCP_FULL=1` lists all 42. The groups are the ones in [Tools](#tools). | Group | MCP default / all | Tools | |---|---|---| | Analysis and inspection | 2 / 3 | **probe**, **look**, scenes | | Editing | 3 / 24 | **cut**, **fit**, **silence**, join, crop, cropdetect, deinterlace, denoise, redact, sphere, straighten, insert, background, reverse, stabilize, sequence, waveform, freeze, pad, speedramp, loop, broll, metadata, grid | | Audio | 2 / 3 | **audio**, **loudness**, sync | | Picture | 2 / 4 | **caption**, **graphics**, overlay, color | | Delivery | 2 / 4 | **export**, **check**, proxy, report | | Orchestration | 1 / 4 | **render**, batch, multicam, verify | | **Total** | **12 / 42** | | Without the other 30, an agent writes raw ffmpeg for those jobs, and a mistake there often still exits 0: - `stabilize.py` runs vidstab in two passes, and the second pass needs the first pass's transforms file. - `color.py` builds the HDR-to-SDR chain. With a wrong colour tag the run still finishes, and the picture comes out washed out. - `join.py` puts transitions between clips that differ in size, frame rate or audio layout. Done by hand, those clips have to be normalised first or xfade fails. - `sync.py` and `multicam.py` find the offset between two recordings by audio cross-correlation. No ffmpeg filter measures it. Every command a tool records as run is in its `--json` `commands` (`batch.py` lists none of its steps' commands, and a measurement pass is listed only where the tool records it), shell-quoted so it can be pasted and run again, except a line that names a file the tool wrote for the run and removed when it exited (such as a concat list, an ffmetadata file, a drawtext text file, a two-pass log or a stage's intermediate), and `--dry-run` on a writing tool prints the commands without writing the output (some dry runs still run a measurement, and `verify.py` ignores `--dry-run`: see below). In the 100-prompt agent eval (1.17.0, [Tested on real footage](#tested-on-real-footage)) the agent made no raw ffmpeg calls and reported no false successes. ### What does `verified` check, and what can it not tell me? `verified` covers what can be measured from the file. Each tool measures its output again: the probe (the file opens, its duration, codecs, size and frame rate) and the tool's own promise. For example, loudness and true peak after `loudness.py` or `export.py`, the length against the asked one, and for `cut.py`, `join.py` and `export.py` the stream count, where picture and sound end, and whether both ends of every stream decode. `check.py` grades a file against a platform's limits. A value that cannot be read fails its step as `not_measured`; it does not pass. It cannot tell you whether the result looks or sounds right, and the result says so: every writing tool lists the properties it did not measure in `unverified`. Examples are `picture_content` (what is in the frame), `subject_framing` after a reframe, `rendered_placement` and `legibility` of captions and titles, `grade_look` after a colour conversion, `removed_span_content` after a silence cut (whether a removed span held speech), `mix_balance` and `lip_sync`. For those, look at frames with `look.py` (a contact sheet, or `--safe` for a platform's UI zones) and listen where the result points you. `silence.py` lists the level at every cut, and `cut_warnings` names the cuts that may have landed in a breath or a word's tail. For a single-file video delivery other than GIF, the call fails if an expected picture or audio stream is missing, the video codec (for an editing master also its profile and pixel format), dimensions or fixed frame rate differ from the preset, or the output exceeds a duration or file size limit. The written file stays available for diagnosis. When a platform preset specifies loudness, a failed loudness check marks the export unverified so the caller can decide whether to normalize or retry. `check.py --content` looks for black frames, freezes, flashes, silence and audio dropouts where the relevant stream exists. Review WARN rows for checks that could not measure a property. Delivery templates run these checks on the written file by default. A single-template render includes the rows in `check.checks` when it reaches the check stage. A dry run records `check_dry_run` and leaves `check` null. A real check adds decode time. For an intentional exception, fill the template with `--write-project` and set `"check": {"platform": "...", "content": false}` in the project before rendering. After a failed check, choose a new output or pass `--overwrite` to intentionally replace the retained file. JSON `commands` records the render's FFmpeg command lines. A single-template render lists content-check commands in `check.commands`. A social pack reports a verdict per output. Run `check.py FILE --platform NAME --content` on an individual file for its full rows and commands. For separate recordings, `sync.py` measures audio offset. Use `--fix-drift` to also request a drift measurement, which may be unavailable for short or low-confidence recordings. Review lip sync by watching and listening to the delivered file. When a real export fits video into a preset frame, `picture` gives the rectangle for pad, blur fill or crop if the measurement succeeds. If it fails, the report carries `measured: false` and a reason. A project render carries its fit and export reports in `stage_pictures` and the final framing report in `picture` when available. Dry runs omit both fields. A contact sheet surveys one file. To inspect a cut's first frame, put the requested source position beside the output start with `python3 scripts/look.py source.mp4 --at 12.5 --compare cut.mp4 --compare-at 0 -o start.png`. Open the PNG to check the two frames. For several cuts, pair the source in-points with their positions in the output by repeating both time flags. ### How do I finish a vertical crop for Reels? On a 1920×1080 source, the first command below centre-crops to **608×1080**. The Reels preset scales it to the **1080×1920** delivery frame and applies audio correction if required. To do the whole delivery in one project, use `render.py --template reels`. ```bash python3 scripts/fit.py source.mp4 --aspect 9:16 --fit crop -o vertical.mp4 python3 scripts/export.py vertical.mp4 --preset reels -o reels.mp4 python3 scripts/check.py reels.mp4 --platform reels ``` When an export returns a `loudness` block, `lufs` is the written file's reading, or `null` if unavailable. `loudness.normalized` records whether export applied correction. `loudness.ok` is true or false when the target can be evaluated, and `null` when it cannot. Since 4.0.0 a platform preset corrects a miss by default (`--no-normalize` measures and reports only, as 3.x did); with `--no-normalize`, use the `loudness.py` command in the warning. A silent track needs usable source audio before its level can be corrected. ### Are silence removal and captions stable? They are the most used tools here, and they are tested on every pull request and every push to `main` on Linux, macOS and Windows, with FFmpeg 6.1 to 9. On 20 test files with known gaps, `silence.py` missed none and left at most 1 ms of silence (see [Tested on real footage](#tested-on-real-footage)). A cut keeps `--margin` seconds of air on each side, 0.2 s by default; raise it to 0.3 s for a speaker who trails off. `--speech-aware` keeps the short breaths inside a sentence. Filler words are removed only from measured word timings (`--words` or a local `--transcribe`), never guessed. `--timemap` writes where each kept and removed range sits in the source and the output, for re-timing subtitles. If `--threshold` is set high enough to cut into a breath or a weak word ending, the result warns at that cut. `caption.py` burns SRT/ASS or muxes them as soft tracks, fits the size to the platform's safe area, and picks a font that covers the script (Japanese, Chinese, Korean, Arabic, Thai, Hindi and others). It needs FFmpeg's `subtitles` filter (libass); `doctor` reports whether this build has it. Placement and legibility are listed as `unverified`, so look at a contact sheet before delivering. Speech-to-text runs on a local engine you install; its first run may download a model. #### Vietnamese captions Check `doctor --json` → `fonts.scripts.vi` for Vietnamese font coverage. Use `caption.py input.mp4 --srt vi.srt --lang vi` to burn reviewed UTF-8 captions. The font lookup also recognizes common Vietnamese accents in unlabelled cues. For local speech recognition, use `caption.py input.mp4 --transcribe --lang vi --engine faster-whisper --model base`. Use a multilingual Whisper model and review its transcript before delivery. The Vietnamese regression tests cover font selection and burn-in from SRT. ### Which engine provides word timestamps for karaoke? With `caption.py --transcribe --karaoke`, the speech engine supplies word timestamps for the highlights. In `--engine auto`, eligible English speech can use Parakeet first. Auto prefers Whisper engines in this order: whisper.cpp, faster-whisper, OpenAI Whisper. An engine's failure can stop automatic selection, for example when the language is known and whisper.cpp fails to produce word timings. Use `--engine` to select an engine explicitly and `--model` to choose a model. Some engines download the selected model on first use. Whisper.cpp needs a local model file. Run `doctor --json` and inspect `speech_engines` for Whisper startup checks and errors. The faster-whisper entry includes the installed PyAV version when readable. Startup checks run without loading a model. Model availability and word timestamps are checked when you transcribe. ### How well does HDR to SDR work, and what should I watch for? `color.py --to-sdr` converts PQ (HDR10), HLG and iPhone Dolby Vision 8.4 to SDR BT.709 with real tone mapping (`zscale` and `tonemap`, `hable` by default; `mobius`, `reinhard`, `clip`, `linear` and `gamma` with `--tonemap`). BT.2020 footage on an SDR transfer gets a gamut conversion only. Watch for four things: - It needs `zscale` (libzimg). The plain Homebrew `ffmpeg` lacks it, so use `ffmpeg-full` (keg-only: see [Install](#install) for putting it on `PATH`); `doctor` reports whether it is there. - `--peak` (default 1000 nits) is the PQ source's brightest level, the one that becomes SDR white: set it to how bright the source was mastered (its MaxCLL or mastering peak). Too high dims the picture; too low clips the highlights. HLG always peaks at 1000 nits, so `--peak` does not apply to it. - Tone mapping is a judgement, and the result says so (`grade_look` in `unverified`). Compare frames with `look.py`, and try another `--tonemap` if skin or skies look off. - An HDR source that only needs to play everywhere may not need converting at all. `--strip-dovi` removes the Dolby Vision layer from an iPhone clip, keeping its HLG picture, with a stream copy. ### How does ffmpeg-skill compare with Remotion? ffmpeg-skill edits footage you already have, on this machine, with FFmpeg tools whose flags are a machine-readable contract (`contract --json`). Remotion renders a video from React components. They complement each other: this repository does not call Remotion, and a file Remotion writes is an ordinary input (`probe.py`, `cut.py`, `fit.py`, `export.py`, `check.py`). [`remotion-ffmpeg-skill`](https://github.com/kajisho5/remotion-ffmpeg-skill) joins the two. It measures the footage with this repo, draws the graphics in Remotion from those measurements, and checks and delivers the result with this repo again. Install both (`npx ffmpeg-skill`, then `npx remotion-ffmpeg-skill`). As with the other skills, the dependency runs one way: it calls these tools, and nothing here calls it. HyperFrames renders a video from HTML and is the same kind of neighbour: a file it writes is an ordinary input too. ### Does it validate the filter graph before running? No. `--dry-run` prints the ffmpeg command a writing tool would run and does not start ffmpeg, so ffmpeg never parses that filter graph. ffprobe still runs when the tool probes an input that exists. Unless `--overwrite` is passed, an existing output is refused (`kind: input`) before ffmpeg. An output that is the same file as an input is refused either way. No media file is written, and `verified` is false; `--plan FILE` does write the plan JSON. A path that is not on disk yet is not measured: the probe is a stub (0×0, duration 0), so a number taken from it is not a measurement. A plan is not a promise of the outcome: `cut.py`'s plan of a stream copy names in `possible_reencode_reason` what a real run may still re-encode it for (`tolerance`: where the copy lands is measured from the written file). A real `render.py` run starts with its own dry run, so when that dry run is refused because a stage needs a filter or an encoder the build lacks, the real run is refused the same way before the first stage encodes. The measuring tools (`probe`, `check`, `sync`, `multicam`, `scenes`, `cropdetect`, `report`, `silence`, `loudness`, `stabilize`) still run their measurements; only the artifact is skipped, and `silence` with `--transcribe` (with `--filler` or a sentence flag) also runs the speech engine, which may download a model. `overlay` measures the lines of a multi-line `--text` with one drawtext on a generated frame on FFmpeg 8.0, 8.0.1 and 8.1.0, where it draws them one by one. `metadata` with `--auto-chapters` and `cut` with `--snap beats` decode the input for their measurement, and `render` and `batch` run each stage or step as its own dry run, so a measuring stage measures an input that exists; a stage or an item a real run would serve from its cache is not run, as the real run does not run it (`render`'s `cache.would_hit`; `batch`'s row `cached: true`, with what the run that stored it measured and verified). `verify` accepts `--dry-run` and ignores it: its steps run, and its document says `dry_run: false`. `--plan FILE` is that dry run written down — the planned argv, the command lines, and a fingerprint of each existing input (size, plus a sha256 of the first and last 8 MiB). `render.py` and `verify.py` refuse `--plan`. `render.py FILE` runs a plan only when those fingerprints still match (a mismatch is refused with each input's expected and actual fingerprint in `error.details`, and logged to `.audit.jsonl`), by running the tool again with the planned argv, not by executing the recorded ffmpeg lines; `--dry-run` on that run only prints them. `doctor` reports whether the filters, encoders and bitstream filters the contract names are in this build (`ffmpeg -filters`, `-encoders`, `-bsfs`) and which fonts are installed. A name in that listing is not a check of the graph this command would build, and a listed GPU encoder is not a successful encode. ### Can it remove burned-in subtitles or logos? A rectangle you already know, sitting still for the whole clip, can be filled from the picture around it with `redact.py --mode delogo` (ffmpeg's `delogo` filter). That is a 1 px border blend. It is not inpainting: a logo that moves, or burned-in subtitles whose position changes, is out of scope. The same known box can be obscured instead, with `--mode blur` or `--mode pixelate`. None of the three finds the box. `delogo` also needs the box at least 1 px inside the frame, and it only interpolates 8-bit YUV, so an HDR or 10-bit source is refused until `color.py --to-sdr`. ### Does it auto-track faces or subjects for reframing? `fit.py --fit crop` centres the crop unless you pass `--crop-x` and `--crop-y`. Check `crop_check.review_points` for sampled moments when luma motion or edge detail falls outside the kept window. Use `look.py OUTPUT --at TIME` with an indicated `output_time_estimate` to inspect one. `crop.py` cuts the rectangle you pass. `cropdetect.py --motion-centre` reports where motion sat each second. `sphere.py` points a 360 view where you aim it. Subject framing still needs visual review. ### Does it encode on the GPU? The encode path a tool will actually take is Apple VideoToolbox, for h264, hevc and prores, and only on Apple Silicon. `--hw` asks for it on that call. `FFMPEG_SKILL_HW=1` makes it the default for every re-encoding tool except `export.py`'s delivery presets, which take `--hw` on their own (or `render.py --hw` for a whole project). AV1 stays on SVT-AV1. nvenc, QSV, VAAPI and AMF are reported by `doctor --json`'s `gpu_encoders` when the ffmpeg build was compiled with them, and no tool encodes with them. One build is the exception to opt-in: with no `libx264` and no `libx265`, and with `h264_videotoolbox` or `hevc_videotoolbox`, those encodes use VideoToolbox without `--hw` and the result says `hw.source` is `"auto"`. `--no-hw` still asks for the CPU encoder. A VideoToolbox job the hardware refuses is re-encoded on the CPU and the result says so (`hw.fallback`). ## FFmpeg compatibility The tools need FFmpeg 6.1 or later and Python 3.10 or later (standard library only). 3.0.0 removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9: every tool refuses an `ffmpeg`/`ffprobe` whose version reads as older than 6.1 (`kind: missing_tool`, `error.reason: ffmpeg_unsupported`; a git build whose version is not a release number is not refused), and `doctor` lists an unsupported FFmpeg or Python under `unsupported` with `ok: false`. What CI actually exercises on every pull request is FFmpeg 6.1 (Ubuntu 24.04 apt), 7.1 (Debian trixie apt), 8.x (macOS Homebrew), 9.x (Windows gyan.dev) and 8.0.1 (Ubuntu 26.04 apt), on Python 3.10 and 3.13 (the two ends of the supported range). The capability parser has been run against the listings of these builds: | FFmpeg | `-filters` row layout | Source | |---|---|---| | 6.1.1 | three flag characters: `..C acompressor A->A` | Ubuntu 24.04 apt, captured | | 7.1.x | same as 6.x | Debian trixie apt in a CI container (plus a constructed fixture in tests/) | | 8.1.2 | two flag characters: `TS aap AA->A`, three-character legend, `------` separator | Homebrew on the macOS CI runner, captured | | 9.0.1 | same as 8.x, CRLF | gyan.dev build on the Windows CI runner, captured | FFmpeg 8 shortened the flag column of `ffmpeg -filters`. A parser anchored on the old width matches nothing on FFmpeg 8 and, if "nothing matched" is read as "nothing installed", reports every filter missing; that is what 0.9.0 did on macOS and Windows. For a long master, pass `--timeout 0` (no limit) or a larger value, or `--fast`, which at the measured rate takes about 16 minutes for the hour. Analysis tools and stream-copy cuts stay far below the limit. ### Plan a long edit or batch 1. Probe the master and make one lightweight copy for review with `python3 scripts/proxy.py master.mp4 --width 640 -o review.mp4`. Use the master for the final cut and check the chosen boundaries on its timeline. 2. Run whole-file analysis once and save the results. For example, `python3 scripts/silence.py master.mp4 --list --json > silence.json` lists the ranges to review. Pass the chosen ranges to `cut.py --segments`. When the delivery uses only selected material, trim before reframing, adding captions, or applying effects. 3. Time a representative segment at the final resolution, codec, and quality to set the export timeout. Watch peak memory across the tool and its FFmpeg children. For a batch, start with `--jobs 1` and increase to `--jobs 2` on the same sample only if throughput improves and the workstation has memory headroom. Each concurrent encode has its own decoder, filter buffers, and encoder threads. A parallel batch shares one timeout across its items. ## Install Where it can be installed from today. Every process finds this one, but `brew doctor` warns about a linked keg-only formula, and an upgrade of the lean `ffmpeg` has been seen to link the lean build back on top without a message. After upgrading, check that `command -v ffmpeg` still resolves into `ffmpeg-full`, and re-run the link if it doesn't. ### Updating Releases are frequent (often several a week), and nothing updates by itself: the tools never go online, so a copy stays at the version you installed until you replace it. ```bash grep '"version"' ~/.claude/skills/ffmpeg-skill/package.json # the version installed (Cursor: ~/.cursor/skills, Codex: ~/.agents/skills) npm view ffmpeg-skill version # the latest release npx ffmpeg-skill@latest setup # replace every installed copy with the latest claude plugin update # when installed as a Claude Code plugin ``` `npx ffmpeg-skill@4.1.3` installs that exact version, for a setup that should not move. Within 4.x an update does not break a call to one of the 12 stable tools (see [Stability](#stability)). ## Requirements - FFmpeg 6.1+ (3.0.0 removed 5.x; an older build is refused). Required by at least one tool (so `doctor`'s `ok` needs them all): `libx264`, `aac`, and the `drawtext`, `subtitles` (libass), `loudnorm`, `xfade`, `acrossfade`, `amix`, `overlay`, `scdet`, `silencedetect`, `cropdetect`, `tile`, `tpad`, `boxblur`, `hqdn3d`, `yadif`, `reverse`, `rotate`, `showwaves`, `v360`, `xstack` and `vidstabdetect`/`vidstabtransform` (libvidstab, `stabilize.py` only) filters; `doctor --json` lists them as `capabilities.required`. Needed only by the flags that use them: `libx265`, `prores_ks`, `libzimg` / `zscale`, `libmp3lame`, `libopus`, `libvorbis`, the `ass` filter. `doctor` tells you which are present. The apt and gyan.dev builds carry all of them; some Homebrew bottles lack `libass` / `libfreetype` / `libzimg`, which `doctor` reports as missing. - Python 3.10+, standard library only (3.0.0 removed 3.9) - Node 16+ only for the `npx` installer `doctor`'s own introspection calls (`ffmpeg -filters`/`-encoders`/`-bsfs`/`-version`) time out after 10s and report `failed` rather than hanging forever — those are meant to be fast. Every tool's actual media-processing `ffmpeg` invocation (cut, fit, caption, ...) runs under `--timeout` (default 1800 s, `FFMPEG_SKILL_TIMEOUT`, `0` = none): past the limit the process is killed, its partial output removed, and the failure reported as `kind: timeout` (exit 124) — a legitimately long `--accurate` re-encode should raise the limit rather than run unbounded. `-nostdin` is always passed, so a hung ffmpeg process waiting on stdin cannot happen. ## Stability 4.x splits the promise by tool: the 12 core tools (`stability: stable` in `contract --json`) keep every tool name, CLI argument, JSON output key and exit code working until 5.0, as every tool did in 3.x; the other 30 (`beta`) may drop or rename an argument or an output key in a minor release after one minor of notice in `deprecated`. The full list of what is promised and what is not, and the three-step deprecation policy, is in [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#stability-guarantee-4x). It is enforced by a test that pins every tool's argument names against a snapshot, so a breaking change fails CI instead of slipping into a patch. Releases are batched: related fixes and features ship together as one version rather than one version per merged pull request, so a dependent project sees fewer, larger steps. Pin a tagged version, not `main`. 2.0.0 made the five changes announced since 1.10.0 -- `--crf` removed in favour of `--quality` (except on `export.py`, whose preset chooses the encoder), an existing output refused without `--overwrite`, `probe`'s `hdr` narrowed to a real HDR signal, `json`/`progress` out of the MCP schema, the `result_v2` preview withdrawn -- listed with what to change in [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-20-changed) and under `removed` in `contract --json`. 3.0.0 is the second break: it removed FFmpeg 5.x and Python 3.9 (announced in 2.14.0 and 2.10.9), made `cut.py` keep an `.mp4`/`.mov` copy's edit list, keep an SDR HEVC source HEVC and use `--vfr-guard sampled` by default (`--no-edit-list`, `--no-keep-hevc` and `--vfr-guard average` restore 2.x), and changed what `cut.py`'s `precision` (now the least exact segment's) and `keyframe_snapped` (now equal to `start_snapped`) mean (`contract_version` 2.0) -- see [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-30-changed). 4.0.0 is the third: it split the promise by tool (above), made `export.py` exit non-zero when a video delivery misses a required property, made `fit.py --duration` ask for `--method` before a retime beyond 1.15x, turned on content checks in the delivery templates, and gave unusable inputs their own `error.reason` -- see [docs/contract.md](docs/contract.md#what-40-changed). ## See [references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md](references/ci-platform-pitfalls.md) for this and other per-OS behaviour differences already diagnosed, before spending a CI cycle re-diagnosing a platform-only failure. **Releasing** is fully automated end to end, including the version number itself — a PR never needs to touch `package.json` or the version in `docs/contract.md`. `CHANGELOG.md` is different: the release writes the version heading and one line per merged PR, but a `feat` PR writes its own notes under `## Unreleased` (CONTRIBUTING.md), and a PR that closes an issue must name that issue in `CHANGELOG.md` or `test_changelog_mentions_every_closed_issue_since_last_tag` fails. Once a PR merges to `main`, `.github/workflows/release.yml` takes it from there: if nobody bumped the version by hand, it resolves the next version with [.github/scripts/resolve_version.py](.github/scripts/resolve_version.py). What that script reads, its rules, their exceptions and the incidents behind them are written once, in its docstring, and `test_release_version_resolver_rules` and `test_release_version_resolver_does_not_depend_on_a_pr_title` pin them; they are not restated here. Most PRs don't need a label added by hand: `release-drafter.yml`'s `autolabel` job applies one automatically from the PR's title/changed files (`Fix ...` → `fix`, `Add ...`/`feat ...` → `feature`, `docs`/`.md`/`.github/`/`build(deps)` changes → `chore`) as soon as it's opened — add a label yourself only to override that. **A major version is never chosen automatically**: no label rule produces `major`, and the workflow refuses to auto-bump across a major boundary even if someone applies that label — a real major release is a deliberate `package.json` bump in a PR, which the manual path below already handles. It bumps `package.json`, `.claude-plugin/plugin.json`, `docs/contract.md` and `docs/roadmap.md`'s released-version sentence, writes a `CHANGELOG.md` section listing those PRs (and any issues they closed), and pushes that commit to `main` itself. If another PR merged while the bump was being prepared, the push is refused and that run releases nothing: the newer merge's own run, queued behind it, starts from `main`'s tip and releases both (the bump is never rebased onto a merge it did not read). After the tag it also asks `pages.yml` to rebuild the site, because the bump commit carries `[skip ci]` and would otherwise leave the site on the previous version. Either way — auto-bumped or hand-bumped in the PR — it then creates the `vX.Y.Z` tag, publishes a GitHub Release with notes extracted from `CHANGELOG.md`'s matching section, and publishes the package to npm. A PR that still wants to write its own version bump and `CHANGELOG.md` prose (e.g. to explain the "why" of a release by hand) can — the automation only fills in when nobody made that call already. A push to `main` with nothing new to release creates no tag, Release or npm publish; its MCP Registry step still asks npm and the registry about `server.json`'s version and publishes the entry only when npm has that version and the registry does not, which is how a later run finishes an entry an earlier one failed to publish. npm publishing needs an `NPM_TOKEN` repo secret (an npm access token with publish rights on this package) — without it the tag and GitHub Release still happen, only the npm step is skipped. A repo that depends on this one (an editing skill, an agent) should pin an `ffmpeg-skill` version by tag or npm version, not by tracking `main` — a merged-but-not-yet-released commit on `main` can be ahead of the last published npm version for the few minutes between merge and this workflow completing. **A version that was tagged but never reached npm** (the npm step failed; a re-run of that release sees the tag and skips the publish) is finished by dispatching the same workflow on its tag: `gh workflow run release.yml --ref vX.Y.Z -f version=X.Y.Z`. That runs only the workflow's `recover` job. It refuses a version that is not `X.Y.Z`, has no tag, or that npm already has, and a run whose commit is not the tagged one: the npm provenance attestation names the run's commit, so it must be the commit the package is built from. It publishes with `--provenance` under the `latest` dist-tag when the version is above every stable (non-prerelease) version npm has, and under `backport` otherwise, so `latest` never moves back. Then it publishes the `plugin` branch when no commit there is for this version and the branch's tip is older, and the MCP Registry entry when the registry does not list the version (never for a `backport`). The GitHub Release is left as it is. A tag cut before the job was added (#448; every tag up to v3.6.3) has no `recover` job at its commit and cannot be recovered this way. repository.readme:
# agent-vitals

**A daily census of the AI agent tooling ecosystem on GitHub: MCP servers, agent
frameworks, skills and the tools around them. It measures which of them are still alive.**

Every awesome-list tells you what was published. None of them tell you what has
been touched since. This repository answers three questions every day, from public
GitHub metadata, and keeps the answers as a time series:

1. How much of the ecosystem is still maintained?
2. How much of it carries a licence you could actually use at work?
3. What appeared, and what went quiet, since yesterday?

## 2026-11-21

- **52,133 repositories** across 13 topic queries in 2 tiers: **mcp** (21,955, 2+ stars), **agents** (30,178, 10+ stars).
- **49.7%** pushed in the last 30 days.
- **5,547 (10.6%) have no licence file at all**, which leaves them under exclusive copyright by default: no permission to use, copy or modify them, whatever the README suggests. A further 4,138 (7.9%) carry a licence GitHub cannot map to a standard identifier. Those are licensed, just not in a way a procurement review waves through.
- Only 10,505 of these repositories are even a year old. Among those, **27.9% have not been pushed since**. The headline 5.6% across the whole index is an artefact of how young this ecosystem is.
- Churn since the previous run: **+269 new**, **-52 gone**.

| slowing | 8,941 | 17.2% | 31-90 days |
| stale | 13,386 | 25.7% | 91-365 days |
| abandoned | 2,934 | 5.6% | no push in over a year |
| archived | 944 | 1.8% | archived by its owner |

## Ask it from an agent

The census is an MCP server too, standard library only, four tools: `lookup` a
repository's status and licence, `search` by words with status and licence
filters, `summary` of the latest run, and the two `candidates` lists.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Keremozdemirra/agent-vitals && cd agent-vitals
claude mcp add agent-vitals -- python3 "$PWD/mcp_server.py"
```

`AGENT_VITALS_REMOTE=1` reads the published index instead of the checkout, so
the clone can stay old. Nothing is written or executed; it answers from
`data/servers.json`.

## Use the data

```bash
curl -sL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Keremozdemirra/agent-vitals/main/data/servers.csv -o servers.csv
```

| File | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `data/servers.json` | Full index, one object per repository, with `first_seen` and `status`. |
| `data/servers.csv` | The same index, flat, for spreadsheets and `pandas.read_csv`. |
| `data/history.csv` | One row per day: totals per status, licence counts, churn. |
| `data/daily/YYYY-MM-DD.json` | That day's snapshot, including which repositories arrived and which went quiet. |
| `data/candidates.csv` | The two acted-on lists from the report: `revive` (quiet, permissive, still asked about) and `contribute` (busy, permissive, with open work). |

Everything is committed, so `git log data/history.csv` is the changelog of the
ecosystem itself.

## Method

- Source: the GitHub REST search API, public repository metadata only. Nothing is
  cloned, downloaded or executed.
- Tiers and their star floors:
  - `mcp` (2+ stars): `topic:mcp-server`, `topic:model-context-protocol`
  - `agents` (10+ stars): `topic:mcp`, `topic:claude-code`, `topic:ai-agents`, `topic:ai-agent`, `topic:agent-skills`, `topic:agentic-ai`, `topic:claude-skills`, `topic:autonomous-agents`, `topic:llm-agents`, `topic:agent-framework`, `topic:llm-tools`
  The MCP topics name one specific thing, so two stars is enough. The broad agent
  topics are also attached to every tutorial and course repository in the field; ten
  stars is where they start describing tools rather than exercises.
- Each query is sliced by star count until every slice fits under GitHub's
  1000-result ceiling, so this is a census rather than a top-1000 sample.
- `status` is derived from `pushed_at` alone. It measures whether a repository is
  being touched, not whether it is good. A finished, correct tool can sit at
  `abandoned` and still work.
- `license_state` is the field that matters. `spdx` means GitHub matched a
  standard licence; `non-standard` means a LICENSE file exists that GitHub reports
  as `NOASSERTION` (n8n's Sustainable Use License, for one); `none` means no
  licence file was detected at all. Only the last of those means "you have no
  permission to use this", and conflating the two would misrepresent projects
  that did license their work.
- A repository leaves the index when it is deleted, renamed, drops below the
  star floor, or has its topic removed. `left_the_index` does not mean `deleted`,
  and this index cannot tell those cases apart.
- Repository descriptions are third-party text. They are stripped of control
  characters, truncated, and escaped at render time.

## What this is not

- **Not a security audit.** Nothing here says a repository is safe or unsafe. The
  fields are dates, counts and licence identifiers: facts from the API. None of
  them judges anyone's code.
- **Not a quality ranking.** Stars measure attention, not merit.
- **Not a recommendation.** Check anything you install yourself.

## What is in here, and whose it is

Nothing in this repository is anyone else's work. No repository is cloned,
downloaded, or copied. Two kinds of thing are published:

1. **Facts from the GitHub API**: name, URL, star and fork counts, creation and
   last-push dates, detected licence identifier, archived flag. Facts about public
   repositories, not expression, and each one links to its source.
2. **The repository's own one-line description**, as its author wrote it, truncated
   and shown next to a link to the original. This is the only third-party text
   here, and it is used the way every package registry and search index uses it.

Everything else (the collector, the renderer, this text, the analysis) was
written for this repository.

- **Code** (`collect.py`, `render.py`, the workflow): MIT.
- **The compilation** (the selection, structure and derived fields in `data/`):
  CC0 1.0. Take it, chart it, fork it, no attribution required.
- **The `description` field**: belongs to whoever wrote it, and is reproduced here
  as a short factual descriptor alongside a link to its source. It is not covered
  by the CC0 grant above, and this index makes no claim over it.
- **The indexed repositories themselves**: their authors', under their own
  licences, which is precisely what this index measures.

# agent-vitals

**A daily census of the AI agent tooling ecosystem on GitHub: MCP servers, agent
frameworks, skills and the tools around them. It measures which of them are still alive.**

Every awesome-list tells you what was published. None of them tell you what has
been touched since. This repository answers three questions every day, from public
GitHub metadata, and keeps the answers as a time series:

1. How much of the ecosystem is still maintained?
2. How much of it carries a licence you could actually use at work?
3. What appeared, and what went quiet, since yesterday?

- **49.7%** pushed in the last 30 days.
- **5,547 (10.6%) have no licence file at all**, which leaves them under exclusive copyright by default: no permission to use, copy or modify them, whatever the README suggests. - Only 10,505 of these repositories are even a year old. Among those, **27.9% have not been pushed since**. The headline 5.6% across the whole index is an artefact of how young this ecosystem is.

## Ask it from an agent

The census is an MCP server too, standard library only, four tools: `lookup` a
repository's status and licence, `search` by words with status and licence
filters, `summary` of the latest run, and the two `candidates` lists.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Keremozdemirra/agent-vitals && cd agent-vitals
claude mcp add agent-vitals -- python3 "$PWD/mcp_server.py"
```

`AGENT_VITALS_REMOTE=1` reads the published index instead of the checkout, so
the clone can stay old. Nothing is written or executed; it answers from
`data/servers.json`.

repository.readme:
# memtomem > Local-first long-term memory for AI coding agents: Markdown files you own, found again with hybrid keyword + semantic search. Core usage is hook-free by default: memory changes happen only when you or your agent call memtomem. [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/memtomem)](https://pypi.org/project/memtomem/) [![Downloads](https://img.shields.io/pypi/dm/memtomem)](https://pypi.org/project/memtomem/) [![GitHub stars](https://img.shields.io/github/stars/memtomem/memtomem)](https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem/stargazers) [![License: Apache 2.0](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-Apache%202.0-blue)](LICENSE) > 🧪 **Beta** — the nine core MCP tools, the `mm` CLI, and the format of your memory and config files change only with an `Upgrading` note in the [CHANGELOG](CHANGELOG.md). Features marked **experimental** can change without one; see [Stability](#stability). Feedback is welcome: [Issues](https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem/issues) · [Discussions](https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem/discussions). ## The session loop Three plugin workflows carry a project's memory from one session to the next, and from one coding agent to another.

Illustrative output — agent wording and results vary. ```text # End of a session, in Claude Code > /memtomem:handoff save codex-cli handoff_id: 3f2a9c1e-7b4d-4e8a-9c2f-1d5e6a7b8c9d scope: project_local · namespace: shared:retry-policy · 1 file written, 2 chunks indexed # Next session, in Codex CLI > $memtomem-brief Recent updates and active handoff IDs - 3f2a9c1e-7b4d-4e8a-9c2f-1d5e6a7b8c9d from claude-code → codex-cli load it with: $memtomem-handoff resume 3f2a9c1e-7b4d-4e8a-9c2f-1d5e6a7b8c9d > $memtomem-handoff resume 3f2a9c1e-7b4d-4e8a-9c2f-1d5e6a7b8c9d git_head matches the live HEAD · worktree clean · in sync with `origin` `refs/heads/main` # After a few commits, back in Claude Code > /memtomem:update mode: incremental · 4 of the latest 10 commits not yet reviewed saved 2 items · commit-derived: 1 · session-derived: 1 ``` `handoff save` writes one Markdown record into the project's own `.memtomem/memories.local`; `brief` only reads; `update` saves decisions, bug fixes, and preferences as separate items. All three run only when you invoke them, and nothing runs in the background. The [Project workflows](docs/guides/project-workflows.md) guide has each one's modes, checks, and host-specific names. ## Why memtomem? - **Your files stay yours.** Memories are plain `.md` files you can read, edit, and version. The search index is rebuilt from them, day-file namespaces included; tag edits and working state live only in the database ([what a rebuild restores](docs/guides/reference.md#what-a-rebuild-restores)). - **Explicit by default.** Memory operations run on your CLI or MCP calls (`mm add`, `mem_add`, `mem_index`). Optional client hooks are separate, removable integrations, not a hidden runtime default. - **One store, many tools.** Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode, Kimi Code, and Antigravity share one local store, and any MCP client can search it. Hermes Agent joins the same store through its [plugin and memory provider](#agent-frameworks), and LangGraph apps get the same search pipeline over a store of their own with [`langchain-memtomem`](packages/langchain-memtomem/). [memtomem-stm](https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem-stm) is a separate, optional proxy that surfaces memories proactively. ## Private by design The memtomem server runs on your machine, and its database and Markdown files stay there. With the defaults (BM25-only search, no LLM, no reranker) the server sends none of your note text anywhere. Some optional providers send text to an outside service, and each one is off until you configure it; a request to a loopback address can still leave your machine if your environment routes HTTP through a proxy or the local server forwards the request to a hosted model. Separately, the MCP tools return note text to the AI client that called them, and memtomem does not control what that client sends to its own model provider. [What leaves your machine](docs/guides/configuration.md#what-leaves-your-machine) lists what each setting sends, when, and where. ## Set it up from your coding agent Paste a prompt into Claude Code, Codex CLI, or another coding agent. The agent runs the [Quick Start](#quick-start) commands for you, asks before the choices that are yours, and shows you the result. **Install and verify:** ```text Install memtomem on this computer by following https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem#quick-start. If a ~/.memtomem folder already exists, memtomem is already set up here: stop and tell me, and change nothing. Otherwise ask me which preset to use (minimal, english, or korean) and which folder should hold my memories, then run `uv tool install --python 3.12 'memtomem[all]'` and `mm init --non-interactive --preset --memory-dir --mcp skip`. Verify with `mm add "memtomem setup check" --file setup-check.md` (pick another file name if that one exists) and a `mm search` that finds it, and show me both outputs. If a command fails, stop and show me the error instead of working around it. Do not edit, move, or delete my existing notes, and do not install any hooks. Finish by telling me which plugin under "Works with" connects this agent. ``` **Something looks wrong:** ```text Check my memtomem setup with read-only commands: run `mm doctor` and `mm memory doctor`, then list each finding with the command that would fix it. Ask me before you run any fix. ``` Prefer to run the commands yourself? The Quick Start below is the same path, step by step. ## Quick Start ### 1. Install ```bash uv tool install --python 3.12 'memtomem[all]' # or: pipx install 'memtomem[all]' mm --version # verify install ``` `--python 3.12` has uv download Python 3.12 when none is installed; without it, uv can pick an older system Python and stop with `No solution found`. `[all]` bundles ONNX dense embeddings, the Korean tokenizer, the code chunker, and the Web UI (about 340 MB installed, before any model download). The Ollama and OpenAI embedding providers need no extra. A smaller install is under [Other install options](#minimal-install) below. ### 2. Setup ```bash mm init # preset picker, then memory_dir + MCP ``` The interactive picker starts with three presets — **Minimal** (BM25, no downloads), **English (Recommended)** (ONNX `multilingual-e5-small` + auto-discover providers), **Korean-optimized** (ONNX `multilingual-e5-small` + `kiwipiepy` tokenizer); no preset turns on a reranker — plus an **Advanced** entry that opens the full 10-step wizard. Preset paths only ask about the memory directory and MCP registration; everything else is set from the preset. Choose **Minimal** for the fastest no-download first proof and rerun `mm init` later to add semantic search. For automation, `mm init --non-interactive` picks the minimal preset without prompts. See [Embeddings](docs/guides/embeddings.md) for the model and provider matrix. The presets keep embedding on your machine; choosing OpenAI embeddings, a cloud LLM, or the Cohere reranker sends note text to that service ([What leaves your machine](docs/guides/configuration.md#what-leaves-your-machine)). ### 3. Verify a complete memory round trip ```bash mm status mm add "Deployment checklist uses blue-green rollout" --tags ops mm search "blue-green" ``` The last command should return the sentence you just added. `mm add` writes to your user memory directory and indexes the entry immediately, so this works without an existing notes directory or a connected editor. To bring existing notes into the same index, run `mm index /path/to/your/notes`. ### 4. Connect your coding agent Install the plugin for your tool — [Claude Code](packages/memtomem-claude-plugin/), [Codex CLI](plugins/memtomem/), [OpenCode](packages/opencode-memtomem/), [Kimi Code](packages/memtomem-kimi-skills/), [Antigravity](packages/memtomem-antigravity-plugin/), or [Cursor](packages/memtomem-cursor-plugin/) — then, in the project you work on, register the memory tier the session loop writes to: ```bash cd && mm mem init --scope project_local ``` Start a new session and run the brief workflow: `/memtomem:brief` in Claude Code, and the name each other host uses is in the [Project workflows](docs/guides/project-workflows.md) guide. The [Claude Code & Codex CLI plugin quickstart](docs/guides/plugin-quickstart.md) ([한국어](docs/guides/vibe-coding-getting-started-ko.md)) walks through plugin installation and a first memory save-and-search round trip in 10–15 minutes. For Windsurf, Claude Desktop, Gemini CLI, other MCP clients, and registering Cursor by hand instead of through the plugin, see [MCP Client Setup](docs/guides/mcp-clients.md); from any client, asking it to call the `mem_status` tool confirms the connection. ### 5. Open the Web UI (optional) ```bash mm web # dashboard on http://127.0.0.1:8080 mm web -b # run in the background; logs go to ~/.memtomem/logs/web.log mm web stop # stop the tracked Web UI process ``` `mm web` shows the polished page set. `mm web --dev` (or `MEMTOMEM_WEB__MODE=dev`) adds maintainer pages such as Sessions, Working Memory, and Health Report.
Other install options **Minimal** (no bundled model, about 50 MB): ```bash uv tool install --python 3.12 memtomem # no extras — no local ONNX model, Web UI or Korean tokenizer until you add them; Ollama/OpenAI embeddings still work ``` Opt in later per feature: `uv tool install --reinstall 'memtomem[onnx,web]'` (see the [extras table](docs/guides/getting-started.md#optional-extras)). List every extra you want to keep, because `--reinstall` replaces the whole set. A plain `mm upgrade` keeps the extras it detects from the current install, but an explicit `mm upgrade --extras` list must name the complete set too. **Project-scoped** (per-project isolation): ```bash uv add 'memtomem[all]' && uv run mm init # all commands need `uv run` prefix ``` **No install** (uvx on demand): ```bash claude mcp add memtomem -s user -e MEMTOMEM_EXTRA_TOOLS=mem_update_coverage -- uvx --python 3.12 --isolated --from "memtomem[all]==0.7.12" memtomem-server ```
Troubleshooting the install - **`mm --version` shows an older version than the [latest release](https://github.com/memtomem/memtomem/releases)** right after installing: `uv` is likely serving cached PyPI metadata. Re-run with `uv tool install 'memtomem[all]' --refresh`, or clear the cache first with `uv cache clean memtomem`. To upgrade an existing uv tool install, use `mm upgrade` rather than re-running `uv tool install`; see the [CLI reference](docs/guides/reference/data-config-cli.md#cli-reference) for what it preserves and stops. - **`mm: command not found`**: `uv tool install` drops the shim into `~/.local/bin`, which is not on `$PATH` in fresh shells on macOS/Linux. Run `uv tool update-shell`, then open a new shell and re-run `mm --version`. - **Duplicate tools after upgrading the Claude plugin**: re-check `/mcp` after reloading. The plugin launches `memtomem[onnx]==0.7.12`. A manual registration whose launch differs — base-only `memtomem`, or the ONNX launch pinned to an earlier release — no longer matches for deduplication. Confirm the manual entry's name and scope, then align its launch command with the plugin or remove the redundant registration. - **Indexing vs. discovery (Claude Code)**: provider memory folders that setup auto-discovers (such as `~/.claude/projects/*/memory/`) are added to the search *index*. That is separate from the Web UI's opt-in Context Gateway scan of `~/.claude/projects/`, which discovers project *roots* for Skills, Commands, and Subagents; see [Configuration → Context Gateway](docs/guides/configuration.md#context-gateway).
## Works with Everything here runs on the [**memtomem**](https://pypi.org/project/memtomem/) core package: the MCP server, CLI, Web UI, hybrid search, and storage.
