Keeping Postgres and Valkey together on a host dedicated to Agent HQ while sharing your lab's existing MQTT broker works well: the first two hold Agent HQ's state, and MQTT is how the rest of the lab talks to it. 2. **Application:** `cp .env.example .env`, fill in the URLs and keys, set up HTTPS (next section), then `docker compose --profile images build` (the desktop and workbench images) and `docker compose up -d --build`. This starts: - `caddy`: HTTPS on 443 (certificate from your step-ca), with http:// redirected - `hq`: API, UI and MQTT bridge (plain HTTP on 8000, for this host only). Its `hq-data` volume holds the knowledge library's uploads and Git clones. NFS shares for the knowledge library are mounted here too, under `/shares` (see Knowledge library). It also reads your step-ca root from `deploy/caddy/root_ca.crt` (`AHQ_EXTRA_CA_FILE`), so Git and web sources on your HTTPS hosts (your Gitea) are trusted. - `worker`: pool `default` - `worker-desktop`: pool `desktop`, for agents that drive desktops - `docker-proxy`: the Docker API `hq` uses to run desktops and workbenches, which you create under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches** (see [Desktops and workbenches](#desktops-and-workbenches)) - `egress`: the workbenches' proxy, which applies each one's network rules (see Workbenches) 3. **More machines:** copy `docker-compose.yml` and `.env` to another host and keep only the worker services you want there, with `--pools` set to whatever runs on that machine (`gpu`, `desktop`, `lab-east`…). Workers show up on the **Settings → System** page with their pools and load, and each pool's queue depth appears next to them. 4. **More workers on one host:** `docker compose up -d --scale worker=3`. **Deploying on every push.** A Gitea Actions workflow can do the upgrade for you whenever `main` changes: pull, build, a `pg_dump` if schema migrations are pending, restart, health check. It runs on a Gitea runner on the server itself and does nothing until you set it up. See [docs/auto-deploy.md](docs/auto-deploy.md). **Upgrading.** Pull, `docker compose up -d --build`. Each process brings the database schema up to date on startup (Alembic revisions, one process at a time). Before upgrading a Postgres install, `docker compose exec hq python -m app.migrate status` shows the pending revisions; take a `pg_dump` if there are any. Workers on other machines need the new image too: an older one refuses to start against a database a newer version has migrated. See [docs/schema-migrations.md](docs/schema-migrations.md). **Worker names.** In Docker, each worker is named `--`, for example `worker-shockwave-7090` and `worker-shockwave-1c2e`. You can tell which machine and which replica it is, and scaled replicas never share a name. The host name comes from the host's `/etc/hostname`, which the compose file mounts read-only. Where that file doesn't exist (Docker Desktop), set `AHQ_HOST_NAME` in `.env`. Set `AHQ_WORKER_NAME` for a fixed name, as `worker-desktop` does, but only on a service you won't scale. A recreated container (after `up --build`) gets a new ID and so a new suffix. Its old entry drops off the System page once its heartbeat stops, and any job it left unfinished is picked up as usual. Valkey settings that matter (already set in the infra compose file): - `appendonly yes`: queued jobs survive a Valkey restart. - `maxmemory-policy noeviction`: Valkey never quietly discards stream entries. - `requirepass`: a password, which goes in `AHQ_REDIS_URL` as `redis://:password@host:6379/0`. ### Sign-in and HTTPS The UI and API need a sign-in. Agents and workers are unaffected, since they talk to Valkey and Postgres directly. **Your account** - **First run:** with no account yet, the API process logs a one-time setup code. Find it with `docker compose logs hq | grep "setup code"`. The first visit to the UI asks for it, so nobody else on your network can claim the instance before you do. - **Passwords** are stored as Argon2id hashes and need at least 10 characters. - **Two-factor sign-in** is optional. Turn it on under **Settings → Security** by scanning the QR code with any authenticator app. - **Sessions** use an HttpOnly cookie that is marked Secure over HTTPS. A session ends after `AHQ_SESSION_IDLE_DAYS` without use (default 7) and after `AHQ_SESSION_MAX_DAYS` in any case (default 30). **Settings → Security** lists your signed-in browsers and can sign any of them out. Changing your password signs out every other browser. - **Locked out?** `docker compose exec hq python -m app.auth set-password `. The same tool can also `reset-2fa `, `sign-out-all` and `unlock`. **Protections** - **Lockout:** 5 failed sign-ins from one address, or 10 for one username, within 15 minutes lock further attempts for 15 minutes. - **Cross-site requests:** writes and WebSockets that use the cookie are refused when they come from another site. - **Sign-in log:** **Settings → Security** shows sign-ins, failures, lockouts, sign-outs, and every password, 2FA, session and token change. **API tokens** are for scripts, Home Assistant or curl. Create one under **Settings → Security**, then send `Authorization: Bearer ahq_…`. A token is shown once and stored only as a hash. It can expire, and you can revoke it. It can use the API but can't change your password, 2FA or tokens. ```bash curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $AHQ_TOKEN" https://shockwave.home.arpa/api/agents ``` **HTTPS with your step-ca.** The `caddy` service terminates TLS and gets its certificate from step-ca over ACME, renewing it automatically (step-ca certificates last 24 hours by default). One-time setup: 1. **On the CA,** add an ACME provisioner if you don't have one: `step ca provisioner add acme --type ACME`, then restart step-ca. 2. **Copy the root certificate** into the repo: `step ca root deploy/caddy/root_ca.crt`. It's git-ignored. 3. **In `.env`:** set `AHQ_SITE=shockwave.home.arpa` and `ACME_CA=https:///acme/acme/directory`. The provisioner name is part of that path. 4. **Network:** step-ca must be able to reach Shockwave on port 80 for the ACME challenge, and `AHQ_SITE` must resolve to Shockwave in your DNS. 5. **Browsers:** your step-ca root needs to be trusted on the machines you browse from. If you already use step-ca certificates elsewhere, it is. Plain HTTP on port 8000 is published for Shockwave itself only (`127.0.0.1`). While you're getting HTTPS working, set `AHQ_HTTP_BIND=8000` in `.env` to reach it from your LAN, then remove the setting. If you set `AHQ_PUBLIC_URL`, change it to the https address. **Desktop viewers are behind the same sign-in.** Their ports are no longer published. Instead, Caddy serves each one at `https:///desktops/desktop-N/` and checks your Agent HQ session first (`forward_auth` to `/api/auth/verify`). Agent HQ sets each desktop's `SUBFOLDER` to match its path and fills in the agent's **Desktop viewer URL** when you give it a desktop. ### Workbenches: an agent's own Python environment A workbench is a small container per agent that gives it somewhere to write and run code. It's like a desktop, but for scripts instead of a browser. Each one (created under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches**) exposes an MCP server on `:8770` with these tools: | Tool | What it does | Approval suggested | |---|---|---| | `run_python` | runs Python in the workbench's own virtual environment | ask | | `run_shell` | runs a bash command in the workspace | ask | | `pip_install` | installs packages into the venv (they persist) | ask | | `run_script` | runs a saved script by name, with JSON arguments | ask | | `save_script`, `list_scripts` | saves a working script as a named, reusable tool | allow | | `read_file`, `write_file`, `list_files` | files in the workspace; `read_file` can return a numbered range of lines | allow | | `edit_file` | replaces one exact piece of a file (or every copy of it), so a small change doesn't mean writing the whole file again | allow | **Storage.** Everything lives in the workbench's volume (`ahq-`), mounted at `/work`: - the agent's files, **one folder per chat** at `/work/chats/` - the venv at `/work/.venv`, so installed packages survive restarts and rebuilds - saved scripts in `/work/scripts` **Each chat starts with an empty workspace.** Agent HQ names the chat on every workbench call (the `X-AgentHQ-Chat` header), and the workbench makes that chat's folder the workspace: the working directory for code and shell, the root for file paths, and where attachments go in and `send_from_workbench` takes files out. A new chat can't stumble on the last one's project and spend its turn going over that instead of the new task. Files stay with their chat, so coming back to a chat finds its work where it was left, and agents sharing a workbench share a chat's folder when they work in the same chat (a delegated task, say). The venv and saved scripts are shared across chats on purpose: those are meant to carry over. This is about focus, not security: `run_shell` can still `cd` anywhere in the volume. A client that names no chat (your own, or an older Agent HQ) gets all of `/work`, as before. Files from before this change are still at the top of `/work`, out of every chat's sight; delete them from the workbench's shell when you no longer need them. **Limits.** - **Runs:** each run has a timeout (default 120 seconds), and the run and any processes it started are killed when it's reached. Output is capped at 20,000 characters. - **Container:** it runs as an unprivileged user with a read-only root filesystem and no Linux capabilities, capped at 2 CPUs, 2 GB of memory and 512 processes. **The network is off by default.** A workbench is only on the internal `workbench` network, which has no route to the internet or your LAN. Its one way out is the `egress` proxy (`deploy/egress/egress_proxy.py`). Each workbench signs in to it with its own name and token (its `HTTPS_PROXY`), so the proxy knows whose rules apply: - **Every workbench** may reach the defaults: PyPI out of the box, so `pip_install` works. Change them under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches → Network**. - **One workbench** may also reach its own rules, under **Network** on its page. - **Internet and LAN access**, ticked on a workbench, lets it reach everything directly. A rule is one of: a host (`pypi.org`, ports 80 and 443), `*.github.com` (the domain and its subdomains), `host:port` (`gitgard.home.arpa:3000`, or `host:*` for any port), an address (`192.168.10.5`), or a network (`192.168.10.0/24:443`; host names that resolve into it count too, and the proxy connects only to those addresses). Rules apply within seconds, without restarting anything: the proxy reads them from Valkey (`AHQ_REDIS_URL`), where `hq` writes them. **Blocked requests.** The proxy logs what it refuses. Each workbench's page lists its recent ones with an **Allow** button, and the Network page lists all of them with **Allow for ** and **Allow for all**. So you can let an agent try something, see what it needed, and allow just that. The proxy carries HTTPS (CONNECT) and plain HTTP, which covers tools that use `HTTPS_PROXY`/`HTTP_PROXY`: pip, git over HTTPS, curl, requests, httpx. Other connections (SSH, database clients, raw TCP) have no way out except **Internet and LAN access**. A workbench whose container predates its token signs in as nobody and gets only the defaults; its page says so, and **Recreate** fixes it (its files are kept). **Set one up:** 1. Build the image and start the proxy: `docker compose --profile images build` and `docker compose up -d egress`. 2. Under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches**, click **+ Workbench**, or **+ Its own workbench** on the agent's page. See [Desktops and workbenches](#desktops-and-workbenches). 3. Its code tools already ask for approval (see the table above). Change that per tool under its server's **Approvals** on **Settings → Tools**. ### Scripts with tools: many tool calls in one step Some jobs take many tool calls: list 40 VMs, check each one's backups, summarise. Done call by call, that's 40-odd model requests, and every result piles into the model's context window, which on a small local model means slow turns and trimmed history. With **Scripts with tools** ticked on an agent (Settings → Agents → Desktops & workbenches), the agent can instead write one Python script and run it with `run_with_tools`. The script calls the agent's tools as functions, the loop runs on the workbench, and only what the script prints (plus anything it hands to `tools.result(...)`) comes back to the model. ```python vms = tools.labtools_proxmox_list_vms() stale = [v["name"] for v in vms if tools.labtools_backup_status(vm=v["name"])["age_days"] > 7] print(f"{len(vms)} VMs, {len(stale)} without a backup this week: {', '.join(stale)}") ``` **What the script can call.** The `tools` module has a function for each tool on the agent's tool servers, with the names and arguments the agent already sees (`tools.list_tools()` prints them). Workbench and desktop tools aren't in it: the script runs on the workbench already, so it reads and writes files with plain Python. A call that fails or is denied raises `tools.ToolError`. **Same rules as a direct call.** Each call from the script goes through Agent HQ exactly as if the agent had made it: - **Approvals:** a tool set to Ask me raises the usual approval card, and the script waits for your decision. Denied, it gets a `ToolError`. - **Blocked tools** aren't in the `tools` module, and a call to one is refused. - **Work started by a webhook** asks before any tool not marked read-only, as usual. - **The script itself** is code on the workbench, so it follows that workbench's rule for `run_python`: Ask me by default (one approval card for the script), Allow, or Block, which turns scripts off too. - **Visibility:** every call shows in live activity and the run's trace. In Phoenix, each one is a `script_tool ` span under the `run_with_tools` tool span. - **The network:** the script's own code runs in the workbench container under its network rules (see above); only its tool calls leave it, through Agent HQ. **How it works.** The workbench has no route to Agent HQ, and doesn't get one. Its script's tool calls wait in a queue on the workbench, and the Agent HQ worker running the turn collects them over the workbench's own MCP connection (`ahq_script_poll`), runs each one through the agent's toolsets, and sends back the result (`ahq_script_reply`). These `ahq_*` tools are hidden from agents. **Limits.** - **Run time:** the `timeout` the agent gives (default 120 seconds, up to the workbench's `WORKBENCH_MAX_TIMEOUT`, 1800). It counts only the script's own time, not time spent waiting on tools or on you to approve something. At the limit, the script and its processes are killed and the agent is told. - **Tool calls per script:** 200 (`WORKBENCH_SCRIPT_MAX_CALLS`). Past that, each call raises `ToolError`. - **Output:** 20,000 characters (`WORKBENCH_MAX_OUTPUT`), for printed output and for the structured result. - **Stopping the turn** stops the script. If Agent HQ stops collecting a script's calls for 3 minutes (`WORKBENCH_SCRIPT_ABANDON`), say because a worker died, the workbench kills it. While a call is waiting on you or on a slow tool, Agent HQ keeps pinging the workbench, so a long wait doesn't count. Scripts can't do anything the agent couldn't do itself. The `ahq_script_*` tools come with the workbench image: a deploy rebuilds it, and each workbench moves to it by itself when idle (see [Automatic recreate](#automatic-recreate-after-a-rebuild)). ### Skills: know-how agents write down and improve A **skill** is a short, named procedure. It has a title, a line saying *when to use it*, the steps in markdown (including what to check and the pitfalls), the tools it relies on, and optionally the name of a saved workbench script that does the mechanical part. A skill is either shared by every agent or belongs to one agent. You can write and edit skills under **Settings → Skills**. Every change is a new version, with who made it and why, and you can restore any earlier version. **How agents use them:** - **Listing:** on each run, an agent's instructions list up to 8 skills that fit the task, each with its name and *when to use* line. - **How they're matched:** by meaning when an embedding model is set (Settings → Memory), and by keywords otherwise. - **Small collections:** with 12 or fewer skills, all of them are listed. - **Loading:** the agent calls `load_skill` to read a skill's full procedure and follows it. `list_skills` searches the rest. - **Tracking:** each time a skill is loaded, the outcome of that job (done, partial or failed) is recorded. **Settings → Skills** shows each skill's uses and success rate. **How agents learn.** When an agent works out how to do something that will come up again, or finds that a skill it used was wrong or incomplete, it calls `propose_skill`. A proposal is either a new skill, or a revision to an existing one with a diff against the current version. What happens next depends on the agent's **Learning** setting (Settings → Agents): - **Propose to me** (the default for every agent): - **Where it shows up:** in the conversation, in the **Requests** inbox (with the sidebar badge), and on your [notification channels](#notifications-telegram-discord-and-mqtt) as a `skill_proposal` notice. - **Your options:** approve it, edit it first, or reject it, with an optional note. - **Revisions** show a diff against the current version, with a warning if the skill changed after the agent wrote its proposal. - **Save automatically:** the change is saved at once and you're told. You can review it or roll it back on the Skills page. If there are test cases for that agent or skill (see Evals), the change is tested first. It's applied only if it doesn't lower the pass rate; otherwise it waits for you. - **Off:** the agent uses skills but can't propose them. Skills can come from three places besides your own writing: an agent's `propose_skill` call, a reflection after a job (see the learning loop), or a document in the knowledge library ("Propose skills" turns a runbook's procedures into proposals). Each proposal records where it came from. Sub-agents use their parent's skills but don't propose any. Skills never grant tools: every call a skill leads to still goes through your tool approvals. ### The learning loop: ratings, corrections and reflections **Rate replies.** Every agent reply has 👍 and 👎 buttons. A 👎 opens a box for *what it should have done*, which is the most useful thing an agent can learn from. Ratings show on each skill's stats. **Corrections count too.** A reply such as "No, use the TrueNAS datastore" or "from now on, failures first" is recognised as a correction of the job the agent just did. **Reflection.** After a job that's worth a look, the agent rereads the conversation, its tool calls, how the job ended and what you said about it. A job is worth a look when: - you rated it 👎, or 👍 on work that took several steps; - you corrected it; - it failed or only partly worked; - or it made 4+ tool calls. It then may do three things: - **propose skills,** new or improved, through the same path as `propose_skill`, so your learning mode applies; - **save lessons** to its memory, and post "noted for next time: …" in the conversation; - **suggest a line for your profile** when you stated a standing rule. **Settings → Learning** controls all of this and keeps a log of every reflection: why it ran, what it concluded, and links to what it proposed. Each reflection has **Run now** and **Cancel**. - **Reasons to reflect:** you choose which ones count, or reflect after every job, or never. - **Waiting:** a reflection waits 10 minutes after a job so your follow-ups are included, and 2 minutes after a rating. - **Daily limit:** 30 by default. - **Model:** each agent's own, unless you pick a reflection model; a stronger one writes better skills for small local agents. - **Who never reflects:** agents whose learning is Off, and sub-agents. **Requests** has a sub-menu like Settings: **Tool approvals**, **Goals** (see [Standing goals](#standing-goals-the-board)), **Skill proposals**, **Profile updates**, **Knowledge** (documents agents suggest) and **Sub-agent requests**. Each has its own count, and the sidebar badge shows the total. ### The current date and time Models have no clock: left alone, they take "now" to be about when their training data ends, so "this weekend" can turn into a date months off. Every agent's instructions therefore end with the current date and time in your time zone, which you set with `AHQ_TIMEZONE` (an IANA name such as `America/New_York`; falls back to `TZ`, then UTC). The line goes last because it changes every minute, and providers that cache prompts reuse everything before the first change. Delegated agents and sub-agents get it the same way. ### Your profile **Settings → Profile** holds what every agent should always know about you: who you are, how you like things done, your environment. Memory comes up when it matches a task; the profile goes into every agent's instructions, every time. - **Size:** keep it short. Anything past the word limit (600 by default) is cut, so it doesn't crowd small models. - **Opting out:** an agent can opt out under Settings → Agents → Learning ("Knows your profile"). - **Suggestions:** reflections suggest additions when you state a standing preference. Suggestions show up in the conversation, in **Requests → Profile updates**, and on your notification channels as a `profile_proposal` notice. Nothing changes your profile without your approval, and you can reword a suggestion first. ### Tool approvals For every tool on every tool server, you choose under **Settings → Tools → (server) → Approvals**: - **Allow:** the call runs. - **Ask me:** the call waits for your OK. - **Block:** the call is refused, and the agent is told it isn't allowed. A rule on `*` covers every tool on that server that doesn't have its own rule. A server can suggest a mode for each tool in the tool's MCP metadata (`{"agent_hq/approval": "ask"}`); the workbench does this for the tools that run code. Your rules always win. A tool with no rule and no suggestion is allowed, so your existing tool servers behave exactly as before. **When a call needs your OK:** - **Where it shows up:** in the conversation, as a card showing exactly what the agent wants to run, with code and commands shown as code. It also appears in the **Requests** inbox (with the sidebar badge) and on your [notification channels](#notifications-telegram-discord-and-mqtt) as a `tool_approval` notice, which you can approve or deny from Telegram or Discord. - **Your options:** approve it; approve it and don't ask again for that tool, from that agent, in that conversation, for an hour; or deny it, optionally with a note the agent sees. - **While it waits:** the agent's worker slot is freed for other work. - **If you don't decide** within `AHQ_APPROVAL_TIMEOUT_MINUTES` (default 30), the call isn't made, and the agent is told it's waiting for approval. - **Sub-agents** follow the same rules as everyone else. - **Work started by a webhook** asks before any tool not marked read-only, even where the rule says allow (see [Inbound webhooks](#inbound-webhooks)). The same table has a **Safe in tests** column. It decides which tools may run for real in an eval when a test case has no recording for the call. Tools the server marks read-only (`readOnlyHint`) start ticked. Only tools set to Allow ever run in a test. ### Desktops and workbenches Desktops and workbenches are **resources**: one container each, plus the tool servers it serves. Package servers from the MCP server catalog are resources too (see [Package servers](#package-servers)). You create them in the UI and give them to agents. Tools that aren't anyone's in particular, like MQTT or the web reader, stay plain tool servers. Tick **All agents** on one under **Settings → Tools** and every agent gets it without you ticking it on each. **Create one.** Under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches**, click **+ Desktop** or **+ Workbench**. Or, on an agent's page, click **+ Its own desktop** / **+ Its own workbench**. Agent HQ then: 1. picks the next free name (`desktop-2`, `workbench-3`…); 2. creates and starts the container through the Docker API (a desktop with 1 GB of shared memory; a workbench read-only, without capabilities, on the internal network behind the egress proxy, capped at 2 CPUs, 2 GB and 512 processes) with a named volume `ahq-` for its data; 3. registers its tool servers: a desktop's screen (`:8765`) and browser (`:8931`, Playwright, unprefixed), or a workbench's `:8770`; 4. ticks them on the agents you chose, and sets a desktop's **Desktop viewer URL** to `/desktops//` (Caddy routes any `desktop-`). **Dedicated or shared.** - **Dedicated:** one agent's own. Agent HQ refuses to give it to another agent, whether from the Resources page or by ticking it on the agent's page. - **Shared:** any number of agents. A shared workbench is shared files. A shared desktop is used by **one conversation at a time**. The first desktop call takes it. Calls from other conversations wait up to `AHQ_DESKTOP_LEASE_WAIT` seconds (600) and then report it busy. It's let go when that run ends, or `AHQ_DESKTOP_LEASE_TTL` seconds (300) after its last desktop call. Agents delegating within the same conversation share it without waiting. **Take control** pauses the desktop for every agent that has it. On an agent's page, **Desktops & workbenches** lists them all: tick one to give it to the agent (all of its servers go together), and dedicated ones belonging to someone else are greyed out. **Running them.** The resource's page has **Start**, **Stop**, **Restart**, **Recreate** (a new container from the current image, same data, e.g. after `docker compose --profile images build`) and **Delete**. Delete takes it from its agents and removes its tool servers and container. Its data volume goes only if you say so. Otherwise a new desktop with the same name picks it up again. #### Automatic recreate after a rebuild A running container keeps the image it was made from, so rebuilding the images (`docker compose --profile images build`, which [auto-deploy](docs/auto-deploy.md) runs when `workbench/`, `desktop/` or `mcp-runner/` change) doesn't change what's running by itself. Agent HQ closes that gap: every minute it compares each running workbench and package server with its image, and recreates the ones on an older image, the same as the **Recreate** button, so files, installed packages and saved scripts stay. - **Only when idle.** It waits until no agent that has the resource (sub-agents included) has a job queued or running. A turn waiting on your approval is still running, so it waits for that too. - **No half-made connections.** While a container is being replaced, it's flagged in Valkey, and a turn that starts then waits for the new container instead of failing to connect. - **Left alone:** stopped containers (you stopped them), ones docker compose runs (take them over first), and desktops, because recreating a desktop closes its browser and you may be using it. Add them with `AHQ_AUTO_RECREATE_KINDS=workbench,package,desktop`. - **Settings:** `AHQ_AUTO_RECREATE=0` turns it off; `AHQ_AUTO_RECREATE_INTERVAL` (60) sets how often it checks. **Docker access.** The `docker-proxy` service gives `hq`, and nothing else, a Docker API limited to containers, images, networks and volumes (`AHQ_DOCKER_URL=http://docker-proxy:2375`). The images come from compose: the build-only services `desktop-image` and `workbench-image` (profile `images`, so they never run) build `agent-hq/desktop:latest` and `agent-hq/workbench:latest` (`AHQ_DESKTOP_IMAGE` / `AHQ_WORKBENCH_IMAGE`). Plain `docker compose up --build` skips them: after changing `./desktop` or `./workbench`, run `docker compose --profile images build`, then **Recreate** each desktop or workbench. Containers join `agent-hq_default` (desktops) or `agent-hq_workbench` (workbenches) under their name (`AHQ_RESOURCE_NETWORK` / `AHQ_WORKBENCH_NETWORK`, for another compose project name). Without Docker access, the page still registers tool servers and tracks resources, but you run the containers yourself. Anyone who controls `hq` can start containers on this host, so leave `docker-proxy` out if you'd rather not allow that. **Desktops you already run in compose.** The page lists `desktop-N` / `workbench-N` it finds (from tool servers pointing at those hosts, and from compose services) under **Import**. Importing makes each one a resource for its existing tool servers and agents. Compose keeps running the container: Start/Stop work, Recreate doesn't. To hand it over, click **Take over**: Agent HQ reads the compose container's data mounts and replaces it with its own container on the same data (bind mounts such as `./desktops/desktop-1` included). Then delete its block from `docker-compose.yml` (and its volume from the `volumes:` list, which keeps the data but stops `docker compose down -v` deleting it) before your next `docker compose up`, which would otherwise start a second one. `docker compose up -d --remove-orphans` cleans up a block you deleted without taking it over first. **Detach** forgets an imported one and leaves its tool servers as plain ones. **One host.** Resources run on the Docker host next to `hq`. The workers that run their agents must be on that host too (any pool there: compose workers reach both networks). Agents that use desktop tools need a vision-capable model. Anyone who can open a viewer can use whatever sessions the agent's browser is logged in to. That's why viewers are reachable only through Caddy, signed in to Agent HQ. For local development without Caddy, give the desktop `ports: ["3000:3000"]` and `SUBFOLDER: /`. ### Taking control of a desktop You can drive an agent's desktop yourself: to log in to a site, solve a CAPTCHA or enter an MFA code. That way the agent works with an authenticated session and never sees your password. ```mermaid sequenceDiagram actor You participant UI as Chat UI participant API as API process participant VK as Valkey participant W as Worker (agent's run) participant D as Agent desktop W->>W: agent hits a login page W->>VK: request: "Log in to the Zabbix web UI" W-->>UI: banner: agent needs you on its desktop Note over W: waits (worker slot released) You->>UI: Open desktop and take control UI->>API: take API->>VK: control = you Note over W,D: any desktop tool call now returns "paused" You->>D: log in through the desktop viewer You->>UI: Hand back ("logged in, 2FA done") UI->>API: release API->>VK: clear control, push hand-back note VK-->>W: note W->>D: screenshot, continue the task W-->>You: result in the conversation ``` - **When the agent asks.** Agents with a desktop get an `ask_user_to_take_over(reason)` tool and are told to use it, never to ask for passwords in chat. The request appears as a banner in the conversation. The agent waits for up to `AHQ_HANDOFF_TIMEOUT` seconds (30 minutes by default), giving up its worker slot while it waits. When you hand back, it continues with your note. - **When you step in on your own.** **Take control** on the desktop panel pauses the agent at any time. While you have control, every call to that desktop's tools, screenshots included, is refused. So the agent neither fights you for the mouse nor sends what you're typing to its model provider. If the agent ran into the paused desktop mid-task, **Hand back** wakes it in that conversation to carry on. - **A forgotten takeover can't block an agent forever.** Control expires after 24 hours. Credentials typed into chat are stored in the transcript, the conversation history and possibly your traces. Logging in yourself on the desktop keeps them out of all three. ## Adding tools Register MCP servers on the **Settings → Tools** page: - **HTTP:** a URL like `http://perceptor:8811/mcp` - **stdio:** a command plus arguments, which is launched **on whichever worker runs the agent**, so it must be installed there Click **Test connection** to list the server's tools (this connects from the API host), then tick the server on any agent, or tick **All agents** on the server to give it to every agent (sub-agents included). Desktops and workbenches aren't registered here: create them under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches** (see [Desktops and workbenches](#desktops-and-workbenches)). Tool names are prefixed with the server name by default (`proxmox_list_vms`) so they never collide. The worker image is a slim Python image without `npx` or `uvx`, so a stdio server you'd normally start with those commands won't run there. Install it from the catalog as a [package server](#package-servers) instead (its own container, served over HTTP), or run it as a container yourself and register it over HTTP, the way the web reader below does. **Headers.** An HTTP server can get headers, one `Name: value` per line, for example `Authorization: Bearer …` for a hosted server that wants an API key. With `AHQ_SECRET_KEY` set they are encrypted in the database (existing ones at the next start), and the form shows a saved value as `(saved, encrypted)`: leave that line as it is to keep it. ### The MCP server catalog Instead of writing a tool server yourself, look for one someone has already published. **Settings → Tools → Catalog** searches the [official MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io), the open, community-run list of MCP servers. Each entry shows its publisher (a GitHub account, or a domain they proved they own), version, repository and how it runs. - **Remote servers** (hosted at a URL) have an **Add** button. It opens the usual form, filled in: name, description, URL and any headers the server asks for (an API key, say), with what each header is for. Fill in the values and save. - **Package servers** (an npm or PyPI package) have an **Install** button. See [Package servers](#package-servers) below. Servers published only as a Docker image are listed but can't be installed yet. **Nothing is trusted by default.** A listing is the publisher's own description, not a review. A server added from the catalog starts with every tool set to **Ask me** and isn't given to any agent, so it does nothing until you've looked at it: save it, click **Test connection** to see its tools, relax the approvals for the ones you trust, then tick it on the agents that need it. Check the repository first, and remember that whatever the server is sent (your agents' tool arguments) goes to whoever hosts it. The Tools list shows which servers came from the catalog, and the catalog shows which entries you've already added. The search runs on the API host, which needs to reach the registry. `AHQ_MCP_REGISTRY_URL` points it at another registry that speaks the same API (a sub-registry, or one you host yourself); set it empty to turn the catalog off. ### Package servers Most published MCP servers are npm or PyPI packages that talk over stdio. Agent HQ runs each one you install in a **container of its own**, from the `agent-hq/mcp-runner` image (`mcp-runner/`), and agents reach it over HTTP like any other tool server. Build the image once (and again after pulling changes to `mcp-runner/`): ```bash docker compose --profile images build ``` **Installing.** In **Settings → Tools → Catalog**, click **Install npm package** (or **pypi**) on an entry. The form shows what it will run (`npx -y @` or `uvx ==`) and asks for what the package needs: its settings (environment variables; required and secret ones are marked), its arguments (anything in `` must be replaced, e.g. a directory or a URL), and the hosts it may reach. Install creates: - a **resource** of kind *package server* under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches**, where you start, stop, restart, recreate and delete its container, change its settings and arguments (saving recreates the container) and see what it was refused; - a **tool server** with the same name at `http://:8790/mcp`, every tool on **Ask me**, given to no agent. Its first start downloads the package, so give it a minute, then **Test connection** on the Tools page, set its approvals and tick it on the agents that need it. **How it is contained.** Each package server runs like a workbench: an unprivileged user, a read-only root filesystem (the package and its caches live in its own volume, `/work`), no capabilities, 1 CPU, 1 GB of memory, and only the `workbench` network. It reaches the outside only through the egress proxy, signed in with its own token: PyPI for every one (the workbench defaults), the npm registry for npm packages, plus the hosts you list. When the server needs a host you didn't list (the API it talks to, say), the request is refused and shows under **Blocked lately** on its page with an **Allow** button. Node servers go through the proxy too (`NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1`). `mcp-proxy` turns the package's stdio into streamable HTTP and only answers requests that carry the server's own bearer token (generated at install, sent by Agent HQ as an encrypted header) and are addressed to its name. That matters because workbenches share its network: code an agent runs in a workbench can't call a package server directly and get around your approvals. **Secrets.** With `AHQ_SECRET_KEY` set, settings marked secret (and any the catalog doesn't describe) are encrypted in the database and shown as `(saved, encrypted)`; leave that line as it is to keep the value. The container gets the real values in its environment, so anyone who can inspect containers on the host can read them. **Versions.** A package server runs the version it was installed with. To move to a newer one, delete it and install it again from the catalog (its approvals start over). ### Web reader: feeds, pages and search The `web-reader` service (in `docker-compose.yml`, code in `webreader/`) gives agents text-only web tools. It's much faster and cheaper than driving a browser, and works fine with small local models: | Tool | What it returns | |---|---| | `read_feed(url, limit)` | The newest items of an RSS or Atom feed: title, link, date, short summary. A site's address works too if its page links to a feed. | | `fetch_page(url, offset)` | A page's readable content as Markdown (the article or documentation, without menus, ads or scripts). Long pages come back in parts: call again with `next_offset`. | | `search_web(query, limit, time_range, categories)` | Results from **your own SearXNG**: titles, links, snippets. Only offered when `SEARXNG_URL` is set. | Register it under **Settings → Tools**: HTTP, `http://web-reader:8800/mcp`, untick **Prefix tool names**, leave **Controls an agent desktop** unticked. Then tick it on your researcher (or tick **All agents**). A good split is for the researcher to use feeds, pages and search first, and delegate to the desktop agent only for pages that need a login, JavaScript, or actually looking at them (charts, dashboards). **Behaviour:** - `fetch_page` honours `robots.txt` (`WEBREADER_RESPECT_ROBOTS=false` to turn that off) and returns at most `WEBREADER_MAX_CHARS` (12,000) characters per call. - Downloads are capped at 5 MB, and redirects are followed hop by hop. - **LAN addresses are refused by default.** Agents read untrusted web content, and a page could try to talk one into probing your network. To let agents read specific internal sites, list them in `WEBREADER_ALLOW_HOSTS` (for example `wiki.home.arpa`). **Search with SearXNG.** `deploy/searxng/` runs a private SearXNG on any host: ```bash cd deploy/searxng cp .env.example .env # set SEARXNG_SECRET: openssl rand -hex 32 docker compose up -d curl 'http://localhost:8888/search?q=proxmox&format=json' # JSON back = ready (403 = JSON not enabled) ``` Its `config/settings.yml` turns on JSON output, which the web reader needs, and turns off the bot limiter, which would otherwise throttle your own agents on a private instance. Then set `SEARXNG_URL=http://:8888` in Agent HQ's `.env` and run `docker compose up -d web-reader`. Agents see `search_web` the next time they start a job. ### MQTT publisher: agents publish back to the lab The `mqtt-publisher` service (in `docker-compose.yml`, code in `mqttpublisher/`) lets agents publish to your MQTT broker: their status for a dashboard such as Home Assistant, or commands to anything in the lab that listens on MQTT. | Tool | What it does | Approval by default | |---|---|---| | `list_publish_topics()` | Shows the agent where it may publish, and the size and rate limits. | Allow (read-only) | | `publish_status(name, state, detail, data, retain)` | Publishes JSON `{"agent", "state", "detail", "data", "at"}` to `agent-hq/agents//status`, retained so subscribers see the latest state straight away. | Allow | | `publish(topic, payload, qos, retain)` | Publishes to one topic on the allow-list. Text is sent as-is; objects and lists are sent as JSON. Not retained unless asked. | **Ask** | **Setup:** 1. On your broker, create a user for the publisher with **write access only to the topics you'll allow**. The broker then enforces the same limits as the publisher. 2. In `.env`, set `MQTT_PUBLISH_URL=mqtt://agent-hq-pub:@:1883` (`mqtts://` for TLS; for a step-ca certificate, mount your root certificate and set `MQTT_PUBLISH_CA_FILE`). Set `MQTT_PUBLISH_ALLOW` to the topic filters `publish` may use, for example `agent-hq/agents/#,homelab/cmd/#`. 3. Run `docker compose up -d mqtt-publisher`. 4. Under **Settings → Tools**, register HTTP `http://mqtt-publisher:8810/mcp`, untick **Prefix tool names**, and leave **Controls an agent desktop** unticked. Then tick it on the agents that should publish, or tick **All agents** on it. **Safeguards:** - Topics with wildcards, broker system topics (`$SYS/…`) and anything matching `MQTT_PUBLISH_DENY` (default `agent-hq/notifications/#`, so agents can't fake your notifications) are refused. - Payloads are capped at `MQTT_PUBLISH_MAX_BYTES` (16 KB), and the server sends at most `MQTT_PUBLISH_RATE_PER_MINUTE` (30) messages a minute across all agents. - `publish` asks for your approval by default, with the usual card in the conversation and the Requests inbox. Once you trust an agent with a topic, set the tool to **Allow** under **Settings → Tools → (server) → Approvals**, or approve with "don't ask again" (an hour, for that agent in that conversation). - **Watch for loops.** If an Events subscription matches a topic agents publish to, every publish wakes an agent again (the cooldown limits the damage). Keep publish topics outside your subscription filters. - The agent passes its own name to `publish_status`; the server can't verify it, so status topics are informational and should not be used for access decisions. ## Model providers Providers live on the **Settings → Model providers** page; nothing about servers or model names is hardcoded. Add a provider once, and its models become choices in every agent's **Model** picker. Different agents can use different models from the same provider: one on `qwen3:14b`, another on `gpt-oss:20b`. | Kind | Base URL | Model list comes from | API key | |---|---|---|---| | **Ollama** | `http://host:11434` (with or without `/v1`) | `GET /api/tags`, with size and quantization | usually none | | **OpenAI** | optional override | `GET /v1/models` | stored, or `OPENAI_API_KEY` on the workers | | **OpenAI-compatible** (vLLM, LM Studio, LiteLLM, llama.cpp server…) | required, the server's `/v1` URL | `GET /v1/models` | only if the server needs one | | **Anthropic** | optional override | `GET /v1/models` | stored, or `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` on the workers | | **ChatGPT plan** (Plus/Pro) | none | `GET /v1/models` on your plan | none: **Sign in with ChatGPT** instead | | **Grok plan** (SuperGrok / X Premium+) | none | `GET /v1/models` on api.x.ai (chat models only) | none: **Sign in with xAI** instead | You can register several providers of the same kind, for example two Ollama servers on different GPUs. - **Picking a model:** the agent editor lists the provider's current models. You can still type a name the provider doesn't list yet, such as a model you're about to pull. - **API keys are write-only.** They're stored in the database and used by the workers, but the API never returns them and exports never include them. To keep keys out of the database entirely, leave the field blank and set the provider's usual environment variable on the workers instead. - **Disabling and deleting:** disabling a provider stops its agents with a clear error in their conversations. A provider can't be deleted while agents still use it. - **Advanced:** with the provider set to *Custom model spec*, the Model field takes a raw PydanticAI spec such as `openai:gpt-4.1`, or `test` for a no-LLM test model. Agents that use desktop tools need a vision-capable model. ### Thinking levels Each agent has two settings under its model (Settings → Agents): **Thinking** (*Model default*, *Off* or *On*) and, when thinking is on, a **Reasoning level** (*Provider default*, *Minimal*, *Low*, *Medium*, *High*, *Extra high* or *Max*). The level box is greyed out for models that only turn thinking on or off, such as Qwen on Ollama. Both are stored as the agent's one `thinking` value (`""`, `off`, `on`, or the level). It controls how much the model reasons before it answers. It's sent to the model as a request setting, not written into the instructions: telling a model to "think hard" in its prompt doesn't change how much it actually reasons. Use the instructions to say *what* the agent should be careful about, and this setting for *how much* it thinks. - **OpenAI, the ChatGPT plan, the Grok plan and Anthropic** get PydanticAI's unified `thinking` setting, which it turns into each provider's own (reasoning effort, thinking budgets, adaptive thinking). Levels a model doesn't offer use the closest one it does. - **Ollama** gets `reasoning_effort` on its OpenAI-compatible endpoint (`none` for Off), because PydanticAI doesn't translate the setting for Ollama. It's only sent to models whose `/api/show` lists the `thinking` capability, so a model that can't think isn't sent a setting it would reject. gpt-oss always thinks a little (Off gives it its lowest effort); Qwen3-style models only do on and off, so every level just turns thinking on. - **OpenAI-compatible servers** get the unified setting too, but PydanticAI only acts on it for model names it recognises; for others the setting is ignored and the model keeps its default. - The editor checks the chosen model and says under the settings whether thinking reaches it and whether it takes levels. - The **fallback model** uses the same level, translated for its own provider, and **sub-agents** inherit the level of the agent that created them. *Model default* sends nothing at all. Higher levels help on hard, multi-step tasks but are slower, and on local models they cost GPU time; a supervisor that mostly routes work is usually fine on Low or Off. ### Your ChatGPT plan instead of an API key A **ChatGPT plan** provider runs agents on your ChatGPT Plus or Pro subscription, using OpenAI's [Sign in with ChatGPT](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source) for open-source and self-hosted apps. There's no API key and no per-token bill: requests count against your plan's usage instead. **Signing in.** On the **Settings → Model providers** page, add a provider of kind *ChatGPT plan*, save it, and choose **Sign in with ChatGPT**. Then: 1. Approve Agent HQ in the OpenAI tab that opens, including permission to use your plan. 2. OpenAI only ever redirects to `http://127.0.0.1:1455/auth/callback`, which is the computer running your browser, not the server running Agent HQ. So that tab ends on a "can't connect" page. That's expected. 3. Copy the whole address from that tab's address bar, paste it into Agent HQ, and choose **Finish sign-in**. The server started the sign-in and holds its PKCE verifier, so the pasted address is only useful to this Agent HQ, and only once, within 15 minutes. **How it works:** - The tokens are stored on the provider in the database, so every worker on every machine uses the one sign-in. Like API keys, they're never returned by the API or included in exports. - Access tokens last an hour and are refreshed automatically. OpenAI's refresh tokens are single-use, so refreshes are serialized across all workers with a Valkey lock: two workers never spend the same refresh token, which could get the sign-in revoked. - **Disconnect** forgets the tokens. To revoke access entirely, also disconnect Agent HQ in your ChatGPT settings, where you can also cap how much of your plan it may use. **Things to know:** - **Limits:** on Plus, a five-hour usage window is shared with every app connected to your plan, and there's a weekly allowance. Give agents on this provider a **fallback model** on your Ollama server: when the plan is exhausted, the request fails and the agent switches to its fallback. - **Not supported here:** embeddings (use Ollama for memory), and settings like temperature or max output tokens, which OpenAI doesn't accept on plan usage. PydanticAI drops those automatically. - **Eligibility:** OpenAI offers this self-serve to open-source apps and personal projects that run locally or self-hosted, which is what Agent HQ is. A paid or hosted service would need OpenAI's approval first. ### Your Grok plan instead of an API key A **Grok plan** provider runs agents on your SuperGrok subscription (or X Premium+, on an X account linked to your xAI account). xAI lets agent tools such as Hermes Agent, OpenCode, Kilo Code and Warp sign in to your xAI account and call the regular API at `https://api.x.ai/v1` on your subscription, with no API key and no per-token bill. Agent HQ does this itself: there's no proxy or extra service to run. **Signing in.** On the **Settings → Model providers** page, add a provider of kind *Grok plan*, save it, and choose **Sign in with xAI**. A tab opens on xAI's site showing a short code, which Agent HQ shows too. Sign in with the account that has your subscription, check the codes match, and approve. The Models page notices by itself and finishes the sign-in: nothing to copy or paste. The code is good for about ten minutes. This is OAuth's device flow, so it works even though Agent HQ runs on a different machine from your browser. Agent HQ asks xAI at most once per the interval xAI sets while it waits, however often the page checks. **How it works:** - The tokens are stored on the provider in the database, so every worker on every machine uses the one sign-in. Like API keys, they're never returned by the API or included in exports. - Access tokens last about six hours and are refreshed half an hour early. xAI rotates the refresh token on every refresh, so refreshes are serialized across all workers with a Valkey lock, as for the ChatGPT plan. - Requests go through the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API with Grok's model profile, so each agent's thinking level becomes the `reasoning_effort` that model accepts (Grok 4.3 can turn thinking off; Grok 4.5 and later always think a little). - **Disconnect** forgets the tokens. To revoke access entirely, also remove the app from your xAI account. **Things to know:** - **The client ID.** xAI only accepts these sign-ins from apps it has allowlisted, and doesn't let apps register their own. Like the other tools, Agent HQ uses the public client ID of xAI's Grok CLI (a public identifier, not a secret), so xAI's approval page may call it *Grok CLI* or *Grok Build*. Set `AHQ_GROK_CLIENT_ID` on the server and workers to use a different one. Because it borrows that client ID, xAI could change or withdraw it at any time. - **Limits:** usage comes out of your subscription's allowance, shared with Grok Build and every other app you've signed in. Give agents on this provider a **fallback model** on your Ollama server. - **Refused accounts:** xAI has been seen to refuse OAuth API access for some subscription tiers (HTTP 403) even while the subscription is active. Agent HQ says so plainly. If it happens, use an xAI API key on an *OpenAI-compatible* provider with base URL `https://api.x.ai/v1` instead. - **Not supported here:** embeddings (use Ollama for memory), and image, video and voice models, which are left out of the model list. ## Long-term memory Agents remember across conversations: how your lab is set up, what went wrong before and what fixed it, and how you like things done. Memory lives in your Postgres (pgvector for meaning-based search, plus Postgres full-text search) and uses an embedding model from your providers. A small model such as `nomic-embed-text` on Ollama runs fine on CPU. ```mermaid flowchart LR J["Job starts
(turn or delegated task)"] --> R["Recall:
search memory with the
message or task"] R --> I["Top matches added to the
agent's instructions,
with dates, as leads to verify"] I --> A["Agent works
remember / recall / forget / confirm"] A --> C["Capture:
delegation results and
handled MQTT events"] C --> D{"near-duplicate
already stored?"} D -- yes --> K["confirm it
(seen N times, fresher date)"] D -- no --> N["new memory"] T["Nightly tidy-up
(optional model)"] -. "merge duplicates,
retire contradicted facts" .-> N ``` - **Recall is automatic.** Before every job, the runtime searches memory with the incoming message or task and gives the agent the best matches, with their dates. Small local models don't have to remember to look things up. Search blends meaning (embeddings), exact keywords (identifiers like `pve1` or an IP address count) and recency. - **Capture is automatic, and doesn't need an extra model call.** Delegation results and handled MQTT events are already concise summaries, so they're stored as **incident** memories as they happen. If a near-duplicate already exists, it's confirmed (fresher date, higher count) rather than stored twice. - **Agents have tools:** `remember` (with *team* or *agent* scope, and optionally which memory it replaces), `recall`, `forget` and `confirm`. - **Nothing is silently overwritten.** Outdated memories are *retired*, with a reason and a pointer to whatever replaced them, so history stays searchable ("show retired"), and a retired memory can be restored. - **Tidy-up** (on demand, or nightly at a set hour) merges duplicates. With a *tidy-up model* configured, it also merges related memories and retires ones a newer memory contradicts. - **Scopes:** *team* (every agent), *agent* (only one agent), or *conversation* (only one thread). Each agent has a **Long-term memory** switch. On the **Settings → Memory** page you can: - search, add and edit memories; - confirm, retire, restore or delete them; - choose the embedding model; - tune recall (how many memories per job, and a minimum match score); - turn automatic capture on or off; - set up the tidy-up. Changing the embedding model re-embeds existing memories in the background. - **On Postgres:** the infrastructure compose file uses the `pgvector/pgvector:pg17` image, and Agent HQ enables the extension, adds the vector column and creates the full-text index on startup. - **On SQLite (single-machine dev):** search runs in Python instead. It's fine for thousands of memories. ## Huddles: several agents in one chat A conversation starts with one agent. **@mention another agent** in a message, or add one with the **+** in the chat header, and it joins: the chat becomes a **huddle** and moves to the sidebar's **Huddles** section, under Conversations, with its history and address unchanged. The sidebar shows each huddle with its members' avatars. **Who answers:** - **@mention an agent** to address it. Typing `@` in the message box suggests agents (members first); an agent not in the huddle yet joins when you send. - **No mention:** the huddle's **lead** answers. That's the agent the chat started with, until you pick another. Click a member's avatar in the header to mention it, make it lead, or remove it. - **Several mentions** answer one after another in the order you wrote them, so each sees the replies before its own: `@Scarlett find the release notes, then @Snake Eyes check the page`. - **Agents can @mention each other** in their replies, for example to ask another member to check their work. The member they mention answers next. Agents are told to write the @. A member addressed by name at the end of a reply without it also gets the hand-off, since models often write it that way: "Duke, want to weigh in?", "Duke: can you check this?", "What do you think, Duke?". A name used in passing, or earlier in the reply, doesn't count. **Settings → System → Long conversations → Huddles** caps how many turns agents can start that way after one message of yours (3 by default; 0 turns it off), so two agents can't keep passing the floor back and forth. The chat notes when the cap stops a hand-off. - **Reports and events** go to the member they belong to: a background delegation reports to whoever delegated it, a sub-agent decision goes to the agent that asked, and a desktop handback goes to that desktop's agent if it's in the huddle. Otherwise the lead takes them. **What each agent sees:** - **Its own model history.** Each member has its own LangGraph checkpoint for the conversation (the starting agent keeps the conversation's own key, so chats from before huddles carry on as they were). One agent never sees another's tool calls or thinking as its own, and agents on different providers can share a huddle. - **A catch-up at the start of its turn:** what you and the others said since it last spoke, as plain text. It's read when the turn runs, so it includes the replies of agents that answered just before. An agent that joins later gets the conversation so far, trimmed from the oldest end to fit its context window. - **Who's in the huddle,** in its instructions: the other members, who leads, and how mentions work. **Delegating from a huddle brings the delegate in.** When a member delegates to another agent from the huddle, that agent joins it. It does the work as an ordinary delegated task, then posts its findings in the chat as its own message, under its name and avatar, marked "findings for" the agent that asked. The delegator gets the result as usual, but is told the findings are already posted: it credits them and adds only its own view, instead of passing the work off as its own. This works whether it waits for the result or it comes back later. Work an agent delegates from inside a delegated task stays in the background, and so do sub-agents, which are one-task helpers. **Unchanged:** each answer is an ordinary turn by that agent. It runs on that agent's model and pool, with its tools, delegation rights, tool approvals and sub-agent limits. Memory recall uses that agent's own scope, plus team memories and the conversation's memories, which every member shares. In Phoenix, each answer is a `turn ` span in the conversation's session. Stop halts whoever is working, and the agents still waiting for their turn. **Leaving and deleting:** removing a member keeps its earlier replies in the chat, and the chat stays a huddle. If the lead leaves, the next member in join order leads. A huddle always keeps at least one agent. Deleting an agent removes the huddles it started, and takes it out of the huddles it joined. Those stay, along with the other agents' work. **API:** `POST /api/threads/{id}/members` `{"agent_id"}` adds a member, `DELETE /api/threads/{id}/members/{agent_id}` removes one, and `PUT /api/threads/{id}/lead` `{"agent_id"}` picks the lead. Threads carry `members`, `lead_agent_id` and `huddle`. `GET /api/threads?agent_id=` lists the chats an agent started and the huddles it's in. Posting a message returns the agent that answers first and the thread as it is now. ## Long conversations Every model call has to fit the agent's **context window**, and Ollama silently drops whatever doesn't. Agent HQ works out each agent's window and fits the conversation into it. **The window comes from, in order:** 1. the agent's own **Context window** setting (Settings → Agents); 2. what the provider reports: for Ollama, the loaded model's context (`/api/ps`), else a Modelfile's `num_ctx` (`/api/show`); for vLLM-style servers, `max_model_len`; 3. a default: 4,096 for Ollama (the smallest it picks), 128K for cloud models. The agent editor shows the window it's using, where the number came from, how many tokens the agent's instructions take, and how much room that leaves for the conversation. **Ollama's window is set on the Ollama server, not per request.** The OpenAI-compatible endpoint Agent HQ uses can't change it. Set `OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH` on the server, or bake `num_ctx` into a Modelfile; otherwise Ollama picks 4K, 32K or 256K depending on GPU memory. Then set the same number on the agent if Agent HQ can't read it. **What happens as a conversation grows:** - **Compaction, between turns.** When the history, the agent's instructions and the new message would take more than 75% of the window, the older turns are summarised and replaced by the summary, and the recent turns stay word for word. - **Who writes the summary:** the agent's own model, unless you pick a summary model. - **Contents:** what you want, decisions and results, open work, and facts found with tools, with exact hostnames, IDs and paths. - **In the conversation:** a note says what was summarised, with the summary itself one click away. - **If the summary can't be written,** the older turns are dropped instead, and the agent is told. - **Trimming, within a turn.** During a long run of tool calls, older tool results are shortened, harder as the run nears the window. The size estimate is self-correcting: each model response reports how many tokens its request really took (tool definitions included, and models such as Qwen count code and JSON at about 3 characters a token, not 3.5), so the trimmer compares that with its own estimate and trims to the real figure. Without this, a long coding run could look 24k tokens to Agent HQ while the model received 32k, and the next tool call came back cut off. - **A warning,** once a day per conversation, when an agent's instructions alone don't fit its window. The instructions include its prompt, your profile, skills, memories, knowledge excerpts and tools. When that happens, Ollama is already cutting them. The thresholds, the summary length, the room kept for tools and the reply, and the default windows are under **Settings → System → Long conversations**. ## File attachments Attach files in the chat: the 📎 button, drag and drop onto the conversation, or paste (a pasted screenshot becomes `pasted-.png`). They upload as soon as you pick them, show as chips above the message box (✕ removes one), and go with your message when you send it. A message can be just files. **Code in replies:** every code block an agent writes has a bar with its language and **Copy** / **Save** buttons. Save downloads the code as a file, named the way the reply names it ("save it as `dungeon_rpg.py`"), or from a `# file: x.py` first line, else `snippet.` from the language. **Storage:** files live in the database (Postgres `bytea`), like avatars, so a worker on any machine reads the same bytes; no shared folder needed. Text is pulled out once, on upload: PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, HTML and EPUB through `markitdown`, plus Markdown, CSV, JSON, logs and code as they are. Scanned PDFs are read with OCR (see *Scanned PDFs* under the knowledge library). Limits: `AHQ_ATTACHMENT_MAX_BYTES` (25 MB) per file and `AHQ_ATTACHMENT_MAX_FILES` (10) per message. **What the agent gets:** the turn starts with a manifest: each file's ID (`att_…`), name, kind and size, and the first lines of each document. Its tools: | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `read_attachment` | A document's text, in pages (`next_offset` to continue) | | `look_at_attachment` | A question about an image, answered by the agent's **vision model** (the same one that looks at its desktop) | | `list_attachments` | Every file in the conversation, the user's and the agents' | | `attachment_to_workbench` | Copies a file to the agent's workbench (`inbox/` by default) so scripts can work on it | | `create_file` | Gives you a file it wrote (a report, CSV, JSON, a script) | | `send_from_workbench` | Gives you a file from its workbench (a chart a script made, an export) | | `attachment_to_desktop` | Copies a file onto the agent's desktop, into `~/Uploads`, and returns its path there, so it can upload it to a website | | `list_desktop_files` | The newest files the desktop downloaded (`~/Downloads` and the browser's download folder) | | `send_from_desktop` | Gives you a file from the desktop, e.g. an invoice the browser downloaded | The reading tools only appear once a conversation has files; `create_file` is always there. The workbench tools appear for agents with a workbench, and the desktop tools for agents with a desktop. **Uploading to a website:** the agent copies the file to its desktop, clicks the page's upload button or file field, then calls Playwright MCP's `browser_file_upload` with the path while the file chooser waits, so there's no dialog to click through. Playwright MCP only reads files inside its working folder; the desktop image starts it in `/config` (the desktop's home), which covers `~/Uploads`. Without the browser tools, the agent types the path into the file dialog. The file is also there for you in `~/Uploads` when you take over the desktop. **Getting downloads back:** pages the browser downloads land in `~/Downloads` or the Playwright MCP output folder (`/tmp/playwright-mcp`). `list_desktop_files` shows the newest of both, and `send_from_desktop` puts one in the chat. Desktop files can only be read from the desktop's home folder and that output folder. **Images, two ways** (Settings → Agents, under *Vision model*): - **Vision tool (the default):** the agent's own model never sees pixels. It asks its vision model with `look_at_attachment`, as it does with its desktop, so a text-only model on Ollama can still "see" a photo. - **Model sees images:** for an agent on a multimodal model (qwen3-vl, gpt-4.1, Claude…), image attachments go straight into its turn. They're taken out of the saved history afterwards (a placeholder stays), so a conversation doesn't carry megabytes of pictures; it can look again with `look_at_attachment`. With neither, the agent can read documents but tells you it can't view images. **Delegation:** every agent working in a conversation can read its files, so a supervisor passes your file on by ID: `delegate(agent_name=…, task=…, attachment_ids=["att_…"])`. The delegate gets the manifest with its task; the file shows on the delegation card. Files a delegate makes appear on its card and are listed in its result, so the supervisor can use them too. **Files agents send back** collect in the **Outputs** panel beside the chat, newest first; images also show as thumbnails under the reply (or on the delegation card for a delegate's files). Text files (code, config, Markdown, CSV, logs…) get a **view →** chip under the reply: it opens the file in Outputs, as does clicking the file there. An open file shows its contents with **Copy** and **Download**, and the panel widens while any file is open; click the file again, or **Collapse all**, to close it and narrow the panel. Archives and other binaries stay a download, with an **in Outputs →** chip under the reply that points at them. **After updating:** rebuild the workbench and desktop images. The file transfers use hidden `ahq_*` tools in them. **Safety:** downloads are served with `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox` and `nosniff`, and only real images (PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, checked by decoding them) open in the browser. An uploaded HTML or SVG file always downloads; it never runs on Agent HQ's origin. Workbench and desktop transfers go through internal `ahq_put_file` / `ahq_get_file` (and, on desktops, `ahq_list_files`) tools on those servers. Agents never see them; they use the tools in the table above. Agents on cloud models send the attachments they read to that provider. **API:** `POST /api/threads/{id}/attachments` (multipart `files`), then `POST /api/threads/{id}/messages` with `{"content": "…", "attachment_ids": ["…"]}`. `GET /api/attachments/{id}` returns the file (`?download=1` forces a download), `GET /api/attachments/{id}/text` its text, `GET /api/threads/{id}/attachments` the list. `DELETE /api/attachments/{id}` removes a file that hasn't been sent. ## Knowledge library **Settings → Knowledge** makes your own documents and notes searchable by agents, with citations. Documents live in **collections**, and each collection says which agents may read it (none ticked means every agent; sub-agents read what their parent can). **Sources:** - **Obsidian vault (Git):** - **Sync:** push the vault to your Gitea with the Obsidian Git community plugin, set to auto commit and push every 10 minutes or so, with `.obsidian/` in `.gitignore`. Agent HQ clones the repo read-only and checks for changes on a schedule (every 15 minutes by default). Only notes that changed are re-read, and deleted notes leave the library. - **Notes are read the Obsidian way:** frontmatter titles, aliases and tags, inline `#tags`, `[[wikilinks]]` (kept as links, shown as text), `%%comments%%` dropped. - **Citations** open the note in Obsidian (`obsidian://`). - **Skipped folders:** `.obsidian`, `.trash` and `.git` always; add your own excludes (`Journal/**`). - **Access:** use a dedicated Gitea user with **Read** access to just that repo, and a token with *repository: Read*. Tokens are never sent back to the browser, and errors are shown with the token redacted. - **Git repository:** the same for any repo of runbooks or docs. Citations link to the file in Gitea. - **Network share (SMB / NFS):** a share on your NAS (TrueNAS, a Windows server, Samba), read in place and never written to. - **SMB:** give the share as `smb://truenas.home.arpa/docs/Runbooks` or `\\truenas\docs\Runbooks` (a folder inside the share is fine), with a user and password. Agent HQ reads it over the network with `smbprotocol`, so the container needs no mount and no extra privileges. On TrueNAS, make a dedicated user (say `agent-hq`) and give it read-only access to the dataset. The password is never sent back to the browser, and errors are shown with it redacted. - **NFS:** mount the export into the `hq` container under `/shares` (`AHQ_SHARES_DIR`) and give that path, e.g. `/shares/docs`. `docker-compose.yml` has a commented-out example that has Docker mount it read-only. Paths outside `/shares` are refused, so a source can't read the app's own data. Symlinks aren't followed. A local folder bind-mounted under `/shares` works the same way. - **Reads:** Markdown, text, PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel and HTML by default (change the include patterns under Edit). Only files whose size or modified time changed are read again, and deleted files leave the library. - **Skipped:** ZFS snapshot folders (`.zfs`), recycle bins (`#recycle`, `.recycle`, `$RECYCLE.BIN`), Office lock files (`~$…`), macOS and Windows clutter, `.obsidian`, `.trash` and `.git`; add your own excludes (`Archive/**`). A source stops with an error past 20,000 matching files: point it at a narrower folder. - **Obsidian vault:** tick it for a vault kept on the share (synced there with Syncthing, say). Notes are read the Obsidian way and citations open in Obsidian. - **Web page:** fetched, turned into text, and re-checked on a schedule if you like. - **Uploaded files:** PDF, Word, PowerPoint, Excel, HTML, Markdown and text (converted with `markitdown`). **Scanned PDFs:** pages that are an image with next to no text layer are read with Tesseract OCR, wherever a PDF comes from: uploads, Git, shares, web pages and chat attachments. A PDF with no such pages is converted as before. Otherwise its text is rebuilt page by page under `## Page N` headings (the text layer where a page has one, OCR where it doesn't), so search sections and citations follow the pages. The image installs Tesseract with English. - **Settings:** `AHQ_OCR` (`auto`, the default, is on when Tesseract is installed; `on`; `off`), `AHQ_OCR_LANGUAGES` (`eng`; Tesseract codes joined with `+`, e.g. `eng+deu`), `AHQ_OCR_DPI` (300) and `AHQ_OCR_MAX_PAGES` (200 scanned pages per file; the rest are skipped with a warning in the log). - **Other languages:** build with `--build-arg OCR_LANGS="deu fra"` (Debian's `tesseract-ocr-` packages) and set `AHQ_OCR_LANGUAGES=eng+deu+fra`. - **Speed:** about a second or two per page on a modern CPU, run in the background. Large scans take a while to show up in the library. - **Without OCR:** a fully scanned PDF is refused with the reason (upload) or skipped and logged (Git, shares), rather than stored empty. **How it's indexed:** documents are cut into sections at their headings and embedded with the embedding model from Settings → Memory. Search is hybrid (meaning plus keywords, with full-text search on Postgres); without an embedding model it matches keywords only. **What agents get:** - matching excerpts automatically, like memories (per collection, with a threshold); - `search_knowledge` and `read_document` tools; - instructions to say which document and section they used. **The page itself** also has: - a test search, run as any agent, showing scores and what would come up by itself; - a document viewer that shows each document's sections; - **Propose skills,** which turns a runbook's procedures into skill proposals. Agents on cloud models send the excerpts they read to that provider. Keep private collections to agents on local models. ### Documents agents suggest Agents can suggest additions to the library: a runbook they worked out, research findings, a summary of a long investigation. **Nothing goes in until you approve it.** **Where suggestions go:** - **Agent Findings,** a collection made for this and open to every agent. Suggestions go here unless an agent is asked to use another collection. - **Your own collections** only take suggestions when you allow it in the collection's settings. Under *Agents may suggest documents*, pick **No** (the default), **Any agent that can read it**, or **These agents**. An agent can also only suggest for collections it can read. **How they're made:** - An agent calls `suggest_knowledge` with a title, a reason, and either Markdown text or a file from the conversation (`attachment_id`). `knowledge_targets` lists the collections it may use. - A reflection can also suggest one document after a job that produced reference material: not a procedure (that's a skill), not a short fact (that's a lesson). - Agents get these tools when their learning mode isn't **off**. **Settings → Knowledge → Agents may suggest documents** turns them off for everyone. **Deciding:** a card appears in the conversation and in **Requests → Knowledge**, plus a `knowledge_proposal` MQTT notice with a link. You can approve or reject from either place: - **Edit** the title and text first. - **Move** it to any collection. Yours to choose, whatever the agent was allowed. - **Replace** a near-copy. If the document looks like one already in that collection, the card says so; when that one also came from an agent, you can replace it instead of adding a second. - **Reject** with a note. The agent is told your note if it suggests the same thing again. **Limits:** at most 5 suggestions waiting per agent, and at most 60,000 characters each. **What's stored:** approved documents go into the collection's **Suggested by agents** source. Each is tagged with the agent's name (`agent/scarlett`), and its citation links back to the conversation it came from. You can delete them like uploads. **Kept separate from your own sources:** suggestions are never written to your Obsidian vault or Git sources. ## Evals **Settings → Evals** shows whether agents, and the skills they learn, actually get better. A **test case** is three things: - a request for an agent; - the checks its answer must pass: a rubric graded by the judge, the reply contains or doesn't contain some text, calls or doesn't call a tool, loads a skill; - the tool results recorded from the job it came from. **Replay, so tests never touch your lab:** - **Recorded calls:** a call that matches the recording gets the recorded result. - **Calls with no recording:** they run for real only if the tool is set to Allow *and* ticked **Safe in tests** (Settings → Tools). Anything else is told "not available in a test run", and the result shows it. - **Ask and Block tools** never run in a test, and no approval requests are raised. - **Agent HQ's own tools:** the read-only ones (skills, knowledge search, memory recall) run normally. Ones that would change something (memories, delegation, proposals) are stubbed. Full tool results are kept for 14 days so you can turn any recent reply into a test. **Where cases come from:** - a 👎 with a note, or a correction, drafts one, and you click **Keep**; - the flask button under any reply ("Make this a test"); - writing one yourself. Feedback never changes a test you've kept: a later note starts a fresh draft. **When they run:** - **On skill changes:** when an agent proposes one, the cases for that agent and skill run without and with the change, and the proposal card shows both pass rates. - **In Auto learning mode:** a change that lowers the pass rate isn't applied; it waits in Requests for you. - **Anytime:** **Run now** on a case, or **Run all**. **The judge** is any provider and model you pick, switchable any time: a strong local model, your ChatGPT plan, or any OpenAI-compatible service. Pick one that isn't grading its own work. ## Scheduled tasks The **Scheduler** (above Settings in the sidebar) gives agents tasks to run on a schedule: every N hours, daily, on chosen days of the week, monthly, or any cron expression. - **Time zone:** each schedule has its own (your browser's by default), and daylight-saving changes are handled: "every day at 7:00 AM" stays at 7:00 AM local time. - **Where results go:** each schedule has its own conversation, `Scheduled: `, which appears in the sidebar like any chat. - **What a run is:** it posts a short "Scheduled run" note, then gives the agent the task as a turn, exactly as if you'd typed it. Delegation, tools and memory all work as usual, and so do the delegation threads. - **Editor:** shows the cadence in plain English and the next three run times as you change it. It also lists recent runs with their status (queued, running, done, failed, skipped), and has **Run now** (doesn't move the schedule) and **Open conversation**. **Reliability:** - **Which process runs it:** the API process checks for due schedules every 20 seconds. Each run is claimed with a Valkey lock, so it fires exactly once even if you run several API processes. - **After an outage:** if Agent HQ was down when a run was due, it runs **once** when it comes back, not once per missed slot, and the note says it ran late. - **Overlapping runs:** with **Skip a run if the previous one is still going** on (the default), a run is skipped rather than piling up behind a slow one. - **Disabled agent:** if a schedule's agent is disabled, its runs are recorded as skipped. - **Turning it off:** set `AHQ_SCHEDULER=0` to stop an API process from running schedules. Monthly schedules can be set for days 1 to 28 only, so they happen every month. For "the last day of the month" or anything else unusual, use a custom cron expression. ## Standing goals (the Board) A **standing goal** is an outcome with a definition of done, given to one agent: "Every VLAN has a note in the vault", "pve2's backups finish inside the window three nights running".
