The agent breaks it into **next actions** and keeps working it, one action at a time, across as many turns as it takes, until it can show the done criteria are met. It's Getting Things Done on a Kanban board: the goal is the project, the actions are its next actions, and the **Board** (in the sidebar, above the Scheduler) is the external memory, so the agent never has to hold the original problem in its context window. ```mermaid flowchart LR B["Backlog
(yours)"] -- "you move it" --> R["Ready"] R -- "free WIP slot:
the agent pulls it" --> P["In progress"] P <-- "delegate, approval,
your answer, a time" --> W["Waiting"] P -- "claim_done
+ evidence" --> V["Review"] V -- "you confirm" --> D["Done"] V -- "you send it back
(with a note)" --> P P -- "no progress, a limit,
or Stop" --> X["Blocked"] X -- "you resume it" --> P ``` **Columns, and who moves cards:** - **Backlog:** captured, not agreed to. Agents never pull from it. - **Ready:** you've said "yes, do this". The agent pulls the highest-priority Ready goal (then board order) when it has a free WIP slot. - **In progress, Waiting, Review:** the agent's and the runner's. Waiting shows what it's waiting on: a background delegation, a tool approval, you on its desktop, your answer, or a check-back time. - **Blocked** (shown in In progress, flagged red): a guard stopped it, or you pressed Stop in its conversation. **Resume** puts it back. - **Done** and **Dropped** (shown in Done): finished, or abandoned. **Reopen** sends either back to Ready. You can drag cards between Backlog, Ready, In progress and Done in the agent's own lane. Errors (a full WIP limit, a proposal not yet approved) show above the board. **WIP limits.** Each agent has a **goal WIP limit** (Settings → Agents → Standing goals; default 1, 0 = it takes no goals). Goals that are in progress, waiting or blocked all hold a slot, so a blocked goal stops that agent pulling new work until you deal with it, which is the Kanban signal to fix it or move it. Inside a goal, only **one next action** can be in progress at a time; the agent has to finish, block or drop it before starting another. That's the guard against losing track of the original problem. **The goal runner** runs in the API process and checks the board every `AHQ_GOALS_TICK` seconds (5): 1. **Pull.** For each agent with free slots, move its next Ready goal to In progress. Each goal gets its own conversation, `Goal: `, in the sidebar. 2. **Advance.** For each goal in progress with nothing running in its conversation, queue a **goal turn**. Its prompt is the card itself: the objective, the done criteria, the next actions with their status and results, the last 12 log entries, and your note if you sent a done claim back. The agent doesn't rely on the conversation's history to know where it is, so compaction can't make it lose the thread. 3. **Wait and resume.** A background delegation shows as Waiting and resumes once the delegate's result has been reported in the conversation. Approvals and desktop hand-offs show as Waiting while they're pending. "Wait for the user" resumes when you post in the goal's conversation; "check back in N minutes" resumes when the time comes. 4. **Guard.** A goal is **blocked** when it goes `stall_turns` goal turns in a row without changing anything on the board (default 3), reaches its **turn** limit (40), its **hours** limit (72, wall clock since it started), or its **model requests** limit (400, counted from the usage ledger for everything that ran in its conversation, delegates included). You get a card in Requests → Goals and a `goal_blocked` MQTT notice. Raise a limit on the card (Edit → Limits) before resuming a goal that hit one. Only one API process should look at a goal at a time; a Valkey lock per goal makes that so, however many API processes run the runner. Set `AHQ_GOALS=0` to stop an API process from running it. **Agent tools,** given only to the goal's owner, in the goal's own conversation (delegates working there don't get them): | Tool | What it does | |---|---| | `board_view` | The card: objective, done criteria, actions with IDs, recent log | | `add_action(title, details, after)` | Adds a next action (to do). `after` lists the actions that must be done before it can start | | `start_action(id)` | Starts one; refused while another of its own is in progress, or while anything in its `after` list isn't done | | `complete_action(id, result)` | Finishes one, keeping what it found or did on the board | | `block_action` / `drop_action(id, reason)` | It can't go on as it is / it isn't needed | | `log_note(text)` | A note on the log; doesn't count as progress | | `wait_for(kind, reason, minutes)` | `user`: asks you something and waits for your answer. `time`: checks back later (5 minutes to a week) | | `claim_done(evidence)` | Moves the goal to Review with the evidence; refused while its team is still working | | `delegate_action(id, agent_name, instructions)` | Agents with a team and agents to delegate to: hands a startable action to one of its existing agents (see below) | | `assign_action(id, role, why_not_existing_agents, instructions, model, tools)` | Agents with a team allowed sub-agents: hands a startable action to a new sub-agent (see below) | The agent can't change the objective or the done criteria; only you can (Edit on the card). If it thinks they're wrong, it's told to say so and wait for you. **Done is your call.** A done claim shows up in the goal's conversation, in **Requests → Goals** (with the sidebar badge) and on MQTT as `goal_review`. **Confirm done** finishes it and frees the slot; **Send back** returns it to In progress with your note, which the agent sees at the top of its next goal turn. **Agents propose goals.** Every agent (not sub-agents) has `propose_goal(title, objective, done_criteria, reason, agent_name)` for multi-step work it notices but wasn't asked to do. A proposal lands in Backlog, flagged *proposed*, for itself or another agent, with a card in the conversation, in Requests → Goals and on MQTT (`goal_proposal`). It can't leave Backlog until you **Approve to Ready**, **Approve to Backlog** or **Reject** it. At most 5 proposals per agent wait at once. **Creating goals:** **+ New goal** on the Board, or the flag button under any agent reply ("Make this a goal"), which opens the form with that reply as the objective. Write the done criteria so anyone could check them: they're what the agent works toward and what you'll review against. **On the card:** the objective and done criteria, the next actions (you can add, start, finish or drop them too), the full log, a box for notes to the agent, and how much of each limit it has used. **MQTT notices** on `AHQ_MQTT_NOTIFY_TOPIC`: `goal_review`, `goal_proposal`, `goal_question` and `goal_blocked`, each with the goal's ID, title, agent and a link (`AHQ_PUBLIC_URL`). ### Teams: your agents and sub-agents working a goal's actions in parallel An agent can form a team for a goal: while it works one next action itself, team members work other actions of the same goal in parallel. Team members are **its existing agents** (the ones it may delegate to) and, if it's allowed them, **new sub-agents**. It's swarming, in Kanban terms: the agent's goal WIP stays where it is (one outcome at a time, by default), and the *action* WIP inside that goal grows by its team. ```mermaid flowchart LR L["Lead: works its own<br/>action, one at a time"] -- "delegate_action(a2, Breaker)" --> A1["Breaker<br/>(your agent) works a2"] L -- "assign_action(a3)" --> S2["Sub-agent<br/>works a3"] A1 -- "result on a2:<br/>done or blocked" --> B[("Board")] S2 -- "result on a3" --> B B -- "a4 (after a2, a3)<br/>becomes startable" --> L ``` **Turning it on:** Settings → Agents → Standing goals → **Team size** (parallel actions per goal: the agent plus its team members; default 1 = no team). It takes effect when the agent has agents under **Can delegate to**, or sub-agents set to *Ask me first* or *Allowed within limits*, or both. With sub-agents only, *Allowed within limits* caps it by the sub-agent limit **At once** (the editor says so when it is); with agents on the team, that limit still applies to the sub-agents it creates, not to the team size. **How it works:** - **Serial stays serial.** When the agent adds an action that needs others' results, or would clash with them, it lists them in `after`. An action is startable, by the agent or its team, only when everything in its `after` list is done (dropped ones don't hold it up). The card shows what each action waits for. - **Your agents first.** `delegate_action` hands an action to one of the agents the lead may delegate to. That agent works it as a background delegated task with everything it already has: its own model, tools, memory, skills, knowledge and desktop. It shows in the conversation as a delegation card with the action and the lead's instructions. Each agent works one action per goal at a time, and the usual delegation rules apply (no loops back up the chain, the depth limit, *ask first* for work a webhook started). The goal turn's instructions name the lead's agents and tell it to use them before creating sub-agents, and to use `delegate_action` rather than `delegate` for a whole action, so it keeps working while they do. - **Sub-agents for the rest.** `assign_action` creates a sub-agent through the normal sub-agent path, so everything already set for sub-agents applies: the mode (in *Ask me first*, the agent asks with `request_subagents` first, and your approval covers the goal's conversation), the models and tool servers it may give them (including a cloud model, which matters when the local GPU is busy), minutes and model requests each, how many at once and per day, and the team-wide limits. Sub-agents on a team never get a desktop and can't create sub-agents of their own. - **No duplicates of your agents.** As with any sub-agent, the lead has to say why none of your existing agents should do the action (`why_not_existing_agents`), and a sub-agent whose role names one of your agents, or whose work is close to one's description, is refused with a pointer to that agent: `delegate_action` when the lead can delegate to it (under an approved *Ask me first* request, only an outright name clash is refused, since the request already showed you any overlap). The comparison uses the role, the action and the lead's instructions for it, not the goal and team context in the briefing, so a long briefing can't water it down. - **What a team member is told:** the goal and its objective, its one action and the lead's instructions for it, and what the team has found so far (the results of the actions it depends on, and the latest others). It's told not to change anything outside its action. - **Results land on the board.** A team member's result goes onto its action, before anything else happens when it finishes: *done* completes it with what it found; *partial* or *failed* blocks it with the reason, for the lead to re-plan. There's no report turn per result: the next goal turn's card shows every result, with who did it, marked *your agent* or *sub-agent*. - **The runner keeps the lead busy.** While its team works, the lead keeps getting goal turns as long as it has something of its own: its action in progress, a blocked action to re-plan, or a startable one to take or hand over. When everything left is either with the team or waiting on it, the goal shows as **Waiting on its team**, and resumes as results come in. - **Same guards, same review.** The goal's model-request limit counts its team too, a team result counts as progress, `claim_done` is refused while any team member is still working, and you still confirm done. Stop (or dropping the goal) stops the whole team, and their actions go back to to-do. - **You can step in:** drop an action a team member is working on, and its late result is noted in the log but not applied. On the board, a card with a team shows **team ×N** while N team members are working, and its action list shows who's working or did each action (tagged *agent* or *sub-agent*), and what each waits for. The goal's detail names who the lead can put on its team. **Built for incidents next.** The board's rows aren't specific to goals: each work item has a kind, a source and a correlation key, and the same columns, runner, next actions and WIP rules will carry incidents (alerts grouped into one problem to solve) later. ## Notifications: Telegram, Discord and MQTT Everything that waits for you shows up in the **Requests** inbox: tool approvals, sub-agent requests, skill, profile and knowledge proposals, done claims, proposed goals, goal questions and desktop take-overs. **Notification channels** (Settings → Notifications) send these to you as well, together with agents' **alerts**. Chat channels also take your answers, so you can handle most of them from your phone. ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Requests and alerts<br/>(tool approvals, proposals,<br/>goal questions, send_alert)"] --> N["Notices<br/>(routing rules:<br/>type × agent × severity)"] N --> T["Telegram bot"] N --> DC["Discord bot"] N --> M["MQTT topic"] T -- "buttons, replies,<br/>messages" --> I["Inbox<br/>(paired accounts only)"] DC -- "buttons, replies,<br/>DMs, mentions" --> I I --> D["the same decisions<br/>as the web UI"] I --> C["your message in<br/>the conversation"] C --> A["the agent's answer<br/>back to the chat"] ``` - **Channels:** **MQTT** publishes each notice's event JSON on a topic, as before (it's set up for you from `AHQ_MQTT_URL` and the old Settings → Sub-agents switch). **Telegram** and **Discord** use a bot of your own. Both are drivers on one framework (`app/channels/`): what to send, who may answer and what an answer does are shared, so they behave the same. - **Routing rules:** each channel has one or more rules. A rule picks notice types (none = all), agents (none = all) and, for alerts, the lowest severity it takes. A notice goes to a channel when any of its rules match, so "tool approvals and goal questions from everyone, plus Breaker's and Mainframe's critical alerts" is two rules. - **No inbound access needed.** Agent HQ reads a Telegram bot's messages by long polling (`getUpdates`), and keeps a Gateway websocket open to Discord (resuming it after a drop, so nothing is missed). Nothing on the internet has to reach Agent HQ. The listeners run in the API process (`AHQ_CHANNELS=1`, the default); a Valkey lock keeps a second API process from reading the same bot. **Setting up Telegram:** 1. Create a bot with @BotFather (`/newbot`) and copy its token. 2. Under **Settings → Notifications**, choose **+ New… → Telegram bot**, paste the token and save. Agent HQ checks it with Telegram (`getMe`) and stores it encrypted when `AHQ_SECRET_KEY` is set; it's never shown again. 3. **Pair an account:** this makes a one-time code that's valid for 10 minutes. Open the `t.me` link it shows and tap **Start**, or send the bot `/start <code>`. Only paired accounts get notices and can answer. Anyone else who finds the bot is ignored without a reply, and logged under **Recent activity**. 4. **Send a test** to check it arrives. **Setting up Discord:** 1. In the [Discord Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications), create an application. On its **Bot** page, **Reset Token** and copy it. 2. Under **Settings → Notifications**, choose **+ New… → Discord bot**, paste the token and save. Agent HQ checks it with Discord and stores it the same way as a Telegram token. 3. Use the channel's **invite link** to add the bot to a server you're in. Discord only lets you DM a bot you share a server with. 4. **Pair an account:** - **In a DM:** send the bot `!start <code>`, and notices come to your DMs. - **In a server channel:** post `@YourBot !start <code>` there, and notices go to that channel. Only paired accounts can press its buttons or talk to the bot; everyone else in the channel is ignored. 5. **Send a test.** Commands start with `!` on Discord (`!new`, `!help`), since Discord keeps `/` for its own commands. Discord only shows a bot the text of some messages unless it has the privileged **Message Content** intent: - **Always visible:** DMs, messages that @mention the bot, and replies to its messages (with *ping on reply* on, which is Discord's default). - **Without the intent:** that's everything above needs, so leave it off. - **With it:** tick **Message Content** on the channel to talk in a paired server channel without mentioning the bot. Turn it on for the bot in the Developer Portal as well (**Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents**), or Discord refuses the connection, and the channel shows that error. On Discord, notices are embeds coloured by kind (alerts by severity), and agents' answers are plain messages, so their Markdown renders. A button press is answered only to the person who pressed it. **Answering from the chat:** - **Buttons decide the request** with the same code the web UI uses: ✅ Approve / ❌ Deny for tool approvals, sub-agent requests (as asked; change the terms in Agent HQ) and proposals; ✅ Confirm done / ↩️ Send back for done claims; To Ready / To Backlog / Reject for proposed goals. - **A reply that starts with approve/yes or deny/no** decides it too, and the rest becomes your note: "no, not on a Friday". - **Any other reply to a notice** (a goal question, an alert, an agent's answer) goes to that notice's conversation as your message. - **A message that isn't a reply** goes to the channel's **default agent**, in a conversation of the channel's own. `/new` (`!new` on Discord) starts a fresh one, and `/help` (`!help`) lists the commands. - **Answers come back:** - The agent's answer to a turn you started from the chat is sent back to the chat. - So is anything in the channel's own conversation. - After you answer from the chat, that conversation's background reports and follow-ups go there too, for **Follow-ups for** minutes (default 30). Goal turns, events and schedules don't follow you there. - **Every copy is settled:** whichever way a request is decided (web UI, Telegram, Discord, another paired account), each message about it is edited to show the outcome ("✅ Approved via Phone (Mike)") and loses its buttons. Tapping a stale button says what already happened. **Decide from the chat** can be turned off per channel. Requests then arrive with a link only, and you decide them in Agent HQ, behind its sign-in and two-factor. Every decision, reply, chat, pairing and refusal on a channel is logged under its **Recent activity**, with the sender. **Alerts.** Tick **Alerts** on an agent (Settings → Agents) to give it `send_alert(message, severity)`. It's for things you should know about now, such as an outage or a failure that needs you, not for routine results. The alert goes to the channels whose rules take `agent_alert` at that severity (info, warning or critical). Replying to it continues the agent's conversation. Each agent may send at most **Alerts per agent per hour** (Settings → Notifications, default 10); beyond that, the tool refuses. ## Sub-agents Agents can create temporary **sub-agents** for parts of their own task (say, reading twelve feeds in parallel). It's off for every agent until you turn it on, per agent, under **Settings → Agents → Sub-agents**: - **Off** (the default): the agent has no sub-agent tools at all. - **Ask me first:** the agent gets `request_subagents`. It sends you a request, like a staffing request: which sub-agents, what each is for, why it needs them, why none of your existing agents fits, which model and tools each needs, and how long. You decide; it can only create them after you approve, and only within what you approve. - **Allowed within limits:** the agent may create sub-agents itself, within the limits set on it. **Limits, all enforced in code:** - **Per agent:** how many at once, per task and per day, minutes each, and model requests each. Also which models sub-agents may use (empty = the agent's own model) and which of its tool servers they may have. - **Team-wide** (**Settings → Sub-agents**): running at once and created per day across all agents, open requests per agent, and how long an unanswered request stays open. - **Enforcement:** every spawn is checked under a Valkey lock, so several workers can't race past a limit. A sub-agent's run stops at its request limit (PydanticAI `UsageLimits`) and its time limit, and the sub-agent retires as soon as it reports back. Anything left over (a crashed worker, say) is retired by a sweep when it expires. - **No nesting:** sub-agents can't delegate or create sub-agents of their own. - **No desktops:** sub-agents are never given a desktop tool server, since two agents can't drive one desktop. **No duplicates of agents you've defined.** If an existing agent is meant for the work, the agent should delegate to it instead. This is enforced three ways: - **A rule** in the agent's instructions, which names your agents. - **A required explanation:** `why_not_existing_agents` must be filled in. - **A refusal check:** a sub-agent whose role reuses an agent's name is always refused. With an embedding model set (Settings → Memory), the role and task are also compared with every agent's description, and anything above the similarity setting (Settings → Sub-agents, default 0.78) is refused. The refusal tells the agent which agent to delegate to. On requests, near misses show up as warnings for you, and approving them is your call. **Requests.** A request appears in three places: - **In the conversation:** an approval card with the agent's reasoning and the system's own estimate. The estimate covers, for each sub-agent: the model and its size (from the provider's model list), whether it runs on your hardware or a cloud plan, free provider slots, and the usage ledger's averages for that model. It also gives the total model-minutes and the expected wall time. - **In the Requests inbox:** under **Requests → Sub-agent requests**, with a badge for pending requests. - **On MQTT**, if `AHQ_MQTT_URL` is set (see below). You can approve as asked or change the terms first: the number of sub-agents, how many at once, minutes, model requests, models, tools, and how long the approval lasts. You can also deny it, with or without a note. An approval is a grant for that agent in that conversation, and it expires. Your decision wakes the conversation: - **If the conversation is the agent's own,** it carries on with (or without) the sub-agents. - **If the agent asked while working on a task delegated to it,** the conversation's owner is told and delegates the task again. **MQTT notifications.** New requests and your decisions are published as JSON to `AHQ_MQTT_NOTIFY_TOPIC` (default `agent-hq/notifications`) on the broker in `AHQ_MQTT_URL`, using a client ID of their own. This is now the **MQTT** channel under Settings → Notifications, where you can turn it off, change its topic or narrow what it gets (see [Notifications](#notifications-telegram-discord-and-mqtt)). Set `AHQ_PUBLIC_URL` (for example `http://shockwave:8000`) to include a link to the request. ```json {"type": "subagent_request", "request_id": "…", "agent": "Duke", "why": "…", "subagents": [{"role": "Feed reader", "purpose": "…", "label": "qwen3:14b @ Einstein Ollama", "est_minutes": 5}], "total_minutes": 5, "hours": 2, "link": "http://shockwave:8000/requests?id=…", "at": "…"} {"type": "subagent_decision", "request_id": "…", "agent": "Duke", "status": "approved", "grant": {…}, "note": "…"} ``` **In the chat,** a sub-agent's work shows as a crumb marked *sub-agent*, with its role and model. Expand it for the task, the reason it was created, and its report. Sub-agents never appear in your agent lists, the New chat menu, teams or exports. ### Provider slots and the usage ledger - **Slots:** each model provider has **Max concurrent requests** (Settings → Model providers; 0 = no limit). It caps how many model calls run against that provider at once, across every worker, so a burst of agents and sub-agents queues instead of swamping a GPU box. Slots are leases in Valkey that are renewed while a call runs, so a crashed worker can't hold one for more than 90 seconds. - **The ledger:** every agent run (chat turn, delegated task or sub-agent task) is recorded with its model, model requests, tokens and wall-clock time. **Settings → Usage** totals these by agent (sub-agent runs count under the agent that created them), by model and by day. Request estimates use the same numbers. - **Daily budgets** aren't built yet, on purpose: watch the real numbers here first. ## Disabling and deleting agents Removing an agent takes two deliberate steps on the **Settings → Agents** page: 1. **Disable** stops the agent: it takes no new work, other agents stop delegating to it, and its conversations stay readable. Tick **Enabled** and save to bring it back. 2. **Delete permanently** appears once the agent is disabled. It shows what will go and asks you to type the agent's name to confirm. It can't be undone. Deleting an agent removes: - its conversations: messages, files, jobs, traces and model history, including huddles it started (it leaves the huddles it joined, which stay) - its schedules and event subscriptions - its own memories and skills, test cases, proposals, ratings, reflections, tool approvals and sub-agent requests - its avatar and any sub-agents it made Some things are kept: - **Usage ledger:** cost history stays intact. - **Shared learning:** team memories, team skills and knowledge-library documents stay. - **Goals it owned:** these go back to your backlog with no owner, and actions it was working go back to Ready. An agent with work queued or running can't be deleted until that work finishes or you stop it. **API:** `DELETE /api/agents/{id}` disables. `GET /api/agents/{id}/delete-plan` returns what a delete would remove and whether it's allowed now. `DELETE /api/agents/{id}/permanent` deletes a disabled agent (`409` with the reason otherwise). ## Avatars Each agent can also have **pronouns** (he/him, she/her, they/them…). Teammates see them in the roster and with delegated results, so a supervisor refers to them correctly. Give each agent a face on the **Settings → Agents** page: **Upload avatar** accepts a GIF (animated is fine), PNG, JPEG or WebP image up to 3 MB (`AHQ_AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`). Avatars appear in the agent list, the conversation list, the chat header, next to each reply, and on desktop-help banners. Agents without one get their initials on a colour derived from their name. - **Storage:** images are kept in the database, so every machine serves the same ones, and they're included in agent export and import. - **Animation:** how animated GIFs behave is a per-browser setting on the **Settings → System** page: - *Always animate* - *Only while the agent is working* - *Never*: shows the first frame; hovering plays the animation. Browsers set to reduce motion default to *Never*. - **Working indicator:** an agent that's currently working also gets a highlighted ring around its avatar. ## Local-first models Three features let local models do most of the work, so frontier models are only used when needed. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Agent's main model<br/>(local, text-only)"] subgraph desktop["Agent desktop container"] PW["Playwright MCP :8931<br/>page as accessibility text"] CH["Chromium<br/>(same window you see)"] DM["desktop MCP :8765<br/>screenshot, click, type"] end V["Vision model<br/>(small local VLM)"] F["Fallback model<br/>(frontier, optional)"] A -- "browser_navigate / snapshot / click by ref" --> PW PW -- CDP --> CH A -- "look(question) / click_on(description)" --> V V -- "screenshots" --> DM V -- "text answer or x,y" --> A A -. "error, runaway loop, or escalate()" .-> F ``` ### 1. Read web pages as text (Playwright MCP) Each desktop container now runs a Chromium window (kept on the desktop, with its profile in `/config/agent-browser`) and a [Playwright MCP](https://playwright.dev/mcp/snapshots) server attached to it over the DevTools Protocol. Agents read pages as an accessibility snapshot, a text tree in which every element has a ref, and click or type by ref. That brings some big advantages: - Any text model can browse; no vision model is involved. - Clicks are exact rather than guessed coordinates. - It costs far fewer tokens than screenshots. - It works in the same browser you see, so a login you do through take-control stays in place for the agent. Every desktop made under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches** registers it for you as `desktop-N-browser` (`http://desktop-N:8931/mcp`, **Controls an agent desktop** ticked, *Prefix tool names* unticked, since its tools are already called `browser_*`). Agents should call `browser_snapshot` after navigating to read the page. ### 2. Vision as a tool (per-agent vision model) Set a **Vision model** on an agent, for example `qwen3-vl:8b` from your Ollama provider. The agent's main model then never sees screenshots, so its context stays small and it can be a text-only model. Instead it gets three tools: - `look(question)`: a text answer about what's on screen, such as "CPU peaked at 87% at 14:20". - `locate(description)`: the x/y position of something described in words. - `click_on(description)`: locate it, then click. The vision model does the looking. Screenshot tools on that agent's desktop servers are hidden from the main model. Two settings tune it for the vision model you pick: - **Coordinates:** *0–1000 scale* for the Qwen-VL family and Holo models; *pixels* for UI-TARS. - **Zoom in to double-check clicks:** after a first guess, the area around it is cropped, enlarged and checked again. That takes one more vision call, but small local models land much more accurately with it. Good local choices are `qwen3-vl:4b` or `qwen3-vl:8b` (in Ollama) for reading screens and graphs, and Holo2 or UI-TARS-1.5 for precise clicking. The last two are served through vLLM or llama.cpp as an *OpenAI-compatible* provider. With 16 GB of VRAM, keep in mind that the main model and the vision model each need to load; a 14B text model plus a 4B vision model fit more comfortably than gpt-oss:20b plus an 8B. ### 3. Fallback model Set a **Fallback model** on an agent, for example `gpt-4.1` from OpenAI. The turn is rerun on it when any of these happens: - the main model errors, for instance because the Ollama server is down; - it runs away, hitting the per-run request limit while looping on tool calls; - it calls `escalate(reason)` itself. Agents with a fallback are told to do this when a task is beyond them. The switch shows up in the conversation and the live activity panel. The fallback can't escalate again. It doesn't start the turn over: it gets everything the main model did up to its last complete step (its tool calls and their results), with a note to take over from there and finish the task, so work already done isn't repeated. **Guardrails for the main model.** Two settings on an agent (Settings → Agents) make a stuck local model fail in minutes instead of running on: - **Max output tokens**: the most one model response may generate, thinking included. A model that thinks without end stops here instead of filling the context window. Leave room for the biggest file the agent writes in one call: 16,384 is a reasonable start for a coding agent. When a tool call is cut off at this limit, Ollama can't read it and answers with a server error (500) instead of saying the model ran out of room. The client would quietly send the request again, and on a local GPU each try can take 5 minutes (8,192 tokens at 25 a second). So when this limit is set, Agent HQ makes a single attempt per request. On a 500, how long the request ran tells the two causes apart, using the model's measured speed: - **Cut off** (it had written close to the limit): Agent HQ says so in the chat and tries once more on the same model, telling it to keep each tool call well under the limit by writing big files in parts (`write_file`, then `write_file` with `append=true`). If that fails too, the fallback takes over as usual. - **Unreadable** (well under the limit: the model got the call's JSON wrong, usually quotes in a shell command with code inside): it tries again on the same model up to 3 times in a turn, naming the tool in the note, and from the second slip on telling the model to keep code out of shell commands. Only a fourth goes to the fallback, since redoing one step costs far less than the local model's whole run. The workbench's `run_shell` description already steers models away from heredocs, towards `write_file` and `run_python`. - **Request time limit**: a deadline in seconds for one model request, every client retry included. Without it, a request can wait for the client's 10-minute timeout and then be retried twice. - **Model requests per run**: the most model requests one run may make, 50 if left blank. It stops a model looping on tool calls, but a coding agent working through a big task (write, run, read, edit, run again) can need more: 150 is a reasonable start. The retry with less thinking and the fallback each get that many again. **Side jobs follow the same settings.** When no separate summary, reflection or judge model is set, Agent HQ names chats, writes compaction summaries, reflects on finished work and grades test runs with the agent's own model. Those calls now carry the agent's thinking level, max output tokens and request time limit too. Before, they got the model's defaults, which on Qwen3.8 is the highest reasoning effort with no cap and no deadline: one reflection could hold a single-GPU server for many minutes while the agent's own requests queued behind it. **A failing tool call doesn't end the run.** When a tool server reports an error (edit_file can't find the text, a command fails), the model gets it back as a failed tool result and carries on. PydanticAI's default would count it as a retry, and the fourth miss on the same tool in a row ended the whole run with no reply. Repeated failures are still bounded by **Model requests per run**. When the main model hits either one, it gets one more try on the same model with less thinking (low effort, or thinking off for Ollama models that only have on/off), carrying on from where it stopped. If that fails too, the fallback takes over. The guardrails don't apply to the fallback. **Keeping a turn going.** Small models often say what they'll do next ("I'll now write the world files…") and stop. A reply whose last paragraph only announces work is sent back with a nudge to do it with tool calls, at most twice per reply. Replies that were cut off at the output limit, and replies that link to files by path (`sandbox:/…`, `/work/…`, `attachment:…`) instead of sending them, are sent back the same way; when the file was already sent, the agent is told to take out the link and not to send it again. So is a reply after the agent changed code (`write_file`, `edit_file`, `save_script`) without running anything since: it's told to run the code or its tests first, unless the reply says plainly that it couldn't test. ## Observability Set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to your OpenTelemetry Collector, for example `http://perceptor:4318`; it uses OTLP over HTTP, so the Collector needs its HTTP receiver. You can also point it straight at Phoenix (`http://phoenix-host:6006`). Agent HQ's traces are shaped for [Arize Phoenix](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix): - **Phoenix's native span types.** The OpenInference span processor reshapes PydanticAI's spans into the agent, LLM and tool spans Phoenix understands, with inputs, outputs and token counts. - **One trace per conversation turn, across machines.** Each job carries the W3C `traceparent` of whatever queued it, through Valkey to the worker. A turn, its delegations on other workers and any background report all form one tree: `turn` → `invoke_agent` → `execute_tool delegate` → `task` → `invoke_agent` → `chat`. - **Sessions.** Every span inside a job has `session.id` set to the conversation ID, so Phoenix's **View Session** shows a whole conversation, every turn included. Job spans also carry agent, agent ID, job ID, pool, worker and attempt, as attributes and as metadata. In a huddle each agent's answer is its own `turn <agent>` span in the same session. - **No screenshots in traces.** Images sent to vision models are never recorded. `AHQ_TRACE_CONTENT=0` also leaves prompts and replies out. - **No HTTP noise.** FastAPI's own request tracing is turned off, so the UI's background polling doesn't bury agent traces. - **No MCP protocol noise.** The MCP Python SDK and FastMCP add their own spans for every tool listing and call (`MCP send tools/call …`, `server/discover`, `tools/list`). These have no OpenInference kind, so Phoenix shows them as *unknown*, and they repeat what the `execute_tool` span already shows: the tool's name, arguments and result. They're left out by default. Set `AHQ_TRACE_MCP=1` to keep them, labelled as tool or chain spans, when you're debugging an MCP server. - **Its own Phoenix project.** Traces go to a Phoenix project named after `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` (`agent-hq` by default) rather than `default`. Set `PHOENIX_PROJECT_NAME` to choose a different one. The project is a resource attribute (`openinference.project.name`), so it passes through a Collector unchanged. The API process reports as `agent-hq` and workers as `agent-hq-worker`, both in the same project. The chat page's live activity panel shows the same activity in real time. ## Layout ``` backend/app/ models.py all the tables: providers, agents, tools, threads, messages, jobs, skills, reflections, feedback, profile suggestions, knowledge, eval cases and runs… runtime.py builds agents from rows; turns; delegation; report-back; Stop huddles.py huddles: members, lead, @mentions, per-agent checkpoints, catch-up clock.py the current date and time every agent is told (AHQ_TIMEZONE) worker.py stream consumer: concurrency, heartbeats, reclaiming, registry broker.py all Valkey access: job streams, results, live-event log, locks, cooldowns, stop flags mqtt_bridge.py MQTT subscriptions -> turn jobs (also routes webhook events) webhooks.py inbound webhooks: sender checks (Gitea HMAC, token), allowed networks, rate limits, secrets encrypted at rest, event topics vision.py look / locate / click_on via a per-agent vision model; questions about attached images attachments.py chat attachments: storage, text, manifests, images to models, workbench transfer memory.py long-term memory: storage, embeddings, hybrid search, capture, tidy-up migrate.py schema migrations on startup (lock, adopt, upgrade, backups) and the `python -m app.migrate` CLI; revisions in migrations/versions/ auth.py sign-in: accounts, sessions, API tokens, TOTP, lockout, audit log, CLI approvals.py tool approvals: allow / ask / block per tool, decisions, timeouts skills.py skills: matching, loading, outcomes, versions, proposals learning.py the learning loop: ratings, corrections, reflections, skills from documents profile.py your profile: in every agent's instructions; suggestions you approve knowledge.py knowledge library: sources (upload, web, Git/Obsidian, shares), chunking, hybrid search, recall knowledge_shares.py NAS shares for the library: SMB over the network, or NFS/folders mounted under /shares ocr.py OCR for scanned PDFs (Tesseract), used by the library and chat attachments knowledge_proposals.py documents agents suggest: where they may, near-duplicates, approving into a collection evals.py evals: cases, replayed tool calls, the judge, testing skill changes context.py long conversations: context windows, compaction, trimming, overflow warnings thinking.py thinking levels: per-agent setting -> model settings per provider, support check scheduler.py scheduled tasks: cadence -> cron, time zones, firing due runs exactly once subagents.py sub-agents: modes, limits, duplicate check, grants, estimates, ledger notifications.py notices for you: building them from events, routing rules, delivery, settling every copy when decided, the inbox for chat answers (pairing, decisions, replies, default-agent chat), replies back to the chat, send_alert, listeners channels/ one driver per kind of channel: mqtt.py, telegram.py (Bot API, long polling), discord.py (REST, and a Gateway websocket that resumes after drops) api/notifications.py Settings → Notifications (/api/notifications) workitems.py standing goals: the board, WIP limits, pulling from Ready, the goal runner and its guards, the card prompt, goal tools, proposals, teams (dependencies, team slots, results on actions from the lead's agents and sub-agents) api/workitems.py the board API (/api/board, /api/work-items) slots.py provider slots: cross-worker limit on concurrent model requests (Valkey leases) api/avatars.py agent avatar upload / serve (animated GIF + still first frame) api/desktop.py take control of an agent's desktop / hand it back resources.py desktops and workbenches: containers via the Docker API, dedicated/shared, leases api/resources.py Settings → Desktops & workbenches api/webhooks.py webhook management (/api/webhooks) and deliveries (POST /hooks/<name>) llm.py model providers: build an agent's model; list a provider's models chatgpt.py ChatGPT plan providers: Sign in with ChatGPT, stored tokens, cross-worker refresh lock grok.py Grok plan providers: Sign in with xAI (device flow), stored tokens, cross-worker refresh lock api/ REST + WebSocket (/ws/threads/{id}) telemetry.py OTLP -> your Collector -> Phoenix frontend/src/app/ app shell (sidebar of conversations), chat, and the Settings pages (agents, model providers, sub-agents, usage, memory, skills, knowledge, learning, evals, profile, tools, events, notifications, system, # Agent HQ: builds the Angular UI, then serves it and the API from one Python container.
FROM node:22-slim AS ui
WORKDIR /ui
COPY frontend/package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY frontend/ ./
RUN npx ng build

FROM python:3.13-slim
# git: the knowledge library's Git sources (your Obsidian vault, runbook repos)
# tesseract-ocr: OCR for scanned PDFs (English included). For more languages, build with
#   --build-arg OCR_LANGS="deu fra" and set AHQ_OCR_LANGUAGES=eng+deu+fra
ARG OCR_LANGS=""
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends git ca-certificates tesseract-ocr \
        $(for l in $OCR_LANGS; do echo tesseract-ocr-$l; done) \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
WORKDIR /app
COPY backend/pyproject.toml ./
COPY backend/app ./app
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir .
COPY --from=ui /ui/dist/frontend/browser ./static
ENV AHQ_DATA_DIR=/data
VOLUME /data
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "app.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# Agent HQ A self-hosted multi-agent system. You add model providers (your Ollama servers, OpenAI, Anthropic, any OpenAI-compatible server, your ChatGPT Plus/Pro plan, or your SuperGrok plan) and create agents in the web UI, giving each one instructions, a provider and one of its models, tools, delegation rights and a **worker pool** that decides which machines run it. Supervisors delegate to other agents; delegated work always reports back to the conversation it came from. Standing goals on a Kanban board keep agents working an outcome, one next action at a time, until it's done. Jobs survive crashes and restarts, and MQTT events from your homelab can wake agents on their own. Requests and alerts reach your phone on Telegram or Discord, where you can decide them, answer agents and chat with them. Bring several agents into one chat with @mentions (a huddle) and they answer in turn, each seeing what the others said. - **Backend:** FastAPI, LangGraph (conversation graph + checkpointing), PydanticAI (agents, typed results, MCP tools) - **Frontend:** Angular 22 (signals, standalone components) - **Shared infrastructure:** - **Postgres:** the source of truth: agents, jobs, transcripts and LangGraph checkpoints. - **Valkey** (or Redis): job delivery through Streams, plus results, locks, live UI events and the worker registry. - **MQTT:** incoming events from monitors, devices, Zabbix, Home Assistant and so on. - **Tools:** any MCP server, registered in the UI - **Desktops:** one `linuxserver/webtop` container each, created from the UI and dedicated to an agent or shared, driven by a small MCP server and viewable in the UI Nothing about specific agents or models is in the code. Providers, names, roles, instructions, models, tools, pools, delegation rights and event subscriptions are all database rows, so renaming or re-tasking an agent takes effect on its next job. **Agents get better with use, under your control:** - **Skills:** written-down procedures agents follow, propose and improve. - **The learning loop:** your 👍/👎 and corrections, and agents looking back at their work. - **Your profile:** what every agent always knows about you. - **A knowledge library:** your documents, runbooks, Obsidian vault and NAS shares, searchable with citations. - **Evals:** they show whether a change actually helps before it's applied. What they learn waits for your approval unless you say otherwise. ## Architecture ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph clients["You and your lab"] UI["Angular UI
(browser)"] SRC["Monitors, Zabbix,
Home Assistant, scripts"] end subgraph hq["API process (one)"] API["FastAPI
REST + WebSocket"] BR["MQTT bridge"] end subgraph infra["Shared infrastructure"] PG[("Postgres
agents, jobs, transcripts,
LangGraph checkpoints")] VK[("Valkey
job streams per pool,
results, locks, live events")] MQ{{"MQTT broker
(Mosquitto)"}} end subgraph workers["Workers (any number, any machine)"] W1["worker
pool: default"] W2["worker
pool: gpu"] W3["worker
pool: desktop"] end subgraph tools["Tools"] MCP["MCP servers
Proxmox, OPNsense, RSS…"] DT["Agent desktop
(webtop + desktop MCP)"] end MODELS["Models
Ollama · OpenAI · Anthropic"] UI -- "REST / WebSocket" --> API SRC -- publish --> MQ MQ -- "subscribed topics" --> BR API -- "read/write" --> PG API -- "enqueue turn jobs,
subscribe to live events" --> VK BR -- "enqueue turn jobs" --> VK VK <-- "pull jobs, ack, reclaim;
delegations, results, live events" --> workers workers -- "agents, history" --> PG workers --> MODELS workers --> MCP W3 --> DT UI -. "watch desktop (VNC)" .-> DT ``` **Every piece of work is a job.** A *turn* job runs one turn of a conversation with the thread's owner agent; your messages, MQTT events and background reports all become turn jobs. A *task* job is a delegation, and the assignee returns a structured `WorkResult` (`status`, `summary`, `details`). Each job is written to Postgres, then its ID is added to the Valkey stream for the assignee's pool (`ahq:jobs:`). **Workers pull, run, then acknowledge.** A worker serves one or more pools. It reads with a consumer group, so each job goes to exactly one worker, and it acknowledges the job only after it finishes. While a job runs, the worker refreshes the entry on a heartbeat. If a worker dies, its unacknowledged entries go idle, and another worker on that pool reclaims and reruns them, up to `AHQ_MAX_ATTEMPTS` times. After that the job is marked failed and reported. **Any worker can run any turn.** Agent definitions and job context are in Postgres, and conversation history is in the shared LangGraph checkpointer. A Valkey lock makes sure two turns of the same conversation never run at once, even on different machines. **Pools place agents on machines.** Set an agent's pool to `desktop` and only workers started with `--pools desktop` run it, for example the worker on the host next to its desktop container. ### Delegation and report-back ```mermaid sequenceDiagram autonumber actor You participant API as API process participant VK as Valkey participant WA as Worker (pool: default) participant WB as Worker (pool: gpu) participant PG as Postgres You->>API: message to the supervisor API->>PG: save message, create turn job API->>VK: XADD ahq:jobs:default VK-->>WA: turn job WA->>WA: supervisor runs, calls delegate(scout, task) WA->>PG: create task job (origin thread, depth, chain) WA->>VK: XADD ahq:jobs:gpu Note over WA: gives up its worker slot while waiting VK-->>WB: task job WB->>WB: scout runs, returns WorkResult WB->>PG: job done + result WB->>VK: RPUSH ahq:result:job (wakes the waiter) and XACK VK-->>WA: WorkResult (BLPOP) WA->>WA: supervisor writes the reply using the result WA->>PG: save reply WA->>VK: publish live events, XACK turn VK-->>API: live events API-->>You: reply over WebSocket alt background=true, or the wait exceeds AHQ_DELEGATE_WAIT_TIMEOUT WB->>VK: queue a report turn in the origin conversation VK-->>WA: report turn WA-->>You: supervisor reports the finished work end ``` How the delegation guarantees hold up: - **Wait mode (default)** returns the delegate's `WorkResult` as the `delegate` tool's return value. The supervisor always has the result in hand when it answers you. While it waits, it releases its worker slot, so even a single-slot worker can't deadlock. - **Background mode,** and waits that exceed `AHQ_DELEGATE_WAIT_TIMEOUT`, queue a **report turn** in the conversation the work came from. The conversation's owner agent is woken there to tell you the outcome. - **Failures are results too.** Model errors, exceptions and jobs abandoned after repeated worker crashes all produce a `failed` WorkResult, which is reported the same way. - **Guards:** an agent can only delegate to agents on its list, a chain can't loop back to an agent already in it, and nesting depth is capped (`AHQ_MAX_DELEGATION_DEPTH`). ### Crash recovery ```mermaid sequenceDiagram participant VK as Valkey stream (pool: scouts) participant A as Worker A participant B as Worker B participant PG as Postgres VK-->>A: job (attempt 1) A->>PG: status running, attempts=1 loop every AHQ_WORKER_HEARTBEAT A->>VK: XCLAIM JUSTID (reset idle time) end Note over A: crashes, so no XACK Note over VK: entry idles past AHQ_CLAIM_IDLE_MS B->>VK: XAUTOCLAIM VK-->>B: same job B->>PG: attempts=2, runs it again B->>VK: result + XACK ``` A rerun starts the job from the beginning. Tools that change systems should therefore be safe to repeat, or should go behind an approval step (see *Next steps*). ### Stopping a conversation's work While anything in a conversation is still running, a **Stop** button sits next to Send. It stops the turn and every task delegated from it (background ones included), on whichever workers they run (`POST /api/threads/{id}/stop`). - **How:** Stop sets `ahq:stop:` in Valkey for each queued or running job. Queued jobs are marked stopped at once and never start. A running job's worker checks for the flag every `AHQ_STOP_POLL` seconds (default 1), cancels the run and acks the job, so it is not retried like a crashed one. - **What you see:** the delegation cards say *stopped*, the conversation gets a "Stopped by you." line, and nobody reports back afterwards. Stopped jobs are saved as `failed` with the error "Stopped by you."; they count against neither skills nor the learning loop. - **Caveats:** a tool call already sent to a system can't be called back; Stop only keeps the agent from carrying on. The conversation's model history keeps only finished turns, so the next message starts from what was there before the stopped turn. ### MQTT events ```mermaid flowchart LR M["homelab/alerts/opnsense
WAN gateway down"] --> B["MQTT bridge"] B --> F{"subscription
filter matches?"} F -- no --> X["ignored"] F -- yes --> C{"in cooldown?"} C -- yes --> X C -- no --> T["turn job in the subscription's
conversation (pool of its agent)"] T --> A["agent investigates,
delegates, reports"] ``` Subscriptions are managed on the **Settings → Events** page: - **Topic filter:** MQTT wildcards, where `+` matches one level and `#` matches the rest. - **Agent:** the agent that handles matching events. - **Conversation:** where that agent reports. Leave it empty to get a dedicated events thread. - **Prompt template:** what the agent is told. `{topic}`, `{payload}` (the whole body), `{event}` (the last topic level), `{source}` and `{hook}` are filled in, and so are JSON fields of the payload: `{payload.repository.full_name}`, `{payload.commits.0.message}`. A field that isn't in the payload becomes empty and is flagged in the delivery log; lists and objects come out as compact JSON. This works for MQTT JSON payloads too. - **Cooldown:** stops an alert storm from turning into hundreds of model calls. Under **Try it**, the editor previews the prompt a template produces for a topic and payload you enter, or for a recent webhook delivery that matches the filter, and can send it as a test event without a broker. It reports what happened per subscription (queued, or skipped for cooldown) and any missing fields. The bridge runs in the API process; run only one API process with `AHQ_MQTT_URL` set, or each event is handled twice. MQTT works in the other direction too. Agent HQ publishes your notifications (requests, alerts and decisions; see [Notifications](#notifications-telegram-discord-and-mqtt)) to `AHQ_MQTT_NOTIFY_TOPIC`, and agents can publish their own status and commands through the [MQTT publisher](#mqtt-publisher-agents-publish-back-to-the-lab). ### Inbound webhooks Anything on your LAN that can send an HTTP POST can wake an agent too: Gitea, Proxmox notifications, Uptime Kuma, Grafana, Zabbix, Home Assistant, or a one-line `curl` in a cron job. A delivery becomes an event on the topic `webhook//` and goes through the same router as MQTT, so the subscriptions, cooldowns, prompt templates and report conversations above apply unchanged. Webhooks work without an MQTT broker. ```mermaid flowchart LR G["Gitea push
POST /hooks/gitea"] --> H{"signature or
token OK?"} H -- no --> R["401, logged in
the sign-in audit log"] H -- yes --> T["topic webhook/gitea/push"] T --> S["Events subscriptions
(same router as MQTT)"] S --> A["agent investigates,
delegates, reports"] T --> OK["202 Accepted
(straight away)"] ``` Create hooks on the **Settings → Events** page, under **Webhooks**: - **Name:** becomes the URL, `https:///hooks/`, served by Caddy like the rest of the UI. - **Source:** the second topic level (empty = the name). - **How the sender proves itself.** `/hooks/*` is outside the sign-in, so each hook checks its sender: - **Gitea signature:** `X-Gitea-Signature`, the HMAC-SHA256 of the body keyed with the hook's secret. In Gitea, add a webhook of type *Gitea* with the URL, content type `application/json`, and the secret in *Secret*. - **Secret token:** in an `X-Webhook-Token` header, an `Authorization: Bearer` header, or `?token=` for senders that can't set headers. - **Event header / event field:** where the last topic level comes from. Gitea hooks use `X-Gitea-Event` (`push`, `issues`, `pull_request`…) by default. Otherwise name a header, or a dotted JSON path such as `heartbeat.status_text`; with neither it is `event`. Values are lowercased and made topic-safe. - **Delivery ID header:** for the duplicate check. Gitea hooks use `X-Gitea-Delivery` by default. A repeat of the same ID within `AHQ_WEBHOOK_DEDUPE_SECONDS` (24 hours) is answered `202` with `"duplicate": true` and runs nothing, so a sender's retries don't wake an agent twice. If Gitea's own redeliver button reuses the ID, use **Replay** in Agent HQ instead. The secret is shown once, when the hook is created or rotated. **New subscription for it** pre-fills a subscription with the filter `webhook//#`. Filters can be broader, e.g. `webhook/+/alert` for alerts from any source. ```bash curl -X POST -H "X-Webhook-Token: $AHQ_HOOK_SECRET" -H "X-Event: done" \ --data-binary @report.txt https://shockwave.home.arpa/hooks/nightly-scan ``` Replies: `202` with `{"delivery": ..., "status": ..., "topic": ..., "queued_jobs": [...]}` (an empty list if no subscription matched or it is in cooldown); `401` for a missing or wrong signature or token; `404` for an unknown or disabled hook (the two look the same); `413` for a body over `AHQ_WEBHOOK_MAX_BODY` (1 MB). At most `AHQ_WEBHOOK_MAX_PAYLOAD` characters of the body (8000) reach the prompt. The default prompt tells the agent the body is data from another system, not instructions; your tool approvals still decide what it may do next. **Delivery log.** The hook editor lists its recent deliveries with their status: *accepted*, *no match*, *cooldown*, *duplicate*, *rejected* (bad signature or token) or *too large*. Opening one shows the matched subscriptions with the prompt each agent got and any missing fields, the body, the headers (without `Authorization`, tokens, signatures or cookies), and a link to the conversation. Rejected and too-large deliveries keep only their time, address, size and reason, never the body. The newest `AHQ_WEBHOOK_KEEP_DELIVERIES` (200) per hook are kept. **Send test and Replay.** *Send a test delivery* routes an event name and body as the hook would, without a signature since you're signed in. *Replay* sends a logged delivery through again as a new row linked to the original. Both skip the duplicate check and, unless you tick *Respect cooldowns*, the cooldown. *Use as test delivery* copies a logged body into the test form to edit. **Safety.** Webhooks are meant for the LAN. Don't expose `/hooks/*` to the internet. Each delivery passes these checks in order: 1. **Address.** The sender must be in the hook's **Accept from** networks, or, if that's empty, in `AHQ_WEBHOOK_NETWORKS` (private and loopback ranges, i.e. your LAN). Otherwise it gets `403`, logged as *blocked address*. The address is the first `X-Forwarded-For` hop, which Caddy sets, so keep the API's own port off the network (`AHQ_HTTP_BIND`); otherwise a sender could claim any address. 2. **Rate.** Each hook accepts **Requests per minute** (60 for new hooks, `AHQ_WEBHOOK_RATE_PER_MINUTE`; 0 = no limit). After that it answers `429`, and only the first refusal each minute is logged. 3. **Size, then signature or token**, as above. 4. **Duplicate check**, then routing. **Webhook turns ask before changing things.** A webhook body carries text other people wrote: an issue title, a commit message, an alert from a device. It can try to give your agents instructions ("ignore previous instructions and restart…"). The default prompt marks the body as data, but the real safety net is your tools. With **Ask before tools that change things** on (the default), turns a hook starts, the work they delegate, and the report-backs that follow ask before any tool not marked read-only (`readOnlyHint`), even where your rules say *allow*. The approval card says it's asking because a webhook started the work. Your *block* rules still win, read-only tools (listing VMs, reading pages, searching) still just run, and "approve, don't ask again" works as usual. Turn it off only for hooks whose senders you trust completely. **Secrets at rest.** Set `AHQ_SECRET_KEY` (any long random string) and hook secrets are encrypted in the database. Existing ones are encrypted at the next start. Keep the key safe and don't change it: if it changes, hooks answer `503` and their log says the secret can't be read; rotate their secrets to fix it. Without a key, secrets are stored as they are, and the Events page says so. **Tracing.** Each delivery is a `webhook ` span in Phoenix, with its topic, status and body. The turns it starts, and everything they delegate, continue that trace. **Cleanup.** Deliveries older than `AHQ_WEBHOOK_KEEP_DAYS` (7) are removed hourly, on top of the per-hook limit. ### Lab tools: MCP servers for your homelab `labtools/` is one image of MCP servers for common homelab systems: MikroTik, SNMP switches, Technitium DNS, Kea DHCP, Proxmox VE, TrueNAS SCALE, Zabbix, Prometheus/Alertmanager, Graylog, allow-listed SSH restarts, and ping/port probes. Run as many instances as you like. Each picks its **integrations** (`LABTOOLS_INTEGRATIONS`), **read or write access** (`LABTOOLS_ACCESS`) and **its own credentials**, so you decide which agents can see what and which can change anything. Read tools are marked read-only. Write tools are typed and narrow, ask you first, and respect guards from the inventory: protected interfaces, SSH allow-lists, bounded silences, no node actions. [docs/labtools.md](docs/labtools.md) covers integrations, configuration and credentials. [docs/lab-alerts.md](docs/lab-alerts.md) covers getting each system's alerts into webhooks. [docs/examples/homelab-crew.md](docs/examples/homelab-crew.md) is a worked example: two read-only watchers and a fixer. Two tool-server settings help with any MCP server, yours or someone else's (Settings → Tools): - **Shown** per tool: untick tools agents never need. Hidden tools aren't listed to the model at all, which matters for small local models; a *blocked* tool is still listed, it just can't run. - **Only reads**: every tool of the server counts as read-only, as if it carried `readOnlyHint`, so webhook-started work doesn't ask before using it. Only tick it for servers you know can't change anything, e.g. `gitea-mcp -r`. ## Quick start (single machine, dev) You need Postgres, Valkey and (optionally) MQTT. The simplest route is the infra compose file, which always starts Postgres and Valkey: ```bash cd deploy/infra cp .env.example .env # set the passwords docker compose up -d ``` MQTT is up to you: - **Use your home lab's broker:** give Agent HQ its own user with read access to the topics you'll subscribe to, and set `AHQ_MQTT_URL` to that broker. Nothing else to run. - **Run the bundled Mosquitto** (handy for dev and testing): it's behind the `mqtt` compose profile. ```bash docker compose --profile mqtt run --rm mosquitto mosquitto_passwd -c /mosquitto/config/passwd agent-hq docker compose --profile mqtt up -d # or set COMPOSE_PROFILES=mqtt in .env ``` - **No MQTT at all:** leave `AHQ_MQTT_URL` empty. Everything except event-triggered agents still works. Backend (one shell for the API, one for a worker): ```bash cd backend python -m venv .venv && . .venv/bin/activate # Windows: .venv\Scripts\activate pip install -e ".[dev]" cp ../.env.example ../.env # point AHQ_* at your infra; export it uvicorn app.main:app --reload --port 8000 # API + UI + MQTT bridge python -m app.worker --pools default # a worker (any number, any machine) ``` To run a worker inside the API process instead of separately, set `AHQ_EMBED_WORKER=1`. Frontend: ```bash cd frontend npm install npx ng serve # http://localhost:4200, proxies /api and /ws to :8000 ``` On the first visit you'll be asked to create your account with a one-time setup code, which the API process prints to its console (see *Sign-in and HTTPS*). The UI keeps your conversations in the left sidebar; everything else (agents, model providers, memory, tools, events and system status) is under **Settings** at the bottom of the sidebar. Start on the **Settings → Model providers** page and add your Ollama server (or another provider), then create agents and pick a model for each. To try the example crew, go to **Settings → Agents → Import** and pick `examples/agents.example.json`. It contains two providers (an Ollama server and OpenAI), the agents with their models and pools, a desktop tool server and an alerts subscription, all as data. Then fix the Ollama URL on the **Settings → Model providers** page and choose models that your server actually has. Without `AHQ_DB_URL`, the system falls back to SQLite files in `AHQ_DATA_DIR`. That's fine for a single machine, but use Postgres as soon as workers run anywhere else. ## Tests ```bash cd backend && pytest cd labtools && pip install -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest # the lab tool servers ``` The tests use scripted fake models (no LLM needed), a real `valkey-server` or `redis-server` started on a free port, an in-process MQTT broker, and a throwaway Postgres cluster when Postgres is installed. With `AHQ_TEST_DB=postgres`, every test runs on a fresh Postgres database of its own instead of SQLite; with `AHQ_TEST_STRICT=1`, a test that would skip because something it needs isn't installed fails instead. `deploy/test/Dockerfile` has everything installed (Valkey, Postgres 17 + pgvector, Tesseract, Chromium, Node), and deploys run the suite in it on both databases, strict, before anything changes (see [docs/auto-deploy.md](docs/auto-deploy.md)): ```bash docker build -t agent-hq-test -f deploy/test/Dockerfile . docker run --rm -e AHQ_TEST_DB=postgres -e AHQ_TEST_STRICT=1 agent-hq-test ``` They cover: - delegation in wait and background modes - single-slot workers (no deadlock) - pinning agents to pools - **a worker crashing mid-job and another reclaiming it** - failure reporting - conversation history persisting across turns - renaming agents - a real stdio MCP server - MQTT matching, cooldowns and a real broker end to end - the Postgres database and checkpointer with two workers - long-term memory: keyword and embedding search, scopes, retire/restore/supersede, recall added to instructions, capturing delegations and events without duplicates, agent memory tools, tidy-up with and without a model, re-embedding, and the same search on Postgres + pgvector (via PGlite) - tracing: one trace across two workers for a turn and its delegation, background reports joining that trace, session IDs and Phoenix span types on every span, and no screenshot data in spans - avatars: animated GIF served untouched plus a still first frame, validation, keeping them through agent edits and export/import - local-first models: a real Chromium driven through Playwright MCP over CDP; vision tools on rendered screenshots (with and without zoom, both coordinate formats, and a not-found case); falling back on errors, runaway loops and escalation - desktop handoff: tools pausing while you have control, an agent asking you to take over and resuming with your note, and the wait timing out - model providers: listing models for each kind, write-only keys, and two agents on two Ollama models answering through a worker - thinking levels: the unified setting for OpenAI/Anthropic, `reasoning_effort` for Ollama only when the model can think, the fallback using its own provider, the support hint, an agent run receiving its level, API validation, and export - MQTT publisher: status and allow-listed publishes reaching a real broker; refusing wildcards, system, reserved and off-list topics, oversized payloads and bursts; and an agent publishing only after you approve - web reader: feeds (and finding a site's feed), readable pages without clutter, paging of long pages, redirects, robots.txt, SearXNG search, refusing LAN addresses unless allowed, and an agent reading a feed through Agent HQ - scheduler: every cadence and its description, bad cadences explained, time zones across a DST change, firing into the schedule's own conversation exactly once (two checkers at once), catching up once after downtime, skipping while a run is still going, run now, and disabled agents - ChatGPT plan providers: the full sign-in by pasted callback (PKCE, state, single use, declined consent), tokens never returned or exported, model listing, an agent turn on the plan through the Responses API (`store: false`, `stream: true`, no unsupported fields), and two workers refreshing at once without ever reusing a refresh token - Grok plan providers: the device sign-in (pending, slow down, declined, a subscription xAI refuses), tokens never returned or exported, switching kind dropping the sign-in, model listing without image and video models, an agent turn on the plan with its thinking sent as `reasoning_effort`, and two workers refreshing at once without ever reusing a refresh token - Postgres upgrades: enum values a newer version adds (such as a new provider kind) are added to an older database's enum type on startup - schema migrations: the revisions building exactly the models' schema (on SQLite and Postgres), adopting a database from before migrations, refusing a database a newer version migrated, waiting instead of migrating, four processes starting at once, ignoring pgvector columns and LangGraph's tables, and a later rename-with-data revision running on startup with a SQLite backup first - import and export - deleting agents: only once disabled, never with work in flight, removing what it owns while keeping usage, team memories and skills, and returning its goals to the backlog - sign-in: setup code, passwords, 2FA, sessions, lockout, API tokens, the audit log, and cross-site refusal - sub-agents: off/ask/allowed, limits, refusing duplicates of existing agents, requests and grants, provider slots and the usage ledger - notifications, against a fake Telegram Bot API: the token checked and never shown, pairing and strangers ignored, routing by type, agent and severity, a tool approval decided by button and by a "no, …" reply, a web UI decision editing the chat message, decisions turned off, chatting with the default agent and replying to continue, a goal question answered from the chat, alerts and their hourly cap, one listener per bot, the delivery log, and the MQTT channel publishing the same JSON to a real broker - Discord, against a fake Discord (REST and Gateway): the token checked and hidden and the invite link, pairing by DM and in a server channel, strangers ignored, a tool approval decided by button (deferred, then answered to the presser) and by reply, the message edited, answers coming back as plain text that pings nobody, chatting with the default agent, a server channel ignoring talk not addressed to the bot, the Message Content intent refused until it's turned on in the portal, and resuming the Gateway after a drop - goal teams: your agents (delegate_action) and sub-agents (assign_action) working actions in parallel, dependencies, team slots, one action per agent per goal, results landing on actions with no report turns, a failed result blocking its action, waiting on the team, the done check, approval mode, duplicate refusals pointing to your agent, and Stop - workbenches and tool approvals: allow/ask/block per tool, waiting for a decision, "don't ask again", timeouts, and a real workbench over MCP - skills: matching, loading, outcomes, versions and rollback, proposals in propose/auto/off modes, diffs and stale warnings - the learning loop: rating replies, corrections, reflections that propose skills and save lessons, the daily cap, and Run now - your profile: in every agent's instructions (or not, per agent), the word cap, and suggestions you approve - the knowledge library: Obsidian notes (frontmatter, tags, links), chunking at headings, uploads, web pages, Git sources and NAS shares (SMB and mounted folders) that only re-read changed files, access per collection, recall and tools, runbooks turned into skill proposals, and the same search on Postgres + pgvector - long conversations: cutting only between turns, summarising older turns (and folding an old summary into a new one), dropping them when the summary fails, compaction in a real conversation, trimming tool results within a turn (calibrated against the token counts the model reports), the warning when instructions don't fit, and reading the window from Ollama (loaded model, Modelfile, or the default) - evals: cases from replies and feedback, replaying recorded tool calls, read-only tools running for real only when allowed, Ask/Block tools never running, the judge, and skill changes tested without and with (Auto-mode changes held when they make things worse) ## Deploy (Docker) 1. **Infrastructure,** once, on one host: `deploy/infra/docker-compose.yml` (Postgres 17 with pgvector, Valkey 8, and optionally Mosquitto 2 via the `mqtt` profile). Keeping Postgres and Valkey together on a host dedicated to Agent HQ while sharing your lab's existing MQTT broker works well: the first two hold Agent HQ's state, and MQTT is how the rest of the lab talks to it. 2. **Application:** `cp .env.example .env`, fill in the URLs and keys, set up HTTPS (next section), then `docker compose --profile images build` (the desktop and workbench images) and `docker compose up -d --build`. This starts: - `caddy`: HTTPS on 443 (certificate from your step-ca), with http:// redirected - `hq`: API, UI and MQTT bridge (plain HTTP on 8000, for this host only). Its `hq-data` volume holds the knowledge library's uploads and Git clones. NFS shares for the knowledge library are mounted here too, under `/shares` (see Knowledge library). It also reads your step-ca root from `deploy/caddy/root_ca.crt` (`AHQ_EXTRA_CA_FILE`), so Git and web sources on your HTTPS hosts (your Gitea) are trusted. - `worker`: pool `default` - `worker-desktop`: pool `desktop`, for agents that drive desktops - `docker-proxy`: the Docker API `hq` uses to run desktops and workbenches, which you create under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches** (see [Desktops and workbenches](#desktops-and-workbenches)) - `egress`: the workbenches' proxy, which applies each one's network rules (see Workbenches) 3. **More machines:** copy `docker-compose.yml` and `.env` to another host and keep only the worker services you want there, with `--pools` set to whatever runs on that machine (`gpu`, `desktop`, `lab-east`…). Workers show up on the **Settings → System** page with their pools and load, and each pool's queue depth appears next to them. 4. **More workers on one host:** `docker compose up -d --scale worker=3`. **Deploying on every push.** A Gitea Actions workflow can do the upgrade for you whenever `main` changes: pull, build, a `pg_dump` if schema migrations are pending, restart, health check. It runs on a Gitea runner on the server itself and does nothing until you set it up. See [docs/auto-deploy.md](docs/auto-deploy.md). **Upgrading.** Pull, `docker compose up -d --build`. Each process brings the database schema up to date on startup (Alembic revisions, one process at a time). Before upgrading a Postgres install, `docker compose exec hq python -m app.migrate status` shows the pending revisions; take a `pg_dump` if there are any. Workers on other machines need the new image too: an older one refuses to start against a database a newer version has migrated. See [docs/schema-migrations.md](docs/schema-migrations.md). **Worker names.** In Docker, each worker is named `--`, for example `worker-shockwave-7090` and `worker-shockwave-1c2e`. You can tell which machine and which replica it is, and scaled replicas never share a name. The host name comes from the host's `/etc/hostname`, which the compose file mounts read-only. Where that file doesn't exist (Docker Desktop), set `AHQ_HOST_NAME` in `.env`. Set `AHQ_WORKER_NAME` for a fixed name, as `worker-desktop` does, but only on a service you won't scale. A recreated container (after `up --build`) gets a new ID and so a new suffix. Its old entry drops off the System page once its heartbeat stops, and any job it left unfinished is picked up as usual. Valkey settings that matter (already set in the infra compose file): - `appendonly yes`: queued jobs survive a Valkey restart. - `maxmemory-policy noeviction`: Valkey never quietly discards stream entries. - `requirepass`: a password, which goes in `AHQ_REDIS_URL` as `redis://:password@host:6379/0`. ### Sign-in and HTTPS The UI and API need a sign-in. Agents and workers are unaffected, since they talk to Valkey and Postgres directly. **Your account** - **First run:** with no account yet, the API process logs a one-time setup code. Find it with `docker compose logs hq | grep "setup code"`. The first visit to the UI asks for it, so nobody else on your network can claim the instance before you do. - **Passwords** are stored as Argon2id hashes and need at least 10 characters. - **Two-factor sign-in** is optional. Turn it on under **Settings → Security** by scanning the QR code with any authenticator app. - **Sessions** use an HttpOnly cookie that is marked Secure over HTTPS. A session ends after `AHQ_SESSION_IDLE_DAYS` without use (default 7) and after `AHQ_SESSION_MAX_DAYS` in any case (default 30). **Settings → Security** lists your signed-in browsers and can sign any of them out. Changing your password signs out every other browser. - **Locked out?** `docker compose exec hq python -m app.auth set-password `. The same tool can also `reset-2fa `, `sign-out-all` and `unlock`. **Protections** - **Lockout:** 5 failed sign-ins from one address, or 10 for one username, within 15 minutes lock further attempts for 15 minutes. - **Cross-site requests:** writes and WebSockets that use the cookie are refused when they come from another site. - **Sign-in log:** **Settings → Security** shows sign-ins, failures, lockouts, sign-outs, and every password, 2FA, session and token change. **API tokens** are for scripts, Home Assistant or curl. Create one under **Settings → Security**, then send `Authorization: Bearer ahq_…`. A token is shown once and stored only as a hash. It can expire, and you can revoke it. It can use the API but can't change your password, 2FA or tokens. ```bash curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $AHQ_TOKEN" https://shockwave.home.arpa/api/agents ``` **HTTPS with your step-ca.** The `caddy` service terminates TLS and gets its certificate from step-ca over ACME, renewing it automatically (step-ca certificates last 24 hours by default). One-time setup: 1. **On the CA,** add an ACME provisioner if you don't have one: `step ca provisioner add acme --type ACME`, then restart step-ca. 2. **Copy the root certificate** into the repo: `step ca root deploy/caddy/root_ca.crt`. It's git-ignored. 3. **In `.env`:** set `AHQ_SITE=shockwave.home.arpa` and `ACME_CA=https:///acme/acme/directory`. The provisioner name is part of that path. 4. **Network:** step-ca must be able to reach Shockwave on port 80 for the ACME challenge, and `AHQ_SITE` must resolve to Shockwave in your DNS. 5. **Browsers:** your step-ca root needs to be trusted on the machines you browse from. If you already use step-ca certificates elsewhere, it is. Plain HTTP on port 8000 is published for Shockwave itself only (`127.0.0.1`). While you're getting HTTPS working, set `AHQ_HTTP_BIND=8000` in `.env` to reach it from your LAN, then remove the setting. If you set `AHQ_PUBLIC_URL`, change it to the https address. **Desktop viewers are behind the same sign-in.** Their ports are no longer published. Instead, Caddy serves each one at `https:///desktops/desktop-N/` and checks your Agent HQ session first (`forward_auth` to `/api/auth/verify`). Agent HQ sets each desktop's `SUBFOLDER` to match its path and fills in the agent's **Desktop viewer URL** when you give it a desktop. ### Workbenches: an agent's own Python environment A workbench is a small container per agent that gives it somewhere to write and run code. It's like a desktop, but for scripts instead of a browser.
