Team members are **its existing agents** (the ones it may delegate to) and, if it's allowed them, **new sub-agents**. It's swarming, in Kanban terms: the agent's goal WIP stays where it is (one outcome at a time, by default), and the *action* WIP inside that goal grows by its team. ```mermaid flowchart LR L["Lead: works its own<br/>action, one at a time"] -- "delegate_action(a2, Breaker)" --> A1["Breaker<br/>(your agent) works a2"] L -- "assign_action(a3)" --> S2["Sub-agent<br/>works a3"] A1 -- "result on a2:<br/>done or blocked" --> B[("Board")] S2 -- "result on a3" --> B B -- "a4 (after a2, a3)<br/>becomes startable" --> L ``` **Turning it on:** Settings → Agents → Standing goals → **Team size** (parallel actions per goal: the agent plus its team members; default 1 = no team). It takes effect when the agent has agents under **Can delegate to**, or sub-agents set to *Ask me first* or *Allowed within limits*, or both. With sub-agents only, *Allowed within limits* caps it by the sub-agent limit **At once** (the editor says so when it is); with agents on the team, that limit still applies to the sub-agents it creates, not to the team size. **How it works:** - **Serial stays serial.** When the agent adds an action that needs others' results, or would clash with them, it lists them in `after`. An action is startable, by the agent or its team, only when everything in its `after` list is done (dropped ones don't hold it up). The card shows what each action waits for. - **Your agents first.** `delegate_action` hands an action to one of the agents the lead may delegate to. That agent works it as a background delegated task with everything it already has: its own model, tools, memory, skills, knowledge and desktop. It shows in the conversation as a delegation card with the action and the lead's instructions. Each agent works one action per goal at a time, and the usual delegation rules apply (no loops back up the chain, the depth limit, *ask first* for work a webhook started). The goal turn's instructions name the lead's agents and tell it to use them before creating sub-agents, and to use `delegate_action` rather than `delegate` for a whole action, so it keeps working while they do. - **Sub-agents for the rest.** `assign_action` creates a sub-agent through the normal sub-agent path, so everything already set for sub-agents applies: the mode (in *Ask me first*, the agent asks with `request_subagents` first, and your approval covers the goal's conversation), the models and tool servers it may give them (including a cloud model, which matters when the local GPU is busy), minutes and model requests each, how many at once and per day, and the team-wide limits. Sub-agents on a team never get a desktop and can't create sub-agents of their own. - **No duplicates of your agents.** As with any sub-agent, the lead has to say why none of your existing agents should do the action (`why_not_existing_agents`), and a sub-agent whose role names one of your agents, or whose work is close to one's description, is refused with a pointer to that agent: `delegate_action` when the lead can delegate to it (under an approved *Ask me first* request, only an outright name clash is refused, since the request already showed you any overlap). The comparison uses the role, the action and the lead's instructions for it, not the goal and team context in the briefing, so a long briefing can't water it down. - **What a team member is told:** the goal and its objective, its one action and the lead's instructions for it, and what the team has found so far (the results of the actions it depends on, and the latest others). It's told not to change anything outside its action. - **Results land on the board.** A team member's result goes onto its action, before anything else happens when it finishes: *done* completes it with what it found; *partial* or *failed* blocks it with the reason, for the lead to re-plan. There's no report turn per result: the next goal turn's card shows every result, with who did it, marked *your agent* or *sub-agent*. - **The runner keeps the lead busy.** While its team works, the lead keeps getting goal turns as long as it has something of its own: its action in progress, a blocked action to re-plan, or a startable one to take or hand over. When everything left is either with the team or waiting on it, the goal shows as **Waiting on its team**, and resumes as results come in. - **Same guards, same review.** The goal's model-request limit counts its team too, a team result counts as progress, `claim_done` is refused while any team member is still working, and you still confirm done. Stop (or dropping the goal) stops the whole team, and their actions go back to to-do. - **You can step in:** drop an action a team member is working on, and its late result is noted in the log but not applied. On the board, a card with a team shows **team ×N** while N team members are working, and its action list shows who's working or did each action (tagged *agent* or *sub-agent*), and what each waits for. The goal's detail names who the lead can put on its team. **Built for incidents next.** The board's rows aren't specific to goals: each work item has a kind, a source and a correlation key, and the same columns, runner, next actions and WIP rules will carry incidents (alerts grouped into one problem to solve) later. ## Notifications: Telegram, Discord and MQTT Everything that waits for you shows up in the **Requests** inbox: tool approvals, sub-agent requests, skill, profile and knowledge proposals, done claims, proposed goals, goal questions and desktop take-overs. **Notification channels** (Settings → Notifications) send these to you as well, together with agents' **alerts**. Chat channels also take your answers, so you can handle most of them from your phone. ```mermaid flowchart LR R["Requests and alerts<br/>(tool approvals, proposals,<br/>goal questions, send_alert)"] --> N["Notices<br/>(routing rules:<br/>type × agent × severity)"] N --> T["Telegram bot"] N --> DC["Discord bot"] N --> M["MQTT topic"] T -- "buttons, replies,<br/>messages" --> I["Inbox<br/>(paired accounts only)"] DC -- "buttons, replies,<br/>DMs, mentions" --> I I --> D["the same decisions<br/>as the web UI"] I --> C["your message in<br/>the conversation"] C --> A["the agent's answer<br/>back to the chat"] ``` - **Channels:** **MQTT** publishes each notice's event JSON on a topic, as before (it's set up for you from `AHQ_MQTT_URL` and the old Settings → Sub-agents switch). **Telegram** and **Discord** use a bot of your own. Both are drivers on one framework (`app/channels/`): what to send, who may answer and what an answer does are shared, so they behave the same. - **Routing rules:** each channel has one or more rules. A rule picks notice types (none = all), agents (none = all) and, for alerts, the lowest severity it takes. A notice goes to a channel when any of its rules match, so "tool approvals and goal questions from everyone, plus Breaker's and Mainframe's critical alerts" is two rules. - **No inbound access needed.** Agent HQ reads a Telegram bot's messages by long polling (`getUpdates`), and keeps a Gateway websocket open to Discord (resuming it after a drop, so nothing is missed). Nothing on the internet has to reach Agent HQ. The listeners run in the API process (`AHQ_CHANNELS=1`, the default); a Valkey lock keeps a second API process from reading the same bot. **Setting up Telegram:** 1. Create a bot with @BotFather (`/newbot`) and copy its token. 2. Under **Settings → Notifications**, choose **+ New… → Telegram bot**, paste the token and save. Agent HQ checks it with Telegram (`getMe`) and stores it encrypted when `AHQ_SECRET_KEY` is set; it's never shown again. 3. **Pair an account:** this makes a one-time code that's valid for 10 minutes. Open the `t.me` link it shows and tap **Start**, or send the bot `/start <code>`. Only paired accounts get notices and can answer. Anyone else who finds the bot is ignored without a reply, and logged under **Recent activity**. 4. **Send a test** to check it arrives. **Setting up Discord:** 1. In the [Discord Developer Portal](https://discord.com/developers/applications), create an application. On its **Bot** page, **Reset Token** and copy it. 2. Under **Settings → Notifications**, choose **+ New… → Discord bot**, paste the token and save. Agent HQ checks it with Discord and stores it the same way as a Telegram token. 3. Use the channel's **invite link** to add the bot to a server you're in. Discord only lets you DM a bot you share a server with. 4. **Pair an account:** - **In a DM:** send the bot `!start <code>`, and notices come to your DMs. - **In a server channel:** post `@YourBot !start <code>` there, and notices go to that channel. Only paired accounts can press its buttons or talk to the bot; everyone else in the channel is ignored. 5. **Send a test.** Commands start with `!` on Discord (`!new`, `!help`), since Discord keeps `/` for its own commands. Discord only shows a bot the text of some messages unless it has the privileged **Message Content** intent: - **Always visible:** DMs, messages that @mention the bot, and replies to its messages (with *ping on reply* on, which is Discord's default). - **Without the intent:** that's everything above needs, so leave it off. - **With it:** tick **Message Content** on the channel to talk in a paired server channel without mentioning the bot. Turn it on for the bot in the Developer Portal as well (**Bot → Privileged Gateway Intents**), or Discord refuses the connection, and the channel shows that error. On Discord, notices are embeds coloured by kind (alerts by severity), and agents' answers are plain messages, so their Markdown renders. A button press is answered only to the person who pressed it. **Answering from the chat:** - **Buttons decide the request** with the same code the web UI uses: ✅ Approve / ❌ Deny for tool approvals, sub-agent requests (as asked; change the terms in Agent HQ) and proposals; ✅ Confirm done / ↩️ Send back for done claims; To Ready / To Backlog / Reject for proposed goals. - **A reply that starts with approve/yes or deny/no** decides it too, and the rest becomes your note: "no, not on a Friday". - **Any other reply to a notice** (a goal question, an alert, an agent's answer) goes to that notice's conversation as your message. - **A message that isn't a reply** goes to the channel's **default agent**, in a conversation of the channel's own. `/new` (`!new` on Discord) starts a fresh one, and `/help` (`!help`) lists the commands. - **Answers come back:** - The agent's answer to a turn you started from the chat is sent back to the chat. - So is anything in the channel's own conversation. - After you answer from the chat, that conversation's background reports and follow-ups go there too, for **Follow-ups for** minutes (default 30). Goal turns, events and schedules don't follow you there. - **Every copy is settled:** whichever way a request is decided (web UI, Telegram, Discord, another paired account), each message about it is edited to show the outcome ("✅ Approved via Phone (Mike)") and loses its buttons. Tapping a stale button says what already happened. **Decide from the chat** can be turned off per channel. Requests then arrive with a link only, and you decide them in Agent HQ, behind its sign-in and two-factor. Every decision, reply, chat, pairing and refusal on a channel is logged under its **Recent activity**, with the sender. **Alerts.** Tick **Alerts** on an agent (Settings → Agents) to give it `send_alert(message, severity)`. It's for things you should know about now, such as an outage or a failure that needs you, not for routine results. The alert goes to the channels whose rules take `agent_alert` at that severity (info, warning or critical). Replying to it continues the agent's conversation. Each agent may send at most **Alerts per agent per hour** (Settings → Notifications, default 10); beyond that, the tool refuses. ## Sub-agents Agents can create temporary **sub-agents** for parts of their own task (say, reading twelve feeds in parallel). It's off for every agent until you turn it on, per agent, under **Settings → Agents → Sub-agents**: - **Off** (the default): the agent has no sub-agent tools at all. - **Ask me first:** the agent gets `request_subagents`. It sends you a request, like a staffing request: which sub-agents, what each is for, why it needs them, why none of your existing agents fits, which model and tools each needs, and how long. You decide; it can only create them after you approve, and only within what you approve. - **Allowed within limits:** the agent may create sub-agents itself, within the limits set on it. **Limits, all enforced in code:** - **Per agent:** how many at once, per task and per day, minutes each, and model requests each. Also which models sub-agents may use (empty = the agent's own model) and which of its tool servers they may have. - **Team-wide** (**Settings → Sub-agents**): running at once and created per day across all agents, open requests per agent, and how long an unanswered request stays open. - **Enforcement:** every spawn is checked under a Valkey lock, so several workers can't race past a limit. A sub-agent's run stops at its request limit (PydanticAI `UsageLimits`) and its time limit, and the sub-agent retires as soon as it reports back. Anything left over (a crashed worker, say) is retired by a sweep when it expires. - **No nesting:** sub-agents can't delegate or create sub-agents of their own. - **No desktops:** sub-agents are never given a desktop tool server, since two agents can't drive one desktop. **No duplicates of agents you've defined.** If an existing agent is meant for the work, the agent should delegate to it instead. This is enforced three ways: - **A rule** in the agent's instructions, which names your agents. - **A required explanation:** `why_not_existing_agents` must be filled in. - **A refusal check:** a sub-agent whose role reuses an agent's name is always refused. With an embedding model set (Settings → Memory), the role and task are also compared with every agent's description, and anything above the similarity setting (Settings → Sub-agents, default 0.78) is refused. The refusal tells the agent which agent to delegate to. On requests, near misses show up as warnings for you, and approving them is your call. **Requests.** A request appears in three places: - **In the conversation:** an approval card with the agent's reasoning and the system's own estimate. The estimate covers, for each sub-agent: the model and its size (from the provider's model list), whether it runs on your hardware or a cloud plan, free provider slots, and the usage ledger's averages for that model. It also gives the total model-minutes and the expected wall time. - **In the Requests inbox:** under **Requests → Sub-agent requests**, with a badge for pending requests. - **On MQTT**, if `AHQ_MQTT_URL` is set (see below). You can approve as asked or change the terms first: the number of sub-agents, how many at once, minutes, model requests, models, tools, and how long the approval lasts. You can also deny it, with or without a note. An approval is a grant for that agent in that conversation, and it expires. Your decision wakes the conversation: - **If the conversation is the agent's own,** it carries on with (or without) the sub-agents. - **If the agent asked while working on a task delegated to it,** the conversation's owner is told and delegates the task again. **MQTT notifications.** New requests and your decisions are published as JSON to `AHQ_MQTT_NOTIFY_TOPIC` (default `agent-hq/notifications`) on the broker in `AHQ_MQTT_URL`, using a client ID of their own. This is now the **MQTT** channel under Settings → Notifications, where you can turn it off, change its topic or narrow what it gets (see [Notifications](#notifications-telegram-discord-and-mqtt)). Set `AHQ_PUBLIC_URL` (for example `http://shockwave:8000`) to include a link to the request. ```json {"type": "subagent_request", "request_id": "…", "agent": "Duke", "why": "…", "subagents": [{"role": "Feed reader", "purpose": "…", "label": "qwen3:14b @ Einstein Ollama", "est_minutes": 5}], "total_minutes": 5, "hours": 2, "link": "http://shockwave:8000/requests?id=…", "at": "…"} {"type": "subagent_decision", "request_id": "…", "agent": "Duke", "status": "approved", "grant": {…}, "note": "…"} ``` **In the chat,** a sub-agent's work shows as a crumb marked *sub-agent*, with its role and model. Expand it for the task, the reason it was created, and its report. Sub-agents never appear in your agent lists, the New chat menu, teams or exports. ### Provider slots and the usage ledger - **Slots:** each model provider has **Max concurrent requests** (Settings → Model providers; 0 = no limit). It caps how many model calls run against that provider at once, across every worker, so a burst of agents and sub-agents queues instead of swamping a GPU box. Slots are leases in Valkey that are renewed while a call runs, so a crashed worker can't hold one for more than 90 seconds. - **The ledger:** every agent run (chat turn, delegated task or sub-agent task) is recorded with its model, model requests, tokens and wall-clock time. **Settings → Usage** totals these by agent (sub-agent runs count under the agent that created them), by model and by day. Request estimates use the same numbers. - **Daily budgets** aren't built yet, on purpose: watch the real numbers here first. ## Disabling and deleting agents Removing an agent takes two deliberate steps on the **Settings → Agents** page: 1. **Disable** stops the agent: it takes no new work, other agents stop delegating to it, and its conversations stay readable. Tick **Enabled** and save to bring it back. 2. **Delete permanently** appears once the agent is disabled. It shows what will go and asks you to type the agent's name to confirm. It can't be undone. Deleting an agent removes: - its conversations: messages, files, jobs, traces and model history, including huddles it started (it leaves the huddles it joined, which stay) - its schedules and event subscriptions - its own memories and skills, test cases, proposals, ratings, reflections, tool approvals and sub-agent requests - its avatar and any sub-agents it made Some things are kept: - **Usage ledger:** cost history stays intact. - **Shared learning:** team memories, team skills and knowledge-library documents stay. - **Goals it owned:** these go back to your backlog with no owner, and actions it was working go back to Ready. An agent with work queued or running can't be deleted until that work finishes or you stop it. **API:** `DELETE /api/agents/{id}` disables. `GET /api/agents/{id}/delete-plan` returns what a delete would remove and whether it's allowed now. `DELETE /api/agents/{id}/permanent` deletes a disabled agent (`409` with the reason otherwise). ## Avatars Each agent can also have **pronouns** (he/him, she/her, they/them…). Teammates see them in the roster and with delegated results, so a supervisor refers to them correctly. Give each agent a face on the **Settings → Agents** page: **Upload avatar** accepts a GIF (animated is fine), PNG, JPEG or WebP image up to 3 MB (`AHQ_AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`). Avatars appear in the agent list, the conversation list, the chat header, next to each reply, and on desktop-help banners. Agents without one get their initials on a colour derived from their name. - **Storage:** images are kept in the database, so every machine serves the same ones, and they're included in agent export and import. - **Animation:** how animated GIFs behave is a per-browser setting on the **Settings → System** page: - *Always animate* - *Only while the agent is working* - *Never*: shows the first frame; hovering plays the animation. Browsers set to reduce motion default to *Never*. - **Working indicator:** an agent that's currently working also gets a highlighted ring around its avatar. ## Local-first models Three features let local models do most of the work, so frontier models are only used when needed. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Agent's main model<br/>(local, text-only)"] subgraph desktop["Agent desktop container"] PW["Playwright MCP :8931<br/>page as accessibility text"] CH["Chromium<br/>(same window you see)"] DM["desktop MCP :8765<br/>screenshot, click, type"] end V["Vision model<br/>(small local VLM)"] F["Fallback model<br/>(frontier, optional)"] A -- "browser_navigate / snapshot / click by ref" --> PW PW -- CDP --> CH A -- "look(question) / click_on(description)" --> V V -- "screenshots" --> DM V -- "text answer or x,y" --> A A -. "error, runaway loop, or escalate()" .-> F ``` ### 1. Read web pages as text (Playwright MCP) Each desktop container now runs a Chromium window (kept on the desktop, with its profile in `/config/agent-browser`) and a [Playwright MCP](https://playwright.dev/mcp/snapshots) server attached to it over the DevTools Protocol. Agents read pages as an accessibility snapshot, a text tree in which every element has a ref, and click or type by ref. That brings some big advantages: - Any text model can browse; no vision model is involved. - Clicks are exact rather than guessed coordinates. - It costs far fewer tokens than screenshots. - It works in the same browser you see, so a login you do through take-control stays in place for the agent. Every desktop made under **Settings → Desktops & workbenches** registers it for you as `desktop-N-browser` (`http://desktop-N:8931/mcp`, **Controls an agent desktop** ticked, *Prefix tool names* unticked, since its tools are already called `browser_*`). Agents should call `browser_snapshot` after navigating to read the page. ### 2. Vision as a tool (per-agent vision model) Set a **Vision model** on an agent, for example `qwen3-vl:8b` from your Ollama provider. The agent's main model then never sees screenshots, so its context stays small and it can be a text-only model. Instead it gets three tools: - `look(question)`: a text answer about what's on screen, such as "CPU peaked at 87% at 14:20". - `locate(description)`: the x/y position of something described in words. - `click_on(description)`: locate it, then click. The vision model does the looking. Screenshot tools on that agent's desktop servers are hidden from the main model. Two settings tune it for the vision model you pick: - **Coordinates:** *0–1000 scale* for the Qwen-VL family and Holo models; *pixels* for UI-TARS. - **Zoom in to double-check clicks:** after a first guess, the area around it is cropped, enlarged and checked again. That takes one more vision call, but small local models land much more accurately with it. Good local choices are `qwen3-vl:4b` or `qwen3-vl:8b` (in Ollama) for reading screens and graphs, and Holo2 or UI-TARS-1.5 for precise clicking. The last two are served through vLLM or llama.cpp as an *OpenAI-compatible* provider. With 16 GB of VRAM, keep in mind that the main model and the vision model each need to load; a 14B text model plus a 4B vision model fit more comfortably than gpt-oss:20b plus an 8B. ### 3. Fallback model Set a **Fallback model** on an agent, for example `gpt-4.1` from OpenAI. The turn is rerun on it when any of these happens: - the main model errors, for instance because the Ollama server is down; - it runs away, hitting the per-run request limit while looping on tool calls; - it calls `escalate(reason)` itself. Agents with a fallback are told to do this when a task is beyond them. The switch shows up in the conversation and the live activity panel. The fallback can't escalate again. It doesn't start the turn over: it gets everything the main model did up to its last complete step (its tool calls and their results), with a note to take over from there and finish the task, so work already done isn't repeated. **Guardrails for the main model.** Two settings on an agent (Settings → Agents) make a stuck local model fail in minutes instead of running on: - **Max output tokens**: the most one model response may generate, thinking included. A model that thinks without end stops here instead of filling the context window. Leave room for the biggest file the agent writes in one call: 16,384 is a reasonable start for a coding agent. When a tool call is cut off at this limit, Ollama can't read it and answers with a server error (500) instead of saying the model ran out of room. The client would quietly send the request again, and on a local GPU each try can take 5 minutes (8,192 tokens at 25 a second). So when this limit is set, Agent HQ makes a single attempt per request. On a 500, how long the request ran tells the two causes apart, using the model's measured speed: - **Cut off** (it had written close to the limit): Agent HQ says so in the chat and tries once more on the same model, telling it to keep each tool call well under the limit by writing big files in parts (`write_file`, then `write_file` with `append=true`). If that fails too, the fallback takes over as usual. - **Unreadable** (well under the limit: the model got the call's JSON wrong, usually quotes in a shell command with code inside): it tries again on the same model up to 3 times in a turn, naming the tool in the note, and from the second slip on telling the model to keep code out of shell commands. Only a fourth goes to the fallback, since redoing one step costs far less than the local model's whole run. The workbench's `run_shell` description already steers models away from heredocs, towards `write_file` and `run_python`. - **Request time limit**: a deadline in seconds for one model request, every client retry included. Without it, a request can wait for the client's 10-minute timeout and then be retried twice. - **Model requests per run**: the most model requests one run may make, 50 if left blank. It stops a model looping on tool calls, but a coding agent working through a big task (write, run, read, edit, run again) can need more: 150 is a reasonable start. The retry with less thinking and the fallback each get that many again. **Side jobs follow the same settings.** When no separate summary, reflection or judge model is set, Agent HQ names chats, writes compaction summaries, reflects on finished work and grades test runs with the agent's own model. Those calls now carry the agent's thinking level, max output tokens and request time limit too. Before, they got the model's defaults, which on Qwen3.8 is the highest reasoning effort with no cap and no deadline: one reflection could hold a single-GPU server for many minutes while the agent's own requests queued behind it. **A failing tool call doesn't end the run.** When a tool server reports an error (edit_file can't find the text, a command fails), the model gets it back as a failed tool result and carries on. PydanticAI's default would count it as a retry, and the fourth miss on the same tool in a row ended the whole run with no reply. Repeated failures are still bounded by **Model requests per run**. When the main model hits either one, it gets one more try on the same model with less thinking (low effort, or thinking off for Ollama models that only have on/off), carrying on from where it stopped. If that fails too, the fallback takes over. The guardrails don't apply to the fallback. **Keeping a turn going.** Small models often say what they'll do next ("I'll now write the world files…") and stop. A reply whose last paragraph only announces work is sent back with a nudge to do it with tool calls, at most twice per reply. Replies that were cut off at the output limit, and replies that link to files by path (`sandbox:/…`, `/work/…`, `attachment:…`) instead of sending them, are sent back the same way; when the file was already sent, the agent is told to take out the link and not to send it again. So is a reply after the agent changed code (`write_file`, `edit_file`, `save_script`) without running anything since: it's told to run the code or its tests first, unless the reply says plainly that it couldn't test. ## Observability Set `OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_ENDPOINT` to your OpenTelemetry Collector, for example `http://perceptor:4318`; it uses OTLP over HTTP, so the Collector needs its HTTP receiver. You can also point it straight at Phoenix (`http://phoenix-host:6006`). Agent HQ's traces are shaped for [Arize Phoenix](https://arize.com/docs/phoenix): - **Phoenix's native span types.** The OpenInference span processor reshapes PydanticAI's spans into the agent, LLM and tool spans Phoenix understands, with inputs, outputs and token counts. - **One trace per conversation turn, across machines.** Each job carries the W3C `traceparent` of whatever queued it, through Valkey to the worker. A turn, its delegations on other workers and any background report all form one tree: `turn` → `invoke_agent` → `execute_tool delegate` → `task` → `invoke_agent` → `chat`. - **Sessions.** Every span inside a job has `session.id` set to the conversation ID, so Phoenix's **View Session** shows a whole conversation, every turn included. Job spans also carry agent, agent ID, job ID, pool, worker and attempt, as attributes and as metadata. In a huddle each agent's answer is its own `turn <agent>` span in the same session. - **No screenshots in traces.** Images sent to vision models are never recorded. `AHQ_TRACE_CONTENT=0` also leaves prompts and replies out. - **No HTTP noise.** FastAPI's own request tracing is turned off, so the UI's background polling doesn't bury agent traces. - **No MCP protocol noise.** The MCP Python SDK and FastMCP add their own spans for every tool listing and call (`MCP send tools/call …`, `server/discover`, `tools/list`). These have no OpenInference kind, so Phoenix shows them as *unknown*, and they repeat what the `execute_tool` span already shows: the tool's name, arguments and result. They're left out by default. Set `AHQ_TRACE_MCP=1` to keep them, labelled as tool or chain spans, when you're debugging an MCP server. - **Its own Phoenix project.** Traces go to a Phoenix project named after `OTEL_SERVICE_NAME` (`agent-hq` by default) rather than `default`. Set `PHOENIX_PROJECT_NAME` to choose a different one. The project is a resource attribute (`openinference.project.name`), so it passes through a Collector unchanged. The API process reports as `agent-hq` and workers as `agent-hq-worker`, both in the same project. The chat page's live activity panel shows the same activity in real time. ## Layout ``` backend/app/ models.py all the tables: providers, agents, tools, threads, messages, jobs, skills, reflections, # Agent HQ application: API/UI + workers (+ an example agent desktop).
# Needs the shared infrastructure in deploy/infra (Postgres, Valkey, Mosquitto).
#   cp .env.example .env   # set AHQ_DB_URL, AHQ_REDIS_URL, AHQ_MQTT_URL, model keys
#   docker compose up -d --build
#
# Workers can also run on other machines: copy this file there and keep only the
# worker services you want on that host (same image, same .env).
name: agent-hq

x-app: &app
  build: .
  restart: unless-stopped
  env_file: [.env]
  # The host's name, for readable worker names like worker-shockwave-7090. (Or set
  # AHQ_HOST_NAME in .env, e.g. on Docker Desktop, where this file doesn't exist.)
  volumes: ["/etc/hostname:/etc/host_hostname:ro"]
  # "workbench" lets workers (and the API, to list tools) reach the agents' workbenches.
  networks: [default, workbench]

services:
  hq:
    <<: *app
    # Plain HTTP for this host only by default: browse through https via the caddy service.
    # Set AHQ_HTTP_BIND=8000 in .env to reach it over the network without HTTPS.
    ports: ["${AHQ_HTTP_BIND:-127.0.0.1:8000}:8000"]
    # "docker-api" reaches docker-proxy, so the Resources page can run desktops and workbenches.
    networks: [default, workbench, docker-api]
    environment:
      AHQ_CORS_ORIGINS: http://localhost:4200
      AHQ_WORKER_PREFIX: hq
      AHQ_DOCKER_URL: http://docker-proxy:2375
      # Your step-ca root, so the knowledge library trusts your Gitea and internal sites
      # over HTTPS (the same root_ca.crt the caddy service uses).
      AHQ_EXTRA_CA_FILE: /etc/agent-hq/caddy/root_ca.crt
    volumes:
      - /etc/hostname:/etc/host_hostname:ro
      - hq-data:/data                          # knowledge library: uploads, repo clones
      - ./deploy/caddy:/etc/agent-hq/caddy:ro
      # Knowledge library NFS shares go under /shares (SMB shares need no mount). See the
      # nas-docs volume at the bottom of this file.
      # - nas-docs:/shares/docs:ro

  # General-purpose worker: runs agents whose pool is "default".
  worker:
    <<: *app
    command: ["python", "-m", "app.worker", "--pools", "default", "--concurrency", "4"]
    # No fixed AHQ_WORKER_NAME, so replicas stay unique: each is named
    # worker-<host>-<last 4 of its container ID>, e.g. worker-shockwave-7090.
    environment:
      AHQ_WORKER_PREFIX: worker
    deploy:
      replicas: 1          # raise for more parallel agent runs

  # Worker for agents that drive desktops (set those agents' pool to "desktop"). Runs on
  # the same host as the desktops, so it reaches http://desktop-N:8765/mcp on this network.
  worker-desktop:
    <<: *app
    command: ["python", "-m", "app.worker", "--pools", "desktop", "--concurrency", "1"]
    environment:
      AHQ_WORKER_NAME: worker-desktop

  # Text-only web tools: RSS/Atom feeds, readable pages, and search via your SearXNG.
  # Register in the UI (Settings -> Tools): HTTP, http://web-reader:8800/mcp, untick
  # "Prefix tool names", leave "Controls an agent desktop" unticked.
  web-reader:
    build: ./webreader
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      SEARXNG_URL: ${SEARXNG_URL:-}                     # e.g. http://searxng.home.arpa:8888
      WEBREADER_ALLOW_HOSTS: ${WEBREADER_ALLOW_HOSTS:-}   # internal hosts agents may read
      WEBREADER_MAX_CHARS: ${WEBREADER_MAX_CHARS:-12000}

  # Outbound MQTT: agents publish their status and allow-listed commands to your broker.
  # Register in the UI (Settings -> Tools): HTTP, http://mqtt-publisher:8810/mcp, untick
  # "Prefix tool names", leave "Controls an agent desktop" unticked. `publish` asks you first.
  mqtt-publisher:
    build: ./mqttpublisher
    restart: unless-stopped
    environment:
      MQTT_PUBLISH_URL: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_URL:-}                       # its own broker user, with write access
      MQTT_PUBLISH_ALLOW: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_ALLOW:-agent-hq/agents/#}  # topics `publish` may use
      MQTT_PUBLISH_DENY: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_DENY:-agent-hq/notifications/#}
      MQTT_PUBLISH_STATUS_PREFIX: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_STATUS_PREFIX:-agent-hq/agents}
      MQTT_PUBLISH_RATE_PER_MINUTE: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_RATE_PER_MINUTE:-30}
      MQTT_PUBLISH_CA_FILE: ${MQTT_PUBLISH_CA_FILE:-}                # e.g. /certs/root_ca.crt for mqtts://
    # For mqtts:// with your step-ca, mount the root certificate:
    # volumes:
    #   - ./deploy/caddy/root_ca.crt:/certs/root_ca.crt:ro

  # Lab tools (docs/labtools.md): MCP servers for your lab's systems, as many instances as you
  # like, each with its own integrations, read or write access and credentials. They live in
  # an overlay: docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f deploy/lab/compose.example.yml up -d

  # HTTPS for the UI (certificate from your step-ca) and sign-in-protected desktop viewers.
  # Setup: deploy/caddy/Caddyfile and the README's "HTTPS" section.
  caddy:
    image: caddy:2
    restart: unless-stopped
    ports: ["80:80", "443:443"]
    environment:
      AHQ_SITE: ${AHQ_SITE:-}
      ACME_CA: ${ACME_CA:-}
      ACME_EMAIL: ${ACME_EMAIL:-admin@home.arpa}   # any address; step-ca sends no mail
    volumes:
      - ./deploy/caddy:/etc/caddy:ro     # Caddyfile + your root_ca.crt
      - caddy-data:/data
      - caddy-config:/config
    depends_on: [hq]

  # Docker API for hq, limited to containers, images, networks and volumes, so the
  # Settings -> Desktops & workbenches page can create, start, stop and remove them.
  # Only hq is on its network. Anyone who controls hq can run containers on this host:
  # leave this service out (and AHQ_DOCKER_URL unset) to manage containers by hand.
  docker-proxy:
    image: tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:latest
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [docker-api]
    volumes: ["/var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock:ro"]
    environment:
      CONTAINERS: 1
      IMAGES: 1
      NETWORKS: 1
      VOLUMES: 1
      POST: 1
      ALLOW_START: 1
      ALLOW_STOP: 1
      ALLOW_RESTARTS: 1

  # Images for Settings -> Desktops & workbenches, which creates every desktop and
  # workbench (and registers their tool servers). These services never run a container:
  # they only build agent-hq/desktop, agent-hq/workbench and agent-hq/mcp-runner. The images are built only
  # with the "images" profile (plain `up --build` skips them):
  #   docker compose --profile images build
  # then click Recreate on each desktop / workbench to move it to the new image.
  # Desktops: no published ports; you reach a viewer only through caddy, signed in.
  # Workbenches: no network but the egress proxy, which applies their rules from the UI.
  desktop-image:
    build: ./desktop
    image: agent-hq/desktop:latest
    profiles: [images]

  workbench-image:
    build: ./workbench
    image: agent-hq/workbench:latest
    profiles: [images]

  # Package servers (Settings -> Tools -> Catalog -> Install): an npm or PyPI MCP server
  # in a container of its own, locked down like a workbench, behind the egress proxy.
  mcp-runner-image:
    build: ./mcp-runner
    image: agent-hq/mcp-runner:latest
    profiles: [images]

  # The workbenches' only way out: a proxy that checks each workbench's rules (PyPI for
  # all of them by default). Edit the rules under Settings -> Desktops & workbenches
  # (Network, and each workbench's page); they apply within seconds, from Valkey.
  egress:
    build: ./deploy/egress
    restart: unless-stopped
    env_file: [.env]          # AHQ_REDIS_URL: where it reads the rules and logs what it blocks
    networks: [default, workbench]
    read_only: true

volumes:
  hq-data:
  # An NFS export from your NAS for the knowledge library, mounted read-only by Docker
  # (no privileges needed in the container). Uncomment this and the line in hq's volumes,
  # then add a Network share source with the path /shares/docs.
  # nas-docs:
  #   driver: local
  #   driver_opts:
  #     type: nfs
  #     o: addr=truenas.home.arpa,ro,nfsvers=4.1,soft
  #     device: :/mnt/tank/docs
  caddy-data:
  caddy-config:
  # Workbench data lives in volumes Agent HQ mounts (ahq-<name>, or agent-hq_workbench-1
  # for the one taken over from compose). They're not listed here, so `docker compose
  # down -v` can't delete them.

networks:
  default:
  # Internal: containers on only this network can't reach the internet or your LAN.
  workbench:
    internal: true
  # Internal: only hq and docker-proxy, so agents' containers can't reach the Docker API.
  docker-api:
    internal: true

![squirrelscan](docs/logo/light.svg)

# squirrelscan

**The website QA tool for your coding agent**

squirrelscan is an Open Source cli tool that audits websites for SEO, performance, security, accessibility, agent experience and other issues, and gives your coding agent exact fixes. Run it from the CLI, inside your coding agent, in the cloud, or over MCP.

Combine your coding agent with a deterministic and extensible audit tool.

[![Add to Cursor](https://cursor.com/deeplink/mcp-install-dark.svg)](https://squirrelscan.com/add/cursor)
[![Add to Claude Code](https://img.shields.io/badge/Add_to-Claude_Code-d97757?style=for-the-badge)](https://squirrelscan.com/add/claude)
[![Add to Codex](https://img.shields.io/badge/Add_to-Codex-000000?style=for-the-badge)](https://squirrelscan.com/add/codex)
[![Add to opencode](https://img.shields.io/badge/Add_to-opencode-383838?style=for-the-badge)](https://squirrelscan.com/add/opencode)
[![MCP Registry](https://img.shields.io/badge/MCP-Registry-1f6feb?style=for-the-badge)](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io)

[![CI](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/squirrelscan/squirrelscan/ci.yml?branch=main&style=for-the-badge&label=CI)](https://github.com/squirrelscan/squirrelscan/actions/workflows/ci.yml)
[![CodeQL](https://img.shields.io/github/actions/workflow/status/squirrelscan/squirrelscan/codeql.yml?branch=main&style=for-the-badge&label=CodeQL)](https://github.com/squirrelscan/squirrelscan/actions/workflows/codeql.yml)
[![npm](https://img.shields.io/npm/v/squirrelscan?style=for-the-badge&label=npm)](https://www.npmjs.com/package/squirrelscan)
[![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-52a852?style=for-the-badge)](LICENSE)

![Terminal demo: squirrel audit on a small test site reports 13 failed checks, the report is piped to Claude Code, which fixes the pages and re-audits from 32/100 (F) to 92/100 (A), then git status lists the files it changed](assets/readme-demo.gif)

<sub>A real run on a tiny test site, with the released CLI (signed out, so free) and Claude Code. We cut the two minutes the agent spent working, because nobody wants to watch an agent think.</sub>

## Features

- **[Built for coding agents](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/developers/agents)** - Skills for Claude Code, Cursor, Codex and any coding agent run the audit, fix and re-audit loop. Connect over the CLI, the hosted or local MCP server, or the API.
- **[Enriched fixes for you and your coding agent](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/fix-your-site-with-an-ai-agent)** - Every finding says how to fix it, in LLM-optimized output your agent can apply, and every rule has its own docs page. Signed in, the report adds an editor's summary of what to fix first and the technology stack the site runs on.
- **[350+ rules, 22 categories](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/rules)** - Audit coverage across SEO, accessibility, performance, security, content and more.
- **[Agent experience](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/rules/ax)** - Audit how well AI agents can read, discover and act on your site: llms.txt, AGENTS.md, Markdown responses, and what AI crawlers are served.
- **[Link checking and monitoring](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/link-checking)** - Perch, the cloud link checker, tells a broken link from a blocked one and confirms a failure before reporting it. On Pro and Team, scheduled audits email you when a link breaks.
- **[Security and site integrity](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/rules/integrity)** - Detect phishing kits, injected pages, leaked credentials and missing security headers.
- **[Entity map](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/entity-map)** - Your site's JSON-LD collapsed into one graph: one identity, or a new one on every page.
- **[Browser rendering in the cloud](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/browser-rendering)** - Signed in, pages are rendered in a real browser in the cloud, so single-page apps and JavaScript-heavy sites are audited as visitors see them, at no extra cost per page.
- **[Cloud audits](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/cloud-audits)** - AI page analysis, scheduled audits, a per-website issue tracker and shareable reports.
- **[Smart crawling](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/crawl)** - Fast and memory efficient, incremental with ETag, Last-Modified and content hashing, and resumable from checkpoints.
- **[Crawl history and changes](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/cli/report)** - Track site evolution, compare crawls, spot regressions.
- **[Developer-first CLI](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/cli)** - Single binary, zero dependencies, shell completions, self-update.
- **[Multiple output formats](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/cli/report#output-formats)** - Console, JSON, HTML, Markdown, Text, LLM, XML.

## Rule categories

Ordered by how much a failure usually costs you, not by how many rules each one has.

| Category | Rules | What it covers |
|----------|-------|----------------|
| Crawlability | 27 | Whether search engines and agents can reach and index you at all: robots.txt, sitemap validity and coverage, indexability conflicts, redirect and canonical chains, soft 404s, a home page that fails to load, pages that answer 5xx |
| Core SEO | 14 | The per-page fundamentals: title, meta description, H1, canonical, charset, doctype, robots meta, Open Graph and Twitter cards, plus canonical form drift across the site |
| Agent Experience | 20 | How ready you are for AI agents to read, discover and act on the site: whether GPTBot and Claude-User get the same content a browser does, AGENTS.md, llms.txt, Markdown responses, API and MCP discovery, licensing and noai signals, WebMCP tools, pay-per-crawl, shop offer completeness, response token weight, answer blocks |
| Site Integrity | 10 | Signs the site has been compromised: injected doorway pages, phishing kit signatures, obfuscated scripts, brand impersonation, cloaking, known-malicious URLs, plus pages left on an outdated site template |
| Security | 32 | Transport and header hygiene: HTTPS and HSTS, CSP, cookie flags, mixed content, subresource integrity, leaked secrets, tokens in web storage, unprotected and downgraded forms, open GraphQL introspection and mutations over GET, API endpoints that return data without authentication, credentials and bulk personal data in JSON API responses, exposed .git, .env and backup files, auth endpoints that leak password hashes or the user record, open redirects, admin APIs that answer without credentials, exposed Spring Boot Actuator endpoints, Supabase tables readable with the public anon key |
| Links | 18 | Internal and external link health: broken and dead links, in-page anchors whose target is gone, redirect chains, anchor-text quality and generic-anchor density, orphan and dead-end pages, pages linked only from sitewide chrome, pages whose navigation is missing links the rest of the site has, HTTPS downgrades |
| Content | 35 | Text quality and honesty: common misspellings, duplicate titles and descriptions, near-duplicate pages, title-template consistency, readability, font consistency, color sprawl, voice consistency, terminology consistency, typography, word count, freshness, stale dated copy, text cut mid-word by a character limit, heading hierarchy, keyword stuffing, hidden text, placeholder media and contact details, money pages with no on-site conversion path, encoding damage |
| Performance | 32 | Core Web Vitals and delivery: LCP, CLS and INP hints, TTFB, compression, caching, render-blocking resources, DOM size, font delivery, legacy and unminified JS/CSS |
| Reliability | 6 | Scripts, stylesheets and fonts that fail to load (a first-party bundle that answers 404 or 500 after a deploy, third-party and font failures), JavaScript errors on rendered pages, and forms that lose submissions |
| Images | 16 | Alt text, modern formats, responsive `srcset`, intrinsic dimensions and aspect-ratio mismatches, lazy loading above versus below the fold, file weight |
| Structured Data | 26 | JSON-LD validity and rich-result eligibility for Article, Product, FAQ, Review, Breadcrumb, Organization, LocalBusiness, Video and site search, the markup a page's classified type should carry, plus thirteen site-wide checks on the entity map: whether the site declares one identity for itself or a new one on every page, and rating markup that is not about the page it sits on |
| Accessibility | 63 | WCAG coverage: ARIA roles and names, form labels and autocomplete tokens, colour contrast, heading order, landmarks, tables and lists, focus visibility, touch targets, captions |
| Mobile | 8 | Viewport configuration, tap-target size, legible font sizes, horizontal scroll, blocked zoom, form fields small enough to zoom the page on focus, intrusive interstitials, the web app manifest and its icons |
| Social Media | 5 | Open Graph and Twitter Card completeness, image dimensions, canonical URL match, social profile links, site-chrome assets that disagree across pages |
| URL Structure | 10 | Length, casing, hyphenation, stop words, query parameters, special characters, trailing-slash consistency, site-wide convention consistency |
| E-E-A-T | 16 | Experience, expertise, authority and trust signals: author bylines and credentials, byline consistency across pages of a type, about and contact pages, citations, editorial policy, disclaimers, YMYL detection |
| Legal Compliance | 4 | Privacy policy, terms of service, real cookie-consent machinery, subprocessor disclosure |
| Internationalization | 4 | hreflang correctness, the document language declaration, and spelling, date and currency conventions that contradict each other on one page |
| Local SEO | 3 | NAP (name, address, phone) consistency across every crawled page, geo metadata, service-area businesses |
| Video | 3 | VideoObject markup, captions and accessibility, thumbnails |
| Analytics | 3 | Google Tag Manager presence, consent-mode wiring, and the same GA4 or GTM ID installed twice |
| Blocking | 3 | Content, links and trackers that ad blockers and privacy filters strip for a large share of your visitors |

**Total: 350+ rules across 22 categories**

Cloud audits also run ten [third-party rules](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/cloud/third-party) (compromised, proxied and unpinned vendor scripts, session replay and tag managers on sign-in and checkout pages, vendor counts). They are cloud-only and are not counted above.

See the [rules reference](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/rules) for full details.

## CLI

### Installation

**Paste into your coding agent** (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, opencode and friends):
```text
Fetch and follow the setup instructions for squirrelscan at https://docs.squirrelscan.com/agent-setup/prompt.md
```
Your agent installs the CLI, connects MCP and runs a first audit. You can [read exactly what it will follow](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/agent-setup/prompt) first.

**macOS / Linux:**
```bash
curl -fsSL https://install.squirrelscan.com | bash
```

**Windows:**
```powershell
iwr -useb https://install.squirrelscan.com/install.ps1 | iex
```

**Homebrew (macOS):**
```bash
brew install --cask squirrelscan/tap/squirrel
```
The cask installs a launcher that runs the regular installer on first use. The CLI then updates itself with `squirrel self update`; `brew upgrade` leaves it alone.

**npm (all platforms):**
```bash
npm install -g squirrelscan
```

**npx (run without installing):**
```bash
npx squirrelscan audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com
```

### Quick start

```bash
# Audit a website
squirrel audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com

# Generate HTML report
squirrel audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com -f html -o report.html

# Pipe to Claude for AI analysis
squirrel audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com --format llm | claude

# Quick audit for a fast first look (other levels: surface, full)
squirrel audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com --level quick

# run only agent experience and performance rules
squirrel audit nutshop.squirrelscan.com --rule-include ax,performance

# login for cloud audits and cloud rendering
squirrel auth login
```

## Reports

A health score and grade, group scores for SEO, performance, security and Agent Experience (AX) colored by score, a ranked list of issues, and a copy fix prompt for each one that you can paste into your coding agent. Publish reports to the web to share with team members or coding agents (fix instructions are embedded).

![A squirrelscan report for squirrelscan.com. The header shows the site, 220 of 220 pages scanned, the Full audit level and a health score of 79 (C). A notice says 912 of 1412 external links were not checked. Four group cards show SEO 86 (B), Performance 59 (F), Security 95 (A) and Agents 42 (F), each with its error and warning counts. Below are pass, warning and fail totals, an auto-generated summary, and the first three ranked issues, each with a Copy fix prompt button.](docs/images/report/example-report.webp)

[See an example report](https://reports.squirrelscan.com/01M5NJH51Q6FNRAA3QGW8GYWB6), or read [how to read your report](https://docs.squirrelscan.com/guides/read-your-report).

## Add to your coding agent

squirrelscan ships as an **MCP server** (hosted at `mcp.squirrelscan.com`), **skills** (autonomous audit + fix workflows), and a **plugin** for Claude Code and Cursor. Cursor installs in one click from the badge above; the rest are a single copy-paste.

### Cursor

Click the **Add to Cursor** badge above, or add it manually to `~/.cursor/mcp.json`:

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "squirrelscan": { "url": "https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp" }
  }
}
```

Skills: `squirrel skills install`

### Claude Code

Install the plugin (bundles skills + the MCP server):

```
/plugin marketplace add squirrelscan/skills
/plugin install squirrelscan@squirrelscan
```

Or add just the MCP server:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http squirrelscan https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp
```

### OpenAI Codex

Add the server to `~/.codex/config.toml`:

```toml
[mcp_servers.squirrelscan]
url = "https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp"
```

Codex reads Agent Skills from `~/.agents/skills`, so skills work too: `squirrel skills install`

### opencode

Add the server to `opencode.json`:

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "mcp": {
    "squirrelscan": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp",
      "enabled": true
    }
  }
}
```

### Any MCP client

squirrelscan is in the [MCP Registry](https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io) as `com.squirrelscan/squirrelscan`. Point any client at the remote server:

```
https://mcp.squirrelscan.com/mcp
```

Authentication is per-user OAuth (or pass a squirrelscan API key as a Bearer token). Skills follow the [Agent Skills standard](https://agentskills.io): `squirrel skills install` puts them in `~/.agents/skills/` and `~/.claude/skills/`.


## Skills

Two skills drive agent workflows. They live in [squirrelscan/skills](https://github.com/squirrelscan/skills), along with the Claude Code, Cursor and Agent Plugins packages that bundle them with the MCP server. `squirrel skills install` downloads and verifies them itself, and from v0.0.99 `squirrel`'s auto-update keeps them current. Installs made earlier with `npx skills` are taken over.

- **`squirrelscan`** - operating the CLI: install, login, keys, credits, running audits, publishing reports, the entity map, MCP setup, config, troubleshooting.
- **`audit-website`** - the full fix loop: audit, map issues to source files, fix in batches, re-audit until the site scores well.

```bash
squirrel skills install
```

Then, in your agent:

```
Use the audit-website skill to audit this site and fix all issues but only crawl 10 pages
```

## Output formats

| Format | Flag | Use Case |
|--------|------|----------|
| Console | (default) | Human-readable terminal output |
| JSON | `-f json` | CI/CD, programmatic processing |
| HTML | `-f html` | Visual reports for sharing |
| Markdown | `-f markdown` | Documentation, GitHub |
| Text | `-f text` | Clean output for piping to LLMs |
| LLM | `-f llm` | LLM optimized output |
| XML | `-f xml` | XML output |

## Source and development

The complete local CLI, crawler, audit engine, rules, report generators, CLI-facing cloud clients, and documentation site are open source in this repository. The hosted API, website, dashboard, and cloud worker implementations are separate private services.

Prerequisites: [Bun 1.4.4](https://bun.sh/) and Git.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/squirrelscan/squirrelscan.git
cd squirrelscan
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run dev -- audit https://nutshop.squirrelscan.com --max-pages 10
```

Run the same checks used in pull requests:

```bash
bun run format:check
bun run lint
bun run typecheck
bun test
bun run build
bun run docs:check
bun run docs:build
```

See [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) before opening a pull request. Contributions require a Developer Certificate of Origin sign-off (`git commit -s`).

## Telemetry

Telemetry is enabled by default and is deliberately minimal: event name, CLI version, a random install ID, and bounded error categories. It does not send API keys, URLs, report contents, or raw error messages. After `squirrel auth login`, telemetry requests carry your login session (the 90-day sign-in token from login, never an API key) so events tie to your account; signed out, they are anonymous. Nothing is sent when telemetry is off.

Disable it permanently with:

```bash
squirrel self settings set telemetry false
```

Or disable all telemetry and install registration for any invocation by defining `NO_TELEMETRY` (any defined value works, including an empty value, `0`, or `false`) or `DO_NOT_TRACK=1` (or `true`). A project can opt out with `"telemetry": false` in `.squirrel/settings.json`:

```bash
NO_TELEMETRY=1 squirrel audit https://nutshop.squirrelscan.com
```

## Links

name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [main]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]
  merge_group:

permissions:
  contents: read

concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

env:
  NO_TELEMETRY: "1"

jobs:
  # Which jobs a change needs. Gating is job-level on purpose, NOT
  # `on.push.paths`: a filtered-out push produces no CI run at all, so every
  # ruleset-required check would sit at "Expected" forever and the PR could
  # never merge. A skipped job satisfies a required check; an absent one does
  # not.
  #
  # scripts/ci-classify.sh maps the changed paths to five outputs. Its header
  # holds the path rules and how to add one; scripts/test-ci-classify.sh is
  # its table test.
  #
  #   code       false for a docs-only change (docs/**, the root README,
  #              CONTRIBUTING, CODE_OF_CONDUCT, SECURITY and TRADEMARKS, issue
  #              and PR templates): only Docs check and build runs
  #   engine     Audit engine golden tests
  #   installer  Installer script syntax
  #   release    Release tooling tests
  #   build      Compile CLI
  #
  # Format, lint, and typecheck, CLI tests and Dependency audit run on every
  # code change: CLI tests is the only job that runs every test file, and bun
  # audit's answer moves with the advisory database, not only with bun.lock.
  #
  # Fail open, twice. This job writes every output `true` when the base is
  # unknown or unreachable, the diff is empty, or the classifier fails or
  # prints anything unexpected. And every gate also runs when this job did not
  # succeed: a job that dies after writing `false` (a failed post-checkout
  # step, say) keeps its outputs, and its outputs are empty if it never ran.
  changes:
    name: Classify changed files
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 2
    outputs:
      code: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.code }}
      engine: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.engine }}
      installer: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.installer }}
      release: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.release }}
      build: ${{ steps.classify.outputs.build }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - id: classify
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' && github.event.pull_request.base.sha || github.event_name == 'merge_group' && github.event.merge_group.base_sha || github.event.before }}
        run: |
          set -u
          run_everything() {
            echo "$1: running every job"
            printf '%s=true\n' code engine installer release build >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"
            exit 0
          }
          # Unknown base (first push, force-push, empty sha) → run everything.
          if [ -z "$BASE" ] || [ "$BASE" = "0000000000000000000000000000000000000000" ]; then
            run_everything "no base commit"
          fi
          git fetch --no-tags --depth=1 origin "$BASE" 2>/dev/null || run_everything "cannot fetch base $BASE"
          # --no-renames: a move lists both paths, so source moved under docs/
          # still counts as the code change it is.
          changed=$(git -c core.quotepath=false diff --name-only --no-renames "$BASE" HEAD) || run_everything "git diff failed"
          echo "$changed"
          result=$(printf '%s\n' "$changed" | bash scripts/ci-classify.sh) || run_everything "classifier failed"
          shape=$'^code=(true|false)\nengine=(true|false)\ninstaller=(true|false)\nrelease=(true|false)\nbuild=(true|false)$'
          [[ "$result" =~ $shape ]] || run_everything "unexpected classifier output"
          echo "$result" | tee -a "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

  changelog-guard:
    name: Changelog guard
    if: ${{ github.event_name == 'pull_request' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 2
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - name: Fetch pull request base
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        run: git fetch --no-tags --depth=1 origin "$BASE"
      - name: Fetch release tags without blobs
        run: git fetch --force --quiet --depth=1 --filter=blob:none origin 'refs/tags/v*:refs/tags/v*'
      - name: Check released changelog sections
        env:
          BASE: ${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }}
        run: bash scripts/check-released-changelog.sh "$BASE"

  quality:
    name: Format, lint, and typecheck
    needs: changes
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.code != 'false') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      # First: it takes ~20ms and it is the check that explains itself. Fails if
      # a test file lands outside every suite, if two suites would run the same
      # file, if a named suite points at a package that no longer exists, or if
      # the CLI tests job stops matching scripts/test-suites.ts.
      - name: Check every test suite is wired into CI
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --check
      - name: Check the CI path classifier
        run: bash scripts/test-ci-classify.sh
      - name: Check formatting
        run: bun run format:check
      - name: Lint
        run: bun run lint
      - name: Typecheck all workspaces
        run: bun run typecheck
      - name: Check third-party notices
        run: bun run notices:check
      # Claude Code reads .claude-plugin/marketplace.json from the default
      # branch: it must keep redirecting the old marketplace to squirrelscan/skills.
      # Checked on every PR because nothing else notices until an install breaks.
      - name: Check manifests are in sync
        run: bun run scripts/sync-plugin-manifests.ts --check
      # install.sh / install.ps1 carry pre-rendered copies of the CLI header
      # (apps/cli/src/cli/brand.ts); this fails when they drift from it.
      - name: Check installer header is in sync
        run: bun run scripts/sync-install-header.ts --check

  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Which test suites run where (#1670):
  #
  #   CLI tests (this job)  every test file in the repo, one step per suite.
  #                         This job was a single bare `bun test`, which walks the
  #                         WHOLE tree — packages/* already gated every PR, just
  #                         invisibly, under a job named for apps/cli. The steps
  #                         below run exactly that set; a red step now names the
  #                         package. `rest` is the complement of the named suites,
  #                         so a new package is covered the day it lands.
  #   Audit engine golden   packages/audit-engine golden/streaming/redirect/deadline
  #                         files, again, on their own — a corpus regression is
  #                         unreadable inside a 400-file log.
  #   Release tooling       scripts/release-version.test.ts, again, next to the
  #                         changelog shell test.
  #   release.yml           still one bare whole-tree `bun test` before a release.
  #
  # The last three deliberately re-run files the steps below already cover.
  #
  # "Every test file" means what bun discovers: *.test.* / *.spec.* / *_test.* /
  # *_spec.* with a js/ts extension, any case, outside dot-directories.
  # scripts/test-suites.ts owns that definition and the split; the quality job's
  # --check step fails if the two ever disagree.
  #
  # Do NOT swap these for `bun run test`: that script is `cd apps/cli && bun test`
  # and would drop every package. The job name is fixed by the "CLI tests"
  # required status check in the repo ruleset; renaming it means updating the
  # ruleset in the same change or every PR blocks on a check that never reports.
  #
  # Wall time, measured on main run 41308096807 (job total 23m, cap 25m; #1518):
  #   apps/cli 603s · audit-engine 372s · rules 143s · rest 125s · crawler 121s
  #   report 2s, plus about 20s of checkout and setup per job
  # One job ran them back to back and sat 2 minutes under the cap (a PR run hit
  # 24m54s; five runs were cancelled at the cap and showed as failed checks). The
  # suites now run as two parallel jobs of about 12 and 11 minutes, grouped so
  # each is balanced, and "CLI tests" is a small aggregate job that needs both and
  # fails unless both passed. The required status check keeps its name and its
  # job id (`build` needs it), so the ruleset needs no edit. Every suite still
  # runs once: `scripts/test-suites.ts --check` in the quality job fails if a
  # test file belongs to no suite or ci.yml has no `--run` step for a suite, in
  # whichever job the step sits.
  # ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
  cli-tests-app:
    name: CLI tests (apps/cli and crawler)
    needs: quality
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - id: setup
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      # Every suite runs even when an earlier one is red, the way the single bare
      # `bun test` reported every failure at once; each still fails the job. The
      # setup guard keeps a broken toolchain to one red step instead of several.
      - name: Report tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run report
      - name: apps/cli tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run cli
      - name: Crawler tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run crawler

  cli-tests-packages:
    name: CLI tests (rules, engine and the rest)
    needs: quality
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 25
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - id: setup
        uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - name: Rules tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run rules
      - name: Remaining package and script tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run rest
      - name: Audit engine tests
        if: ${{ !cancelled() && steps.setup.outcome == 'success' }}
        run: bun run scripts/test-suites.ts --run audit-engine

  # The required status check. Skipped exactly when the old single job was (quality
  # not green); otherwise it passes only when both test jobs passed, so a cancelled
  # or skipped half is a red check, never a green one.
  cli-tests:
    name: CLI tests
    needs: [quality, cli-tests-app, cli-tests-packages]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - name: Both test jobs passed
        env:
          APP: ${{ needs.cli-tests-app.result }}
          PACKAGES: ${{ needs.cli-tests-packages.result }}
        run: |
          echo "apps/cli and crawler: $APP; rules, engine and the rest: $PACKAGES"
          [ "$APP" = success ] && [ "$PACKAGES" = success ]

  installer-scripts:
    name: Installer script syntax
    needs: [changes, quality]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.installer != 'false') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      # install.ps1 only ever runs on Windows machines, and the install test
      # workflow fetches the PUBLISHED script from main — so nothing here ever
      # exercised a change to it before users did. pwsh ships on the
      # GitHub-hosted ubuntu image and exposes the same parser and runtime
      # Windows PowerShell uses.
      #
      # The step runs from bash and probes for pwsh rather than declaring
      # `shell: pwsh`. That declaration is resolved before the step's command
      # runs, so on a runner without pwsh (a self-hosted or slimmed image) the
      # step fails with a shell-not-found error that reads like an installer
      # bug. Probing degrades to a skip with a notice instead.
      #
      # The script parses install.ps1 in full and then runs its download helpers
      # against a stubbed Invoke-WebRequest. Parsing alone proved only that the
      # file is syntactically PowerShell, which is how a script-scope Join-Path
      # on a null LOCALAPPDATA got through review: it parses, and it kills the
      # installer on its first line.
      - name: Check install.ps1
        run: |
          if ! command -v pwsh > /dev/null 2>&1; then
            echo "::notice::pwsh is not available on this runner; skipping the install.ps1 checks"
            exit 0
          fi
          pwsh -NoProfile -File ./scripts/install-ps-contract.test.ps1
      - name: Parse install.sh
        run: bash -n install.sh

  dependency-audit:
    name: Dependency audit
    needs: quality
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run audit:dependencies

  engine-tests:
    name: Audit engine golden tests
    needs: [changes, quality]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.engine != 'false') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 10
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run test:engine

  release-tooling:
    name: Release tooling tests
    needs: [changes, quality]
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && needs.quality.result == 'success' && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.release != 'false') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run test:release

  # Runs on every change (docs cross-reference rule ids and CLI flags), and is
  # the only build job a docs-only change triggers. Deliberately not behind
  # `quality`, or `changes`: nothing in docs:check depends on the code lint
  # passing, and a dead classifier must not take the docs check with it.
  docs:
    name: Docs check and build
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run docs:check
      # The code tests that read docs/ pages. CLI tests runs them too, but a
      # docs-only change skips CLI tests, and these are the ones it can break.
      # A new test that reads docs/ belongs in this list.
      - name: Code tests that read docs pages
        run: >-
          bun test
          ./packages/rules/tests/docs-rule-pages.test.ts
          ./packages/rules/tests/docs-category-table.test.ts
          ./apps/cli/tests/mcp/docs-sync.test.ts
      - run: bun run docs:build

  build:
    name: Compile CLI
    needs: [changes, cli-tests, engine-tests, release-tooling]
    # engine-tests and release-tooling may be skipped by their own gates; a
    # failure in any of the three still stops the build.
    if: >-
      ${{ !cancelled()
      && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.build != 'false')
      && needs.cli-tests.result == 'success'
      && contains(fromJSON('["success", "skipped"]'), needs.engine-tests.result)
      && contains(fromJSON('["success", "skipped"]'), needs.release-tooling.result) }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 15
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run build
      - name: Verify compiled rules version
        run: |
          expected=$(bun -e 'import { fingerprintRuleSources } from "./apps/cli/src/audit/rules-fingerprint"; console.log(fingerprintRuleSources(process.cwd(), undefined, { strict: true }))')
          # An empty value would make `grep -F ""` match any file.
          if ! [[ "$expected" =~ ^[0-9a-f]{64}$ ]]; then
            echo "Could not compute the rules fingerprint for this checkout: '$expected'" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          if ! grep -aFq "$expected" apps/cli/build/squirrelscan; then
            echo "Compiled CLI does not embed the rules version for this checkout: $expected" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          echo "Compiled CLI embeds rules version $expected"
      - name: Verify the compiled binary ignores a working-directory bunfig.toml and .env
        run: bun run apps/cli/scripts/check-compiled-autoload.ts apps/cli/build/squirrelscan

  psl-freshness:
    name: Public suffix data freshness
    needs: changes
    if: ${{ !cancelled() && (needs.changes.result != 'success' || needs.changes.outputs.code != 'false') }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    continue-on-error: true
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
      - uses: ./.github/actions/setup-bun
      - run: bun run check:psl-freshness
